dishes.title: Lecsó
dishes.summary: Hungary's summer stew of pale wax peppers and onion softened in fat, coloured with sweet paprika and cooked down with peeled tomatoes until syrupy, finished by stirring in beaten eggs. It shows paprika's character in fat, how long cooking sweetens peppers, and when to salt a watery vegetable.
skills: cooking down with tomato and paprika
equipment: wide 12 inch (30 cm) heavy sauté pan or casserole with a lid
saucepan of boiling water and a bowl of iced water for peeling tomatoes
small bowl and fork for the eggs

ingredients.item: Hungarian wax peppers, banana peppers or pale green Cubanelle peppers
ingredients.note: Thin walled pale peppers collapse beautifully; bell peppers are a poor substitute.

mise: Bring a saucepan of water to the boil and set a bowl of iced water beside it.
Score a small cross in the base of each tomato.
Halve, seed and cut the peppers lengthways into strips about 3/4 inch (2 cm) wide.
Slice the onions.
Beat the eggs lightly with a pinch of salt.

timeline.do: Blanch and peel the tomatoes; slice peppers and onions.
Soften the onion in fat 8 to 10 minutes.
Paprika off the heat; peppers in, covered, 10 to 15 minutes.
Tomatoes and salt; cook uncovered until syrupy.
Stir in the eggs until just set.
Serve with bread.

steps.do: Drop the scored tomatoes into the boiling water for 20 to 30 seconds, until the skin at the cross starts to curl back. Lift them into the iced water for 1 minute, then slip off the skins, core and chop the flesh roughly.
steps.look: Skins peeling away easily from firm, uncooked flesh.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in the boiling water too long, so the flesh cooks and turns mushy.
steps.fix: Thirty seconds at most; it is the skin you are loosening, not the tomato you are cooking.

steps.do: Heat the oil or lard in the sauté pan over low heat. Add the onions and cook gently, stirring, for 8 to 10 minutes until glassy and soft but not coloured.
steps.look: Translucent, soft onions, glossy with fat.
steps.mistake: Browning the onions, which changes the clean, sweet character of the dish.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low; add a spoonful of water if they begin to colour.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the paprika until the fat turns red. Then return it to low heat and add the pepper strips and hot pepper.
steps.look: Brick red fat coating the onions, smelling sweet and warm.
steps.mistake: Adding paprika over the flame, where it burns in seconds and turns bitter and brown.
steps.fix: Always off the heat; the hot fat blooms it on its own.

steps.do: Cover the pan and let the peppers sweat in their own moisture over low to medium low heat for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then.
steps.look: Peppers limp and softened, their skins slack, a little liquid in the pan.
steps.mistake: Salting the peppers now, which draws their water out early so they boil to mush before the tomato reduces.
steps.fix: Hold the salt until the tomatoes go in.

steps.do: Add the chopped tomatoes and the salt. Cook uncovered over medium heat, stirring occasionally, for 10 to 15 minutes, until the liquid has reduced to a thick red sauce that clings to the strips.
steps.look: No pooling liquid; a thick, glossy red sauce coating soft pepper strips.
steps.mistake: Stopping while it is watery, which makes a thin soup when the eggs go in.
steps.fix: Keep reducing until a spoon dragged across the pan leaves a clear trail.

steps.do: Taste and adjust the salt. Lower the heat, pour in the beaten eggs and stir gently but constantly for 1 to 2 minutes, until the eggs are just set in soft curds through the peppers.
steps.look: Soft yellow curds of egg threaded through the red peppers, moist and glossy.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the eggs into dry, rubbery pieces.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat while the eggs still look slightly wet; they finish in the pan's heat.

steps.do: Serve hot in warm bowls with crusty bread.
steps.look: A glossy red and yellow stew of soft peppers and egg.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit on the heat, which toughens the eggs.
steps.fix: Serve straight away.

dishes.science: Pale wax peppers are thin walled and full of water, so they collapse into silky strips rather than roasting. Salt draws water from vegetable cells by osmosis; added to the peppers alone, it pulls their juices out early so they stew and fall apart before the tomatoes have reduced, which is why it goes in with the tomatoes. Paprika is ground dried pepper whose red carotenoid pigments and flavour compounds dissolve in fat; heating it in the fat blooms that colour and aroma, but paprika's sugars burn quickly, so it goes in off the heat. Blanching tomatoes for seconds heats the layer just beneath the skin, loosening it so it slips off. Long, gentle cooking breaks down the peppers' cell walls and concentrates their sugars.
dishes.plating: Spoon the lecsó into warm, shallow bowls, mounding it so the egg curds show among the peppers. Finish with a light dusting of paprika and a few thin rings of fresh hot pepper, and serve thick slices of bread alongside.

pairing.drink: A peppery Austrian Grüner Veltliner or a dry Hungarian Furmint: bright acidity and a white pepper note that match the peppers.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Alte Reben’ Grüner Veltliner 2023: an Austrian Grüner on the Brennan's list with the peppery freshness this dish wants.

variations: Add sliced Hungarian smoked sausage (kolbász), browned first, instead of or as well as the eggs.
Serve without eggs as a side dish for grilled meats.
Stir in a little cooked rice at the end for a heartier version.
safety: Lift tomatoes from boiling water with a slotted spoon, never your fingers.
Eggs stirred until just set are fully cooked through; for vulnerable guests, cook until no wet egg remains.
Wash hands after handling hot peppers.

dishes.title: Tomato and Egg Stir-Fry with Rice
dishes.summary: The everyday home cooking of China: eggs set in seconds in a smoking wok until puffed and soft, lifted out, then folded back into a quick, sweet and savoury sauce of tomatoes, served over steamed rice. The first wok dish in the course teaches high heat, speed and doing every bit of preparation before the flame goes on.
skills: soft eggs cooked fast in hot oil
equipment: carbon steel wok or a 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan
wok spatula or wide metal spatula
medium saucepan with a tight lid for rice

ingredients.item: neutral oil with a high smoke point
spring onions, white and green parts separated, sliced

ingredients.note: Optional, common in Chinese homes for colour and depth.

ingredients.item: cornflour mixed with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water

mise: Rinse the rice until the water runs clear and soak it 15 minutes.
Beat the eggs with 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) salt and the Shaoxing wine until smooth.
Cut the tomatoes into wedges about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick.
Mince the garlic; slice the spring onions.
Mix the cornflour slurry; measure sugar, salt and ketchup into a small bowl.
Line everything up beside the wok in the order it goes in.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice.
Cook the rice: boil, cover, lowest heat 12 minutes, rest 10.
Prepare every ingredient; line them up.
Cook the eggs in a smoking wok; lift them out.
Cook the tomatoes; return the eggs; fold together.
Serve over rice.

steps.do: Drain the soaked rice, put it in the saucepan with 1 1/4 cups (300 ml) water, bring to the boil, cover tightly and cook on the lowest heat for 12 minutes. Turn off the heat and rest, covered, for 10 minutes.
steps.look: Fluffy, separate grains with steam holes on the surface.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid during cooking.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; the steam is doing the cooking.

steps.do: Put every prepared ingredient within reach of the stove. A stir-fry happens in under five minutes and there is no time to chop once the wok is hot.
steps.look: Bowls of beaten egg, tomato wedges, garlic, spring onion and the seasoning lined up in order.
steps.mistake: Starting to cook before everything is ready.
steps.fix: In Chinese kitchens, preparation is the cooking; the wok is the last few minutes.

steps.do: Heat the wok over the highest heat until it just starts to smoke, about 1 to 2 minutes. Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and swirl it round the sides.
steps.look: A wisp of smoke from the wok; the oil shimmering and flowing like water.
steps.mistake: A wok that is not hot enough, so the eggs soak up oil and turn flat and greasy.
steps.fix: Wait for the first smoke before adding oil.

steps.do: Pour in the beaten eggs. They will puff up immediately. Let them set for 5 seconds, then push and fold them gently from the edges into the centre with the spatula for 15 to 20 seconds, until they form large, soft curds that are still wet in places. Tip them onto a plate.
steps.look: Puffy, golden-edged curds, soft and glossy, about two thirds set.
steps.mistake: Cooking the eggs until fully set, so they turn rubbery when returned to the sauce.
steps.fix: Lift them out while they look underdone; they finish in the sauce.

steps.do: Add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil to the wok over high heat. Add the garlic and white spring onion and stir for 10 seconds, then add the tomato wedges and stir-fry for 1 to 2 minutes, pressing a few against the wok, until they soften and release their juices.
steps.look: Tomatoes collapsing at the edges, a red, juicy sauce forming in the wok.
steps.mistake: Cooking the tomatoes until they disappear into a paste.
steps.fix: Stop when some wedges still hold their shape.

steps.do: Add the sugar, the remaining 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt, the ketchup if using, and 2 tbsp (30 ml) water. Stir and let it bubble for 30 seconds. Stir the cornflour slurry and add it if you want a glossier, thicker sauce; it thickens in seconds.
steps.look: A glossy, bright red sauce that coats the spatula.
steps.mistake: Too sour a sauce.
steps.fix: Add sugar a little at a time; it should taste sweet, sour and savoury in balance.

steps.do: Return the eggs to the wok and fold gently a few times so they soak up the sauce without breaking into small bits. Turn off the heat, add the sesame oil and green spring onion.
steps.look: Large soft curds of egg coated in red sauce, flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which breaks the egg into crumbs.
steps.fix: Fold two or three times only.

steps.do: Fluff the rice and serve it in bowls with the tomato and egg spooned over the top.
steps.look: White rice under glossy red and yellow tomato and egg.
steps.mistake: Leaving the stir-fry in the hot wok while the rice is served.
steps.fix: Serve immediately from the wok.

dishes.science: In a smoking wok, eggs meet oil at around 400°F (205°C). Water in the egg flashes to steam, which puffs the curds while the proteins on the outside set almost instantly and brown slightly at the edges. Lifting them out while still partly liquid prevents the proteins from tightening and squeezing out water, so they stay tender when returned to the sauce. Tomatoes are acidic and contain plenty of glutamate; brief, hot cooking breaks their cells and releases juice, and sugar balances their acidity. A cornflour slurry thickens almost instantly when it reaches the boil, because the starch granules swell and bond with water, giving a glossy sauce that clings to the egg.
dishes.plating: Fill a bowl with rice, pressing it lightly into a dome, then spoon the tomato and egg over half the rice so both colours show, letting the sauce run down one side. Finish with the green spring onion and serve with chopsticks.

pairing.drink: A light, crisp Chinese lager or a dry Alsace Riesling: refreshing and bright against sweet and sour tomato.

variations: Add a few slices of fresh ginger with the garlic for warmth.
Stir-fried egg with prawns: cook peeled prawns quickly after the eggs and return them with the eggs.
Make it saucier with a little chicken stock to soak into the rice.
safety: Hot oil in a smoking wok can flare; keep the wok handle steady and add wet ingredients carefully.
Have a lid nearby; never put water on an oil fire.
Eggs cooked until set in the sauce are fully cooked.

dishes.title: Kimchi Fried Rice (Kimchi Bokkeumbap)
dishes.summary: Day-old rice fried hard with sour, well fermented kimchi and its juice, a little pork belly, gochujang and sesame oil, topped with a crisp-edged fried egg and strips of seaweed. Fried rice teaches why cold, dry rice separates and fresh rice clumps, and how frying a fermented ingredient deepens its flavour.
equipment: carbon steel wok or 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan
small nonstick pan for the eggs

ingredients.item: cooked short grain rice, cold from the fridge, at least a day old

ingredients.note: Older kimchi is better for cooking.

ingredients.item: pork belly, bacon or Spam, diced 1/2 inch (1.2 cm)
ingredients.note: Optional; use 1 tbsp (15 ml) more oil without it.
Optional, if the kimchi is very sour.

ingredients.item: roasted seaweed sheet (gim) and toasted sesame seeds

mise: Break up the cold rice so there are no clumps.
Chop the kimchi into 1/2 inch (1.2 cm) pieces and measure its juice.
Dice the pork.
Slice the spring onions.
Mix gochujang, soy and sugar in a small bowl.
Cut the seaweed into thin strips with scissors.

timeline.do: Prepare everything and line it up.
Render the pork; fry the kimchi until its edges catch.
Rice in; fry with kimchi juice and gochujang mix.
Fry the eggs with crisp edges.
Rice into bowls, egg on top, seaweed and sesame.

steps.do: Heat the wok over medium high heat with 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil. Add the pork and cook, stirring occasionally, for 3 to 4 minutes, until it has rendered its fat and is browned and crisp at the edges.
steps.look: Browned, crisp pork pieces sizzling in their own fat.
steps.mistake: A crowded or cool pan, so the pork steams pale.
steps.fix: Spread it in one layer and let it sit between stirs.

steps.do: Add the chopped kimchi to the pork and fat and fry for 3 to 4 minutes, stirring now and then, until the kimchi softens and its edges catch and caramelise.
steps.look: Kimchi turning darker red, glossy and slightly browned at the edges, smelling sweet and tangy rather than sharp.
steps.mistake: Rushing the kimchi, which leaves a raw, sharp sour taste.
steps.fix: Give it the time; this is where the flavour of the dish is built.

steps.do: Turn the heat to high. Add the rice and the kimchi juice. Press the rice against the wok with the back of the spatula to break up any clumps, then toss everything together.
steps.look: Rice turning evenly pink-red from the juice, grains separate.
steps.mistake: Using freshly cooked warm rice, which turns mushy and sticky.
steps.fix: Use day-old, cold rice; spread fresh rice on a tray and chill it uncovered for an hour if you must.

steps.do: Add the gochujang mixture and stir-fry for 3 to 4 minutes, pressing the rice against the hot wok and letting it sit for 20 to 30 seconds between tosses so some grains toast.
steps.look: Evenly coloured, glossy rice with a few toasted, slightly crisp grains; a smoky, savoury smell.
steps.mistake: Constant stirring, which never lets the rice toast.
steps.fix: Spread and press, wait, then toss.

steps.do: Taste and adjust with a little more soy or sugar. Turn off the heat, add the spring onions and sesame oil and toss to combine.
steps.look: Glossy, fragrant rice flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Adding sesame oil early, where its delicate aroma burns off.
steps.fix: Always finish with sesame oil off the heat.

steps.do: Heat the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil in the small pan over medium high heat until it shimmers. Fry the eggs for 2 minutes, spooning hot oil over the whites, until the edges are brown and crisp and the yolks still runny.
steps.look: Lacy, crisp, golden brown edges, set whites, glossy liquid yolks.
steps.mistake: Too low a heat, giving pale, soft edges.
steps.fix: Heat the oil until shimmering before the egg goes in.

steps.do: Press the rice into a bowl, turn it out onto a plate as a dome, slide an egg on top and finish with seaweed strips and sesame seeds.
steps.look: A red dome of rice with a fried egg crowning it and dark seaweed strips scattered over.
steps.mistake: Seaweed added long before eating, which goes limp.
steps.fix: Add at the very end.

dishes.science: Freshly cooked rice is soft and wet on its surface, so in a hot pan the grains stick together and steam. As cooked rice cools in the fridge, its starch retrogrades, the molecules realigning into a firmer structure, and its surface dries, so the grains stay separate and can fry and toast. Kimchi is fermented by lactic acid bacteria; older kimchi is more sour and more deeply flavoured. Frying it in fat drives off water and starts caramelisation and Maillard browning of its sugars and amino acids, softening the sourness into a rounder, savoury sweetness. Gochujang adds fermented chilli, sweetness and glutamates. A fried egg cooked in hot oil develops crisp, browned edges as the thin white dries and browns.
dishes.plating: Pack the rice into a bowl and turn it out onto a plate as a neat dome. Set the fried egg on top, yolk centred, and scatter seaweed strips and sesame seeds over and around it, with a few slices of spring onion for colour.

pairing.drink: A cold Korean lager or a soju highball with soda and lemon: clean and fizzy against chilli and fermentation.

variations: Add a handful of grated mozzarella over the top and cover until melted, a popular modern style.
Tuna kimchi fried rice: stir in canned tuna instead of pork.
Vegetarian: use diced firm tofu and mushrooms, and a little extra gochujang.
safety: Cooked rice must be cooled quickly and kept in the fridge; bacteria from spores that survive cooking can grow if it sits warm.
Pork belly should be cooked until browned and crisp throughout.
Runny yolks have not reached 160°F (71°C); use pasteurised eggs for vulnerable guests.

dishes.title: Pad Kra Pao Moo (Thai Holy Basil Stir-Fry)
dishes.summary: Thailand's favourite quick lunch: pork mince stir-fried hard with pounded garlic and bird's eye chilli, seasoned with oyster, soy and fish sauces, finished with holy basil and served over jasmine rice with a puffed, crisp-edged fried egg. It is fast, loud wok cooking where pounding, searing and seasoning happen in under five minutes.
equipment: carbon steel wok or 12 inch (30 cm) heavy frying pan
small bowls for the sauce and basil
saucepan with a tight lid for rice

ingredients.note: Cooked as in the tomato and egg stir-fry.
Two is warm, six is Thai street heat.
Thai basil works, with a sweeter, anise flavour.

ingredients.item: neutral oil, for frying the eggs

mise: Cook the rice and keep it covered.
Pound the garlic and chillies to a coarse paste.
Mix the oyster sauce, both soy sauces, fish sauce, sugar and water in a small bowl.
Pick the basil leaves; keep them dry.
Crack each egg into its own small bowl.
Line up everything beside the stove.

timeline.do: Rinse and cook the rice.
Pound garlic and chilli; mix sauce; pick basil.
Fry the eggs in hot oil; drain.
Stir-fry paste, pork and sauce; wilt the basil off the heat.
Rice, stir-fry and fried egg on each plate.

steps.do: Put the garlic and chillies in the mortar with a pinch of salt and pound for 30 to 60 seconds into a coarse paste, with some pieces still visible. Use short, firm strokes, with your other hand cupped over the mortar to stop splashes.
steps.look: A rough, juicy paste of garlic and red chilli flecks, smelling strongly.
steps.mistake: Pounding wildly, so chilli juice splashes into your eyes.
steps.fix: Cup your hand over the mortar, keep strokes short, and wash hands straight after.

steps.do: For the eggs, heat the 1/2 cup (120 ml) oil in the wok over high heat to about 375°F (190°C), when a drop of egg white puffs and sizzles instantly. Slide in one egg. It will bubble violently and puff. Spoon hot oil over the white for 1 to 2 minutes until the edges are brown and crisp and the white is set, with the yolk still runny. Lift out onto paper towel. Repeat.
steps.look: A puffed, blistered white with deep golden, crisp, lacy edges and a glossy yolk.
steps.mistake: Oil not hot enough, so the egg sits flat and greasy.
steps.fix: Heat the oil properly first, and stand back as the egg goes in: it spits.

steps.do: Carefully pour off all but 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil into a heatproof bowl. Return the wok to high heat. Add the garlic and chilli paste and stir for 10 to 15 seconds until fragrant.
steps.look: The paste sizzling and turning pale gold; a sharp, pungent smell that may make you cough.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic, which turns it bitter.
steps.fix: Move straight to the pork after 15 seconds.

steps.do: Add the pork, press it flat against the wok with the spatula and leave it for 30 to 45 seconds to sear before breaking it up. Keep stir-frying and pressing for 2 to 3 minutes until no pink remains and it is browned in places.
steps.look: Browned, crumbled pork with crisp edges, not grey and wet; cooked through to 160°F (71°C).
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly from the start, which stews the pork grey in its own liquid.
steps.fix: Press it into the hot wok and let it sit to sear.

steps.do: Pour the sauce mixture down the side of the hot wok so it sizzles, then toss the pork for 1 minute until the sauce reduces and coats the meat in a glossy glaze.
steps.look: Dark, glossy pork with almost no liquid in the wok.
steps.mistake: A pool of sauce left in the wok, which makes the rice soggy.
steps.fix: Toss over high heat until it reduces to a glaze.

steps.do: Turn off the heat. Add the holy basil and toss for 10 to 15 seconds until just wilted.
steps.look: Basil leaves just collapsed and glossy, smelling peppery and clove-like.
steps.mistake: Cooking the basil too long, so it turns black and loses its aroma.
steps.fix: Add it off the heat and toss briefly.

steps.do: Spoon rice onto each plate, add the pork alongside or on top and lay the fried egg on the rice. Serve at once, with fish sauce and sliced chillies on the side if you like.
steps.look: White rice, glossy dark pork and green basil, a puffed crisp egg on top.
steps.mistake: Frying the eggs after the stir-fry, so the pork sits and cools while they cook.
steps.fix: Fry the eggs first, as here; their crisp edges hold for the few minutes the stir-fry takes.

dishes.science: Pounding garlic and chilli in a mortar crushes their cells more completely than chopping, releasing more of their aromatic and pungent compounds, which then bloom in hot oil. A wok at full heat reaches far above the boiling point of water, so the surface of the pork browns through the Maillard reaction before its juices can pool; pressing the meat flat increases contact with the metal. Crowding or constant stirring lowers the temperature so the meat releases liquid and stews. Pouring the sauce down the hot side of the wok caramelises its sugars on contact. The fried egg puffs because water in the white turns to steam in oil at about 375°F (190°C), and the thin edges dry and brown into a crisp lace.
dishes.plating: Press the rice into a small bowl and turn it out to one side of a warm plate. Spoon the pork beside it, letting a little glaze touch the rice, and lay the fried egg on top of the rice dome. Add a small dish of fish sauce with sliced chillies (prik nam pla) at the side.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling or a cold Thai lager: a touch of sweetness and low alcohol to cool the chilli.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: a German Riesling on the Brennan's list whose fruit and acidity calm chilli heat.

variations: Pad kra pao gai: use chicken thigh mince or finely chopped chicken thigh.
Add sliced long beans or onion with the pork for extra vegetables.
Pad kra pao talay: use prawns and squid, cooked only until just opaque.
safety: Pork mince must reach 160°F (71°C), with no pink remaining.
Deep frying eggs in a wok: hot oil can spit and flare; keep a lid nearby, stand back and never leave it unattended.
Pour off the hot oil into a heatproof container, never plastic, and let it cool before discarding.
Wash hands after pounding chillies and avoid touching your eyes.

dishes.title: Oyakodon
dishes.summary: Chicken thigh and onion simmered in a seasoned dashi of soy, mirin and sake, with barely beaten eggs poured in two stages and set under a lid until just done, slid over a bowl of hot rice. Eggs set gently in a seasoned broth bring dashi and egg control together in one bowl, the course's closing lunch.
equipment: saucepan with a tight lid for rice
8 inch (20 cm) frying pan with a lid, or a small oyakodon pan
small bowl and chopsticks for the eggs

ingredients.item: boneless chicken thighs, skin on or off

ingredients.note: Homemade as in the miso soup lesson, or instant.

mise: Rinse the rice until the water is clear and soak it in the measured water for 20 minutes.
Cut the chicken into even 3/4 inch (2 cm) pieces.
Slice the onion.
Mix the dashi, soy, mirin, sake and sugar until the sugar dissolves.
Crack the eggs into a bowl and beat just 8 to 10 strokes with chopsticks, leaving streaks of white.
Chop the mitsuba or spring onion; warm the bowls.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice.
Cook the rice: boil, cover, lowest heat 12 minutes, rest 10 to 15.
Cut chicken and onion; mix the sauce; beat the eggs lightly.
Simmer onion, then chicken, in the sauce until cooked through.
Pour the eggs in two stages; cover; take off the heat while the top is still soft.
Slide onto hot rice, garnish and serve.

steps.do: Bring the soaked rice and its water to the boil in the covered saucepan over medium high heat, then turn to the lowest heat and cook for 12 minutes without lifting the lid. Turn off and rest, covered, for 10 to 15 minutes. Fluff gently with a damp spatula.
steps.look: Glossy, plump, slightly sticky grains that hold together lightly.
steps.mistake: Peeking during cooking, which lets out the steam.
steps.fix: Trust the timer; the rest finishes the cooking.

steps.do: Pour the sauce into the frying pan and add the onion. Bring to a simmer over medium heat and cook for 3 to 4 minutes until the onion softens and turns translucent.
steps.look: Soft, glossy onion slices in a bubbling, amber broth smelling sweet and savoury.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce hard, which reduces it too much before the chicken goes in.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer.

steps.do: Add the chicken pieces in a single layer. Simmer for 5 to 7 minutes, turning once, until cooked through: the thickest piece reads 165°F (74°C) and the inside is white with no pink.
steps.look: Opaque chicken, slightly firm, the broth bubbling gently around it.
steps.mistake: Adding the eggs before the chicken is cooked, since the eggs then overcook while the chicken catches up.
steps.fix: Check a piece with the thermometer before moving on.

steps.do: Make sure the broth is simmering. Pour about two thirds of the lightly beaten eggs over the chicken in a slow circle, starting from the centre and spiralling out. Do not stir. Cover with the lid and cook for 40 to 60 seconds.
steps.look: The egg setting around the edges and over the chicken, streaks of yellow and white, still soft and wet on top.
steps.mistake: Beating the eggs smooth and stirring them in the pan, which gives uniform scrambled egg instead of silky, marbled layers.
steps.fix: Barely beat the eggs and leave them alone once poured.

steps.do: Pour the remaining egg over the top, especially where it looks thin. Scatter the mitsuba or spring onion, cover again and cook for 15 to 30 seconds, then turn off the heat.
steps.look: Three textures at once: set at the edges, soft in the middle, glossy and barely set on top.
steps.mistake: Cooking until all the egg is firm and dry.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat while the top still trembles; it keeps cooking on the way to the bowl.

steps.do: Fill the warm bowls with hot rice. Tilt the pan and slide half the chicken and egg onto each bowl of rice with the help of the spatula, spooning over some of the broth.
steps.look: A soft, glossy blanket of egg and chicken sliding onto white rice, broth soaking into the rice beneath.
steps.mistake: Breaking up the egg while transferring.
steps.fix: Cut the omelette in half in the pan with the spatula, then slide each half off in one movement.

steps.do: Serve immediately with shichimi togarashi at the table, and a bowl of miso soup if you like.
steps.look: A steaming bowl, glossy egg and tender chicken over rice, flecked with green.
steps.mistake: Letting the bowls stand so the egg sets hard.
steps.fix: Eat at once; this is a dish for the moment.

dishes.science: Seasoned dashi carries umami from kombu and bonito, salt from soy and sweetness from mirin and sugar; simmering chicken in it seasons the meat while the chicken adds its own savoury juices. Chicken thigh stays moist because its fat and connective tissue protect it from drying as it reaches 165°F (74°C). Egg proteins set between about 145°F and 160°F (63°C and 71°C), and in a simmering broth they set from the bottom up. Pouring in two stages and stopping while the top is still glossy gives the layered textures the dish is known for. The lid traps steam, which sets the surface gently. Barely beaten eggs keep white and yolk partly separate, so they set at slightly different rates, creating marbled streaks.
dishes.plating: Use deep, warm donburi bowls. Mound the rice, slide the chicken and egg over it in one piece so the glossy surface is unbroken, spoon a little broth around the edge to soak in, and scatter the mitsuba or spring onion over the top. Serve with chopsticks and a spoon.

pairing.drink: A chilled junmai sake or a cup of roasted green tea: soft, savoury and clean beside sweet soy and egg.

variations: Katsudon: use sliced fried pork cutlet in place of the chicken, set in egg the same way.
Tanindon: use thinly sliced beef instead of chicken.
Add sliced shiitake mushrooms with the onion for extra depth.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) before the eggs go in; check the thickest piece.
Soft-set eggs may not reach 160°F (71°C); for vulnerable guests, use pasteurised eggs or cook until set.
Wash hands, board and knife after cutting raw chicken.
Cool leftover rice quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.

dishes.title: Spaghetti al Pomodoro
dishes.summary: Spaghetti in a quick sauce of tomatoes, olive oil, garlic and basil, finished in the pan with its own cooking water. It opens the dinner course because it teaches two habits every later dish leans on: reducing a sauce to the right body, and marrying pasta to sauce rather than spooning one over the other.
equipment: Large pot, at least 6 quarts (6 litres)
12 inch (30 cm) skillet or sauté pan, wide enough to toss the pasta
Heatproof measuring jug for pasta water

ingredients.note: San Marzano style if you can; whole tomatoes are better quality than crushed
1/4 cup (60 ml) for the sauce, the rest to finish
peeled and sliced thin, about 1/16 inch (2 mm)
half for the sauce, half torn to finish
bronze cut dried pasta holds sauce best

ingredients.item: Kosher salt for the pasta water

mise: Fill the large pot with 4 quarts (4 litres) of water, cover and set it over high heat.
Tip the tomatoes and their juice into a bowl and crush them by hand to rough 1/2 inch (1 cm) pieces, pulling out any hard stem cores.
Peel and slice the garlic thin and even so every slice cooks at the same speed.
Pick the basil leaves; keep them dry and whole until the last minute so they do not blacken.
Grate the cheese and set a heatproof jug beside the stove for the pasta water.
Weigh the pasta and the salt for the water.

timeline.do: Water on to boil. Crush the tomatoes, slice the garlic.
Garlic into the cold oil, then the tomatoes; start the simmer.
Salt the boiling water and drop the spaghetti.
Scoop out a cup of pasta water. Move the pasta into the sauce two minutes short of done.
Toss over high heat until the sauce clings. Finish off the heat with basil, oil and butter.
Plate in twisted nests and serve at once.

steps.do: Put 1/4 cup (60 ml) of the olive oil and the sliced garlic into the cold skillet, then set it over medium-low heat. Starting cold lets the garlic warm with the oil so it cooks evenly instead of scorching at the edges.
steps.look: After 2 to 3 minutes the garlic sizzles gently with small, steady bubbles, turns soft and pale gold at the edges and smells sweet, not sharp.
steps.mistake: Starting the garlic in hot oil, or walking away, so it turns brown and bitter in seconds.
steps.fix: If any slice goes darker than light gold, tip the oil out, wipe the pan and start again: burnt garlic flavours the whole sauce and cannot be covered.

steps.do: Add the chilli flakes for 10 seconds, then pour in the crushed tomatoes and their juice all at once. They will spit, so stand back. Add 1/2 tsp (3 g) fine salt and 6 whole basil leaves, and raise the heat to bring it to a lively simmer.
steps.look: A loud hiss as the tomatoes land, then steady bubbling across the whole surface within a minute or two.
steps.mistake: Adding the tomatoes slowly, which lets the garlic keep frying and browning while you pour.
steps.fix: Pour in one go; if the garlic darkened while you hesitated, taste and judge whether to start over.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium and simmer uncovered for 15 to 20 minutes, stirring and scraping the base every few minutes. Crush any large pieces against the side with the spoon.
steps.look: The sauce reduces by about a third, darkens from bright red to a deeper brick red, and small beads of orange oil gather on the surface. A spoon dragged across the pan leaves a track that slowly closes.
steps.mistake: Boiling it hard so it catches on the base, or pulling it while it is still thin and watery.
steps.fix: If it catches, move it to a clean pan without scraping up the burnt layer. If it is thin, give it 5 more minutes; it should coat a spoon, not run off it.

steps.do: When the sauce has about 12 minutes left, salt the boiling water with the 2 tbsp (24 g) of kosher salt. It should taste pleasantly salty, like a well seasoned soup. Drop in the spaghetti and stir for the first full minute so the strands do not glue together.
steps.look: The water returns to a rolling boil within a minute. The strands soften and sink within 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Adding oil to the water, or not stirring, so the pasta clumps in a mat.
steps.fix: Separate any clump with tongs immediately; oil in the water only makes the sauce slide off later.

steps.do: Cook the pasta 2 minutes less than the packet says. Bite a strand to check: it should bend but still have a thin, firm, slightly white core. Just before it is ready, scoop 1 cup (240 ml) of the cloudy water into the jug.
steps.look: The cut strand shows a pinpoint of pale core in the centre. The water is milky with starch.
steps.mistake: Cooking the pasta fully in the water, so it goes soft and swollen once it meets the sauce.
steps.fix: If it is already fully cooked, toss it in the sauce for only 30 seconds and use less water.

steps.do: Remove the basil leaves from the sauce. With tongs, lift the spaghetti straight from the pot into the skillet, letting some water cling. Add 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the reserved water and turn the heat to high.
steps.look: The pasta lands with a hiss and the sauce loosens into a glossy, bubbling liquid.
steps.mistake: Draining the pasta in a colander and letting it sit until it sticks and dries.
steps.fix: If it has stuck, loosen it with a splash of hot pasta water before it meets the sauce.

steps.do: Toss and stir constantly for 1 to 2 minutes, lifting the pasta with tongs and shaking the pan, until the sauce thickens and clings to every strand. Add more pasta water a splash at a time if it tightens.
steps.look: The sauce turns from loose and watery to creamy and glossy, coating each strand with nothing pooling in the pan. You hear a soft sputter, not a dry sizzle.
steps.mistake: Leaving the pasta still, or letting the pan dry out so the sauce becomes sticky and dull.
steps.fix: Loosen with 2 tbsp (30 ml) pasta water and keep tossing; starch plus movement is what binds it.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Add the butter if using, the remaining 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil and half the torn basil, and toss for 20 seconds more. Taste a strand and adjust the salt.
steps.look: The sauce gains a high shine and the basil smells bright and peppery.
steps.mistake: Adding the finishing oil over high heat, which drives off its fresh flavour.
steps.fix: Always finish off the heat. If it tastes flat, add salt a pinch at a time; if sharp, a little more butter softens it.

steps.do: Plate immediately: lift a portion with tongs, hold it over the plate and twist it into a tall nest. Spoon any sauce left in the pan over the top, add the remaining basil and a little cheese.
steps.look: A neat, high nest with sauce on every strand and a little gloss on the plate around it, not a puddle.
steps.mistake: Letting the pasta sit in the pan while you set the table; it keeps absorbing sauce and goes stodgy.
steps.fix: Have warm plates ready before the pasta goes in the sauce. If it has tightened, a splash of pasta water and a quick toss revives it.

dishes.science: Tomatoes are mostly water, so a quick sauce depends on evaporation: simmering uncovered drives off water and concentrates sugars, acids and the savoury glutamates tomatoes are rich in. Frying the garlic in oil first matters because many of its flavour compounds dissolve in fat, not water, so the oil carries garlic through the sauce. The magic at the end is starch. Pasta sheds starch into its cooking water, and when that cloudy water meets the oil and tomato over high heat, the starch acts as a binder, holding fat and water together in a light emulsion that clings to the pasta. Finishing the pasta in the sauce also lets each strand absorb flavoured liquid in its final two minutes instead of plain water.
dishes.plating: Use a warm, wide, shallow bowl. Twist the pasta into a tall nest in the centre with a carving fork or tongs inside a ladle, spoon the remaining sauce over the top so it slides down the sides, then finish with torn basil, a thread of raw olive oil and a fine snow of Parmigiano. Wipe the rim with a clean cloth before it goes out.

pairing.drink: A young Chianti Classico. Sangiovese has bright acidity that matches tomato rather than fighting it, and light tannin that will not clash with the olive oil.
pairing.brennans: Fattoria di Fèlsina Chianti Classico 2022: the Sangiovese on the list, bright enough for tomato

variations: Pomodoro with fresh tomatoes in high summer: score, blanch 30 seconds, peel and chop 2 lb (900 g) ripe plum tomatoes, and simmer 10 minutes only.
Arrabbiata: double the chilli flakes and leave out the butter and cheese.
Pomodoro e ricotta: dot each plate with a spoon of fresh ricotta at the table.
safety: Carry a full pot of boiling water with both hands and a clear path, or lift the pasta out with tongs instead of draining it.
Tomato sauce spits when it boils; keep your face back and stir with a long spoon.

dishes.title: Ratatouille
dishes.summary: The Provençal summer stew of aubergine, courgettes, peppers, onion and tomato, with each vegetable browned on its own before they meet. It is in the course because it trains an even 3/4 inch (2 cm) dice and teaches the most useful lesson in vegetable cookery: different vegetables cook at different speeds, so they get separate turns in the pan.
equipment: Heavy pot or Dutch oven, about 4 quarts (4 litres)
Chef’s knife and a large board
Two sheet pans or large plates to hold the browned vegetables

ingredients.note: or one 14 oz (400 g) can whole tomatoes, crushed
used in rounds, a few tablespoons per vegetable

ingredients.item: Herbes de Provence or dried thyme

mise: Wash and dry all the vegetables; wet vegetables spit and steam.
Cut the aubergine into 3/4 inch (2 cm) cubes. Do this first, toss with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt in a colander and leave 20 minutes to draw out water.
Halve the courgettes lengthways, cut into 3/4 inch (2 cm) strips, then into cubes the same size as the aubergine.
Core and seed the peppers, remove the white ribs, and cut into 3/4 inch (2 cm) squares.
Cut the onion into 3/4 inch (2 cm) pieces. Slice the garlic.
Score the tomatoes with a shallow X, blanch in boiling water 20 seconds, cool in iced water, peel, seed and chop into 1/2 inch (1 cm) pieces, keeping the juice.
Set out two sheet pans to hold each vegetable after browning.

timeline.do: Cut the aubergine and salt it. Cut everything else.
Brown the aubergine, then the courgettes, then the peppers, each on its own.
Soften the onion and garlic in the pot, add the tomatoes and herbs.
Return all the vegetables and stew gently, partly covered.
Taste, adjust salt, tear in the basil and rest.
Serve warm, or chill overnight and serve the next day at room temperature.

steps.do: Pat the salted aubergine dry with a towel, pressing gently. Heat 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers and a cube dropped in sizzles at once.
steps.look: The oil ripples like a heat haze and moves freely when you tilt the pan. The test cube sizzles loudly.
steps.mistake: Adding the aubergine to oil that is not hot enough, so it soaks up oil like a sponge and turns greasy.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer. If the aubergine drinks all the oil immediately, do not add more straight away: keep cooking, and it releases the oil as it browns.

steps.do: Add the aubergine in a single layer with space between pieces, cooking in two batches if needed. Leave it untouched for 2 minutes, then turn and cook 6 to 8 minutes in total until browned on several sides and creamy inside. Lift onto a sheet pan.
steps.look: Deep golden brown faces, a sweet roasted smell, and a cube pressed with a spoon yields completely with no squeak.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan so the aubergine steams grey and stays spongy.
steps.fix: Cook in batches. Grey, steamed pieces can go back in a hot pan alone to take colour.

steps.do: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and the courgettes in one layer. Cook over medium-high heat 4 to 5 minutes, turning once or twice, until browned on two faces but still holding their shape. Season with a pinch of salt and lift onto the sheet pan.
steps.look: Golden patches on the cut faces, edges just softening, the centre still slightly firm when pressed.
steps.mistake: Cooking courgettes until soft in the skillet; they finish in the stew and will turn to mush.
steps.fix: Pull it earlier than you think. If it has gone soft, add it only in the last 5 minutes of the stew.

steps.do: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and the peppers. Cook 6 to 7 minutes over medium heat, turning occasionally, until the skins blister and the pieces bend. Season lightly and add to the tray.
steps.look: Blistered, slightly charred spots on the skin and a sweet smell. The pieces flop when lifted.
steps.mistake: Undercooking peppers, which then taste raw and green in the finished dish.
steps.fix: Give them the full time; peppers need longer than courgettes.

steps.do: In the pot, heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil over medium heat and cook the onion with a pinch of salt for 8 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent. Add the garlic for 1 minute more.
steps.look: The onion is glassy and slumped with only faint gold at the edges; the garlic smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Browning the onion hard; it should be soft and sweet here, a background flavour.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water if the onion is colouring too fast.

steps.do: Add the chopped tomatoes and their juice, the herbes de Provence and the bay leaf. Simmer 5 minutes, stirring, until the tomatoes collapse into a loose sauce.
steps.look: The tomatoes break down and the liquid turns glossy and orange red.
steps.mistake: Adding the browned vegetables before the tomatoes have cooked down, so the stew is watery.
steps.fix: Let the sauce thicken for a few more minutes first.

steps.do: Return the aubergine, peppers and courgettes to the pot and fold together gently with a wide spoon. Partly cover and simmer on low heat 20 to 25 minutes, folding once or twice.
steps.look: Small lazy bubbles at the edge only. The vegetables keep their shape and the liquid thickens to a glossy, oil-slicked juice.
steps.mistake: Stirring hard, which breaks the vegetables into a common pulp.
steps.fix: Fold from the bottom with a wide spoon and stir as little as possible.

steps.do: Taste a piece of aubergine and a piece of tomato. Adjust the salt and add black pepper. Remove the bay leaf, tear in the basil and drizzle with a little raw olive oil. Rest 10 minutes off the heat.
steps.look: Every vegetable is still recognisable, each seasoned, the herbs tasting cooked and perfumed rather than grassy.
steps.mistake: Serving it piping hot straight from the stove, when the flavours are at their least settled.
steps.fix: Let it rest, or better still, cool and refrigerate overnight and serve it the next day at room temperature.

dishes.science: Each vegetable holds a different amount of water and a different cell structure. Aubergine is a sponge of air pockets that soaks up oil until its cells collapse, then releases it again; salting it first draws out water so it browns rather than steams. Courgette is very wet and goes soft quickly, while peppers have tougher skins that need longer heat to soften and sweeten. Browning needs a surface hotter than boiling water, which only happens when moisture can escape: a crowded pan traps steam and holds the vegetables near 212°F (100°C), too cool for the browning reactions that build roasted flavour. Cooking each in its own batch keeps the pan hot and gives every vegetable its own colour and texture before the gentle stew lets their juices mingle.
dishes.plating: Serve in a warm shallow bowl or on a plate as a ring with a hollow in the centre. Spoon it rather than pour it so each vegetable stays distinct, finish with whole small basil leaves, a thread of olive oil and a twist of pepper. As a main course, set it beside a soft pile of polenta or a slice of grilled bread rubbed with garlic.

pairing.drink: A dry Provence rosé. Its red fruit and fresh acidity match the sweet peppers and tomato without overwhelming the herbs, and it is the wine of the same hills.
pairing.brennans: Minuty ‘Prestige’ Côtes de Provence Rosé 2024: a Provence rosé on the list, from the same hills as the dish

variations: Baked tian: slice the same vegetables into 1/8 inch (3 mm) rounds, layer them in overlapping rows over the tomato sauce and bake at 375°F (190°C) for 45 minutes.
With eggs: make four hollows in the finished ratatouille, crack in eggs and cover until the whites set, about 6 minutes.
Cold, as the next day’s lunch: on toast with soft goat’s cheese.
safety: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and refrigerate; they keep 4 days.
Hot oil spits when wet vegetables go in: pat everything dry and lay pieces away from you.

dishes.title: Pollo al Ajillo
dishes.summary: Spanish garlic chicken: small bone-in pieces browned hard in olive oil with whole garlic cloves, then glazed with dry sherry. It is the course’s first real browning and deglazing lesson, and it shows how to cook garlic slowly so it turns sweet instead of burnt.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet, stainless or cast iron, with a lid
Wooden spoon or flat spatula for scraping
Cleaver or heavy knife if cutting thighs in half

ingredients.note: ask the butcher to cut each in half across the bone, or use thighs whole
about 12 cloves, lightly smashed with the skin left on

mise: Pat the chicken completely dry with paper towels and season both sides with the salt and pepper. Leave it at room temperature for 20 minutes while you prepare everything else.
Smash each garlic clove once with the flat of a knife so it splits but stays in its skin.
Measure the sherry and stock into one jug.
Chop the parsley. Set a plate lined with paper towels by the stove.

timeline.do: Season the chicken, smash the garlic.
Brown the chicken skin side down with the garlic.
Turn the chicken, then deglaze with sherry.
Simmer uncovered, turning, until glazed and cooked through.
Check the temperature, scatter parsley, rest briefly.
Serve from the pan with bread.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Lay in the chicken skin side down, spacing the pieces so they do not touch. Work in two batches if they will not fit.
steps.look: An immediate, loud, even sizzle the moment each piece touches the pan.
steps.mistake: Putting the chicken into oil that is not hot, so it sticks and stews without browning.
steps.fix: If the sizzle is weak, lift the pieces out, let the oil heat for another minute and start again.

steps.do: Leave the chicken alone for 6 to 8 minutes, adjusting the heat to keep a steady sizzle, until the skin is deep golden and releases from the pan on its own. Do not tug it free.
steps.look: The skin is evenly deep golden brown and comes away cleanly when nudged with tongs. Rendered fat pools around the pieces.
steps.mistake: Moving or turning the chicken too early, tearing the skin and leaving it stuck to the pan.
steps.fix: If a piece resists, give it another minute; skin that is properly browned lets go by itself.

steps.do: Scatter the smashed garlic cloves into the gaps between the chicken pieces after the first 3 minutes, along with the bay leaves. Turn the garlic now and then so it colours evenly.
steps.look: The cloves sizzle gently, their skins bronze and the kitchen fills with a sweet, nutty garlic smell.
steps.mistake: Using peeled or minced garlic, which burns black in the time the chicken takes to brown.
steps.fix: Keep the skins on. If any clove blackens, pick it out so it does not turn the sauce bitter.

steps.do: Turn the chicken skin side up and cook 3 minutes on the second side. If more than 3 tbsp (45 ml) fat has collected, spoon off the excess, keeping the garlic in the pan.
steps.look: Golden flesh side, clear fat bubbling around the pieces, browned bits stuck to the pan floor.
steps.mistake: Leaving a pool of fat, which turns the sherry glaze greasy.
steps.fix: Tilt the pan and spoon fat into a heatproof bowl, leaving the browned bits behind.

steps.do: Stand back and pour in the sherry and stock. Scrape the pan floor hard with the wooden spoon to lift the browned bits (the fond) into the liquid. Add the herb sprigs.
steps.look: A burst of steam and sizzle, then the liquid turns from pale to amber brown as the fond dissolves. The sharp alcohol smell fades within a minute.
steps.mistake: Pouring the sherry over the skin, which softens the crust you worked to build.
steps.fix: Pour into the gaps between pieces, keeping the skin above the liquid.

steps.do: Simmer uncovered over medium heat 15 to 20 minutes, turning the pieces in the sauce every 5 minutes and finishing skin side up, until the liquid has reduced to a few spoonfuls of glossy glaze.
steps.look: Bubbles turn from thin and fast to slow and syrupy, and the sauce coats the chicken in a shine.
steps.mistake: Reducing until the pan is dry, so the glaze burns and the garlic catches.
steps.fix: Add 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) water and scrape; the glaze should be loose enough to spoon.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece with an instant-read thermometer near, but not touching, the bone. It must read at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are at their best at 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C), when the connective tissue has softened.
steps.look: Juices run clear when pierced and the meat pulls cleanly from the bone.
steps.mistake: Judging doneness by colour alone, which is unreliable near the bone.
steps.fix: If short of temperature, cover with the lid and cook on low 4 to 5 minutes, then check again.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat, remove the herb stalks, scatter the parsley and rest 3 minutes. Serve from the pan with bread, and show your guests how to squeeze the soft garlic out of its skin onto the bread.
steps.look: The garlic cloves are soft enough to squeeze like paste; the glaze clings to the chicken.
steps.mistake: Leaving the garlic underdone and firm.
steps.fix: If cloves are still firm, simmer them a few minutes more in the glaze with a splash of water while the chicken rests.

dishes.science: Browning is the Maillard reaction, in which proteins and sugars react above about 285°F (140°C) to form hundreds of new flavour compounds and a deep brown colour. Skin browns well only when it is dry, because surface water must boil off before the temperature can climb; that is why you pat it dry and leave it untouched. The browned residue on the pan floor, the fond, is concentrated flavour, and liquid dissolves it in seconds: that is deglazing. Garlic left in its skin is insulated, so its sugars caramelise slowly while the inside steams to a soft, sweet paste. Peeled garlic has no such protection and its natural sugars burn quickly, turning acrid.
dishes.plating: Bring it to the table in the skillet on a board, the pieces skin side up and glistening, the garlic cloves scattered among them and parsley over the top. For individual plates, set two pieces slightly overlapping, spoon the glaze over, add three garlic cloves and a wedge of bread to the side.

pairing.drink: A chilled glass of fino or manzanilla sherry. The same dry, nutty, saline wine that is in the sauce matches the garlic and cuts the richness of the skin.
pairing.brennans: La Cigarrera Manzanilla Sanlúcar de Barrameda NV (375 ml): the dry manzanilla on the list, the same style as the sherry in the pan

variations: With potatoes: add 1 lb (450 g) small waxy potatoes, halved and browned, with the sherry, and simmer until tender.
Pollo al ajillo with chilli: add one dried guindilla or a pinch of chilli flakes with the garlic.
Shrimp al ajillo: the same garlic oil with peeled shrimp cooked 2 minutes, a direct preview of the scampi to come.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point. Use a thermometer.
Wash hands, board and knife with hot soapy water after handling raw chicken, and never put cooked chicken back on the plate that held it raw.
Pour the sherry away from the flame on a gas stove; alcohol vapour can catch.

dishes.title: Chicken Piccata
dishes.summary: Thin, flour-dredged chicken cutlets sautéed golden, then served in a sharp pan sauce of white wine, lemon and capers mounted with butter. It is here because the pattern of cutlet, fond, deglaze and butter finish is the backbone of brigade cooking, and because a butter sauce teaches the one moment you must take the pan off the heat.
skills: a lemon and caper pan sauce mounted with butter
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) stainless steel skillet (not non-stick, so a fond forms)
Meat mallet or a small heavy pan for pounding
Plastic wrap or a zip-top bag
Tongs and a fish slice or thin spatula
Wire rack set over a sheet pan, in a 200°F (95°C) oven to hold the cutlets

ingredients.note: 1 tbsp (14 g) for cooking, 3 tbsp (42 g) cold and cubed for the sauce

mise: Lay each breast flat and slice it in half horizontally into two thinner fillets, keeping your flat hand on top and the knife parallel to the board.
Put each piece in the bag or between sheets of plastic wrap and pound from the centre outward to an even 1/4 inch (6 mm). Aim for even thickness, not a large shape.
Season both sides with salt and pepper just before dredging.
Put the flour in the shallow dish. Turn the oven on to 200°F (95°C) with the rack and sheet pan inside.
Mince the shallot, juice the lemon, rinse the capers, cube the cold butter and keep it in the fridge until the end.

timeline.do: Butterfly and pound the chicken. Prepare the sauce ingredients.
Season and dredge; heat the pan.
Sauté the cutlets in two batches, 2 to 3 minutes a side; hold them warm.
Shallot, wine, stock: reduce by half.
Lemon and capers in; butter swirled in off the heat.
Cutlets back through the sauce, parsley on, serve.

steps.do: Dredge each seasoned cutlet in flour, pressing lightly so both sides are coated, then lift and tap it firmly to shake off the excess. Dredge just before cooking, not ahead.
steps.look: A thin, even, dusty film with no clumps or bare patches.
steps.mistake: Dredging minutes ahead, so the flour soaks up moisture and turns gummy.
steps.fix: If the flour has gone pasty, re-dredge in fresh flour.

steps.do: Heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and 1 tbsp (14 g) butter in the skillet over medium-high heat until the butter foam subsides and the fat shimmers.
steps.look: The foam settles, the fat smells nutty and a pinch of flour sizzles immediately.
steps.mistake: Starting cold, which glues the coating to the pan.
steps.fix: Wait for the foam to drop and the sizzle test to pass.

steps.do: Lay in two cutlets, away from you. Cook 2 to 3 minutes undisturbed until the underside is golden, then turn and cook 2 minutes more. Transfer to the rack in the warm oven. Add the last 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and repeat.
steps.look: Golden brown edge to edge with no pale patches; the cutlet feels firm and springy when pressed. Golden brown bits are forming on the pan floor.
steps.mistake: Overcrowding, which steams the coating pale and soggy.
steps.fix: Cook two at a time. If the fond starts going black rather than brown, lower the heat for the second batch.

steps.do: Check one cutlet at its thickest part with the thermometer: it should read 165°F (74°C). Thin cutlets get there quickly and carry a few degrees more as they rest.
steps.look: Opaque white all the way through with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Leaving thin cutlets in the pan to be safe, so they turn dry and stringy.
steps.fix: Trust the thermometer. If a cutlet is short, it can finish in the warm oven for a few minutes.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 1 tsp (5 ml) of fat. Lower the heat to medium, add the shallot and stir 30 seconds until it softens.
steps.look: The shallot sizzles gently and turns translucent, picking up some of the brown fond.
steps.mistake: Burning the shallot in a pan still too hot from the cutlets.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat for 20 seconds if it is smoking before the shallot goes in.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and scrape the floor of the pan hard with a wooden spoon until all the fond has lifted. Boil until reduced by half, about 2 minutes. Add the stock and reduce by half again, 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: The liquid turns light brown, the raw wine smell disappears and the sauce looks slightly syrupy. About 1/2 cup (120 ml) remains.
steps.mistake: Not reducing enough, so the sauce is thin and tastes of raw wine.
steps.fix: Keep boiling and measure by eye: the bubbles become larger and slower as it thickens.

steps.do: Add the lemon juice and capers and simmer 30 seconds. Take the pan completely off the heat. Add the cold butter one cube at a time, swirling the pan constantly until each melts into the sauce before adding the next.
steps.look: The sauce turns opaque, creamy and glossy and coats the back of a spoon. No yellow butter oil separates at the edges.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter over live heat or letting it boil, which splits it into a greasy yellow slick.
steps.fix: If it splits, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) cold water or stock off the heat and whisk hard; it often comes back together.

steps.do: Taste: it should land sharp first, then rich. Adjust with salt or a few drops more lemon. Return the cutlets and any resting juices to the pan, turn them once through the sauce and scatter the parsley.
steps.look: Each cutlet wears a thin glaze and the coating stays on the meat, not in the sauce.
steps.mistake: Leaving the cutlets to soak in the sauce, which softens the crust.
steps.fix: Turn them through once and plate at once.

dishes.science: The flour does three jobs: it browns faster than bare chicken, it insulates the thin meat from the full force of the pan, and the starch it leaves behind thickens the sauce when the wine goes in. Pounding to an even thickness means every part reaches a safe temperature at the same moment. The butter finish is an emulsion: cold butter melting slowly into a little reduced liquid disperses as tiny droplets, held in suspension by the milk proteins and the flour starch, which is why the sauce turns creamy rather than oily. Heat is the enemy here. Much above about 140°F (60°C) the emulsion breaks, the fat separates from the water and the sauce turns greasy, which is why the butter goes in off the heat.
dishes.plating: Warm the plates. Lay two cutlets slightly overlapping on the left of the plate, spoon the sauce over so a few capers land on top, and set a thin lemon slice and a pinch of parsley on each. Add a neat spoon of buttered pasta, mashed potato or sautéed spinach to the right. Keep the sauce on the meat rather than flooding the plate.

pairing.drink: A crisp, unoaked Italian white such as Verdicchio or Pinot Grigio. Its lemony acidity matches the sauce and its lightness respects the delicate chicken.

variations: Veal piccata: the original, with thin veal scaloppine cooked 1 minute a side.
Fish piccata: sole or flounder fillets dredged and cooked 90 seconds a side.
Chicken francese: dip the floured cutlets in beaten egg before frying for a softer, eggy crust.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C). Use a fresh board after pounding raw chicken, and wash the mallet and bag area well.
Discard any flour left after dredging raw chicken; it is contaminated.
When pouring wine into a hot pan, stand back and pour away from you to avoid steam burns.

dishes.title: Shrimp Scampi
dishes.summary: Shrimp sautéed briefly, then finished in a sauce of garlic, white wine, lemon and butter and tossed with linguine. Shrimp go from tender to rubbery in under a minute, so this dish is the course’s best teacher of doneness by sight, by curl and by colour.
skills: a garlic, wine and butter sauce
equipment: Large pot, at least 6 quarts (6 litres)
Paring knife or kitchen shears for deveining
Bowl of iced water to keep shrimp cold while you peel

ingredients.note: about 16 to 20 per pound (35 to 45 per kg)

ingredients.item: Kosher salt for the pasta water

ingredients.note: zest finely grated, plus 2 tbsp (30 ml) juice

mise: Keep the shrimp cold in a bowl set over ice while you work.
Peel each shrimp, leaving the tail on if you like. Run a paring knife 1/8 inch (3 mm) deep along the back and lift out the dark vein with the tip of the knife. Rinse and pat completely dry.
Optional but worth it: simmer the shells in 1 cup (240 ml) water for 10 minutes and strain for a quick stock to use in place of some pasta water.
Season the shrimp with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and keep them in the fridge.
Slice the garlic, zest and juice the lemon, chop the parsley, cube the cold butter.
Put the pasta water on to boil.

timeline.do: Water on. Peel and devein the shrimp; make the shell stock if using.
Salt the water and drop the linguine.
Sear the shrimp in batches and lift them out underdone.
Garlic and chilli, then wine; reduce.
Pasta into the pan with butter and pasta water; toss.
Shrimp back for the final minute with lemon and parsley.

steps.do: Salt the boiling water and cook the linguine 2 minutes less than the packet time, stirring in the first minute. Reserve 1 cup (240 ml) pasta water before draining or lifting.
steps.look: A pinpoint of firm white core when you bite a strand.
steps.mistake: Fully cooking the pasta in the water, so it goes soft in the sauce.
steps.fix: Shorten the sauce toss if it is already done.

steps.do: While the pasta cooks, heat 2 tbsp (30 ml) olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Add half the shrimp in a single layer and cook 1 minute without moving, until the underside turns pink with golden spots.
steps.look: A brisk sizzle; the undersides turn from grey translucent to coral pink.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan, so the shrimp poach in their own liquid and never colour.
steps.fix: Cook in two batches with space between every shrimp.

steps.do: Turn each shrimp and cook 30 seconds more, then lift them onto a plate while still slightly translucent in the centre. Repeat with the rest.
steps.look: The shrimp are pink outside, bending into a loose C, with a grey translucent centre if you cut one.
steps.mistake: Cooking them through now. They will finish in the sauce and turn rubbery if already done.
steps.fix: Pull them early. Underdone at this stage is correct.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium-low, add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil, the garlic and chilli flakes. Cook 1 to 2 minutes, stirring, until the garlic is soft and fragrant but has not taken colour.
steps.look: Garlic slices are pale straw coloured and limp, and the oil smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Browning the garlic in a pan still very hot from the shrimp.
steps.fix: Take the pan off the heat for 30 seconds before adding the garlic; if it browns, start the garlic again.

steps.do: Pour in the wine, raise the heat to medium-high and simmer 2 minutes, scraping up any browned bits, until reduced by about half.
steps.look: The sharp alcohol smell fades and the liquid looks slightly thicker.
steps.mistake: Skipping the reduction, so the sauce tastes of raw wine.
steps.fix: Keep reducing; taste a drop and it should be mellow.

steps.do: Add the drained linguine, 1/2 cup (120 ml) pasta water (or shell stock) and the cold butter. Toss continuously over medium heat 1 to 2 minutes until the butter melts into a creamy sauce that coats the pasta.
steps.look: The sauce turns opaque and glossy, every strand slick, no free butter pooling at the edge.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil hard after the butter goes in, so the sauce splits into oil.
steps.fix: If it looks greasy, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) pasta water and toss hard off the heat.

steps.do: Return the shrimp and their juices to the pan with the lemon zest and juice. Toss over low heat for 1 minute only, until the shrimp are just opaque throughout.
steps.look: Each shrimp is a loose C shape, opaque to the centre, the flesh firm with a slight snap when bitten.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the shrimp curl into tight O rings, which means they are overcooked.
steps.fix: If you overshoot, serve at once; the longer they sit in the heat, the tougher they get.

steps.do: Add the parsley, taste and adjust salt and lemon. Plate straight away.
steps.look: The lemon lands behind the garlic, the sauce clings, and the shrimp sit on top in loose curls.
steps.mistake: Holding the dish while you finish other things.
steps.fix: Have the plates warm and the table set before the shrimp go back in.

dishes.science: Shrimp muscle proteins set over a narrow range: they turn opaque at around 120°F (49°C), are perfectly tender near 135 to 140°F (57 to 60°C), and squeeze out water and turn tight and rubbery beyond about 150°F (66°C). Because shrimp are small, they cross that range in seconds, and a tight O shape tells you the muscle has contracted too far. Searing them briefly and finishing them in the gentler heat of the sauce gives control. The sauce is a butter emulsion, kept stable by starchy pasta water, which coats the fat droplets and stops them merging. Garlic cooked low and slow keeps its sweetness; brown it and it turns bitter, a flavour impossible to hide in a sauce this light.
dishes.plating: Use warm shallow bowls. Twist the linguine into a nest with tongs, arrange five or six shrimp on and around it in loose curls, tails pointing the same way, and spoon the remaining sauce over. Finish with parsley, a little lemon zest and a lemon wedge on the side.

pairing.drink: A crisp Albariño from Rías Baixas. Its saline edge and citrus match the shrimp and lemon, and its acidity cuts the butter.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: the Albariño on the list, saline and citrus for shrimp and lemon

variations: Without pasta: serve the shrimp and sauce in a bowl with crusty bread for mopping.
Gulf shrimp scampi with a pinch of Creole seasoning in place of the chilli flakes.
Langoustine or prawn scampi, the original, split in the shell and grilled with garlic butter.
safety: Keep raw shrimp refrigerated below 40°F (4°C) until cooking, and cook them until opaque throughout, which is about 145°F (63°C).
Thaw frozen shrimp overnight in the fridge or in a sealed bag under cold running water, never at room temperature.
Discard any shrimp that smell of ammonia.

dishes.title: Garides Saganaki
dishes.summary: A Greek taverna dish of shrimp poached in a thick tomato sauce with ouzo, crowned with melting feta and served bubbling in its pan. After scampi, it shows a second way to protect a delicate protein: rather than searing it, you let it cook gently in a sauce, and judge the sauce’s reduction before the shrimp ever go in.
skills: a quick tomato sauce with ouzo
equipment: 10 to 12 inch (25 to 30 cm) ovenproof skillet or two-handled pan with a lid
Small saucepan if making shell stock
Long matches or a lighter if flaming the ouzo (optional)

ingredients.note: peeled and deveined, tails on, shells kept
or one 28 oz (794 g) can whole tomatoes, crushed
broken into large chunks, not crumbs
season lightly; the feta is salty

mise: Peel and devein the shrimp, leaving tails on. Simmer the shells in 2/3 cup (160 ml) water for 10 minutes, strain and keep the liquor.
Halve the tomatoes and grate the cut sides on the large holes of a box grater over a bowl until only the skin is left in your hand. Discard the skins.
Dice the onion fine, mince the garlic, break the feta into 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) chunks.
Pat the shrimp dry and keep them cold.

timeline.do: Peel the shrimp and start the shell stock. Grate the tomatoes.
Soften the onion; add garlic, chilli and tomatoes.
Simmer the sauce until it is thick and the oil rises.
Shrimp in; ouzo over and cooked off.
Feta on, lid on.
Oregano and parsley over; to the table bubbling.

steps.do: Warm the olive oil in the pan over medium-low heat. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 7 to 8 minutes, stirring often, until soft and translucent with no colour.
steps.look: The onion is glassy and limp and smells sweet. No gold at the edges.
steps.mistake: Cooking over high heat so the onion browns; browned flecks taste bitter against the tomato.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and add a splash of water to stop browning.

steps.do: Add the garlic and chilli flakes and stir 1 minute until fragrant.
steps.look: The garlic softens and the oil turns faintly red from the chilli.
steps.mistake: Letting the garlic colour.
steps.fix: Move straight on to the tomatoes if it begins to colour.

steps.do: Add the grated tomatoes and the shell liquor. Raise the heat to medium and simmer 12 to 15 minutes, stirring now and then, until the sauce is thick and sweet.
steps.look: The sauce reduces by about half, darkens, and orange oil rises to the surface. A spoon dragged across the pan leaves a track that holds for a moment.
steps.mistake: Stopping while the sauce is thin. The shrimp and the feta release liquid, and a thin sauce turns into a watery pan.
steps.fix: Keep simmering until the track holds; this is the step that decides the dish.

steps.do: Taste and season the sauce lightly with salt, remembering that the feta will add more. Nestle the shrimp into the sauce in one layer and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: The shrimp begin to turn pink at the edges where they touch the sauce.
steps.mistake: Salting fully before the feta goes in, which makes the finished pan too salty.
steps.fix: If it is over salted, add a little unsalted tomato or water and simmer briefly.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and pour the ouzo over. To flame it, return the pan to the heat, tilt it away from you and touch the edge of the liquid with a long match; let the flame burn out on its own, about 10 seconds. Otherwise simply simmer 1 minute to cook off the alcohol.
steps.look: A soft blue flame that dies down by itself, or a fading anise and alcohol smell as it simmers.
steps.mistake: Pouring ouzo from the bottle over a hot pan, which can draw flame back to the bottle.
steps.fix: Always measure into a cup first and pour off the heat. If the flame lingers, cover the pan with the lid to put it out.

steps.do: Turn the shrimp over, scatter the feta chunks on top and cover with the lid. Cook on low heat 2 to 3 minutes.
steps.look: The feta softens and slumps with glossy shoulders, still in chunks; the shrimp are opaque and curled into loose C shapes.
steps.mistake: Stirring the feta in so it dissolves into a grainy pink sauce.
steps.fix: Leave the feta on top and do not stir. If it dissolved, call it a creamy sauce and serve it proudly, but next time leave it alone.

steps.do: Uncover, scatter the oregano (crumble it between your palms to wake it up) and the parsley, and drizzle with a little more olive oil.
steps.look: A bubbling red pan dotted with white feta and green herbs.
steps.mistake: Leaving the lid on longer, so the shrimp overcook in the steam.
steps.fix: Serve straight away.

steps.do: Take the pan to the table on a board with bread. Taste the sauce with a crumb of feta on the spoon: together they should be well seasoned and bright.
steps.look: Anise in the background, tomato sweet, feta salty, shrimp tender.
steps.mistake: Leaving it to sit before serving.
steps.fix: This dish is at its best within minutes.

dishes.science: Poaching in a sauce protects shrimp because the liquid never rises above its simmering point, around 200°F (93°C), and the shrimp cook from all sides at once rather than from one scorching surface. The trade is that the sauce must be reduced before the shrimp go in, since shrimp release water as they cook and the closed lid traps more as condensation. Ouzo carries anethole, the aromatic compound that gives anise its scent; it dissolves in fat and alcohol and bridges sweet tomato and salty feta. Feta is a brined cheese whose structure softens with heat but resists fully melting, which is why it slumps into glossy chunks rather than flowing like mozzarella.
dishes.plating: Serve in the pan it was cooked in, set on a wooden board, with bread on the side. For plated portions, spoon sauce into a warm shallow bowl, arrange four or five shrimp tails up, set two feta chunks between them and finish with oregano, parsley and a thread of olive oil.

pairing.drink: Santorini Assyrtiko, bone dry with a mineral, salty edge. It cuts through feta and tomato the way a squeeze of lemon would.
pairing.brennans: Gaia ‘Wild Ferment’ Assyrtiko Santorini 2023: the Santorini Assyrtiko on the list, a Greek white for a Greek pan

variations: Baked: assemble in an ovenproof dish and bake at 400°F (200°C) for 10 minutes until the feta softens.
With orzo: stir 1 cup (180 g) cooked orzo into the sauce before the shrimp.
Mussels saganaki: the same sauce with 2 lb (900 g) cleaned mussels, covered until they open.
safety: Cook shrimp until opaque throughout, about 145°F (63°C).
When flaming, turn off the extractor fan, keep hair and sleeves back and keep the lid nearby to smother the flame.
