dishes.title: Blackened Redfish
dishes.summary: Redfish fillets dipped in butter, packed with a Cajun spice blend and seared on a smoking hot cast-iron pan until the spices form a dark crust while the fish stays moist inside. It is the hottest pan in the course, so it teaches heat safety and the exact line between blackened spice and burnt fish. It is also a dish of your city, popularised in New Orleans in the 1980s.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet (only cast iron takes and holds this heat)
Outdoor burner or grill if you can; otherwise every window open and the extractor on full
Shallow dish for melted butter, another for the spice
Heavy oven mitt or welder’s glove

ingredients.us: 4 fillets, each about 6 oz and 1/2 inch thick
ingredients.note: or black drum, snapper or catfish; thicker than 3/4 inch (2 cm) will burn outside before cooking through
melted; 6 tbsp (84 g) for dipping, 4 tbsp (56 g) to serve

mise: Mix all the dry spices in a small bowl until evenly coloured, then spread them on a plate.
Pat the fillets very dry with paper towels. Keep them in the fridge until 10 minutes before cooking.
Melt the butter gently; pour 6 tbsp (85 g) into a shallow dish for dipping and keep the rest warm.
Open windows, turn the extractor to its highest setting and plan where the smoke will go: if indoors, close the kitchen door to the rest of the house and leave the smoke alarm working.
Clear the stove of anything flammable: towels, paper, plastic.
Lay out the spatula, mitt and a warm platter.

timeline.do: Mix the spice. Dry the fish. Ventilate the kitchen.
Set the dry cast iron over the highest heat.
Dip and coat the fillets.
Sear the first side, about 2 minutes.
Turn and sear the second side.
Plate with butter and lemon.

steps.do: Set the empty, dry cast-iron skillet over your highest heat and leave it for 8 to 10 minutes. Do not add any oil to the pan.
steps.look: The pan begins to smoke faintly and a drop of water flicked in skitters and vanishes in under a second. If you have an infrared thermometer, it reads about 500°F (260°C) or above.
steps.mistake: Not heating long enough; the spice then steams instead of blackening, and the fish sticks.
steps.fix: Give it the full time. Cast iron heats slowly but holds heat once there.

steps.do: Dip one fillet into the melted butter, turning to coat both sides, then lay it on the spice plate and press gently so a thick, even layer sticks. Turn and coat the other side. Repeat with all fillets.
steps.look: A complete, even coat of red spice with no bare patches; the butter helps it cling.
steps.mistake: Coating minutes ahead, so the spice turns pasty.
steps.fix: Coat right before cooking. If the coating is thin, dip again lightly and recoat.

steps.do: Wearing the mitt, lay two fillets in the pan, laying them away from you. Drizzle 1 tsp (5 g) of melted butter over the top of each fillet. Stand back: there will be a burst of smoke and loud sizzling.
steps.look: Immediate loud sizzle and thick smoke. The butter on top bubbles.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan with all four, which drops the temperature.
steps.fix: Cook two at a time; let the pan recover 1 to 2 minutes between batches.

steps.do: Cook without moving for 2 minutes, until the underside is a very dark, mahogany crust, nearly black in places.
steps.look: The edge of the fillet turns opaque about a third of the way up. The crust smells toasty and spicy, not acrid like burnt hair.
steps.mistake: Moving the fish early, which tears the crust.
steps.fix: If it smells acrid and the crust is turning grey-black and dry, the pan is too hot: lower the heat slightly for the next batch.

steps.do: Slide the fish spatula flat under the fillet in one confident push and turn it. Drizzle a little more butter over the cooked side. Cook 1 1/2 to 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Both sides are dark, the fillet is opaque through the edges, and it begins to flake at the sides when pressed gently.
steps.mistake: Using tongs or a thick spatula, which breaks the fish.
steps.fix: If the fillet breaks, put it back together on the plate; the crust hides it.

steps.do: Check the thickest part with the thermometer: 140 to 145°F (60 to 63°C). The flesh should flake with gentle pressure and be opaque white with no glassy centre.
steps.look: Moist, opaque white flakes under a dark crust.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the flesh is dry and chalky.
steps.fix: Thin fillets cook fast: lift them as soon as they reach temperature.

steps.do: Move the fillets to the warm platter. Let the pan recover heat for 1 to 2 minutes and cook the second batch the same way. Turn off the heat and leave the pan on a cold burner well out of reach; it stays dangerously hot for 30 minutes.
steps.look: The second batch sizzles as loudly as the first.
steps.mistake: Putting the next fillets into a pan that has cooled.
steps.fix: Wait for faint smoke again before the second batch.

steps.do: Spoon the remaining warm butter over each fillet and serve at once with lemon wedges.
steps.look: The butter pools glossy on the dark crust; the fish smells of toasted spice and lemon.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit; the crust softens as it waits.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the pan to the plate.

dishes.science: Blackening is not burning the fish. It is the butter solids and spices browning and charring on a surface around 500°F (260°C), far hotter than a normal sauté. The milk solids in butter brown fast, and paprika is rich in sugars and pigments that darken into a deeply flavoured crust in seconds. Because the fillet is thin and the heat so intense, the crust forms before the heat has time to travel through and dry out the centre. Cast iron is essential because it is heavy and stores a lot of heat, so it does not cool much when the cold fish lands. A thin pan would drop in temperature and steam the fish. The smoke is butter fat and spice combusting, which is why ventilation matters.
dishes.plating: Set the fillet crust side up across the centre of a warm plate, slightly off centre. Spoon a line of melted butter over it, add a lemon wedge at one end and a neat spoon of rice or a crisp green salad at the other. A classic New Orleans plate adds a pat of herb butter melting on top. Keep the crust dry and visible: no sauce over it.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling. A touch of sweetness tames the cayenne, its acidity cuts the butter, and low alcohol does not inflame the heat.
pairing.brennans: C.H. Berres ‘Old Vines’ Riesling 2022: an off-dry German Riesling on the list to calm the cayenne

variations: Blackened chicken: pound boneless thighs to an even 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) and cook 3 to 4 minutes a side to 165°F (74°C).
Blackened tofu: press extra-firm tofu, slice into 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) slabs and use the same method, 2 minutes a side.
Blackened shrimp over grits, a bridge to the last dinner of this level.
safety: This is the most dangerous pan in the level. Cook outdoors if you can. Indoors, ventilate fully and expect the smoke alarm to sound.
Never add water to a smoking hot pan, and never leave it unattended.
Keep a lid or a sheet pan beside the stove to smother a fat fire. Never use water on burning fat. Know where your fire extinguisher is.
The handle of cast iron is as hot as the pan: always use a heavy mitt.
Fish is safe at 145°F (63°C), opaque and flaking easily.

dishes.title: Pan-Fried Fish with Chermoula
dishes.summary: Skin-on white fish fillets marinated briefly in chermoula, the Moroccan herb, spice and lemon sauce, then pan-fried skin side down until the skin shatters, with more chermoula spooned over at the table. After blackening, this is fish cookery at moderate heat: crisp skin, moist flesh, and the habit of judging doneness by the flake rather than the clock.
skills: a herb, spice and lemon marinade
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) non-stick or well seasoned carbon steel skillet
Food processor, blender or mortar and pestle
Small dry pan for toasting cumin
Paper towels and a sharp knife for scoring

ingredients.item: Skin-on white fish fillets (sea bass, snapper or bream)
ingredients.note: scaled, pin bones removed, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) thick

ingredients.item: Fresh coriander, leaves and tender stems

ingredients.note: 1/2 tsp (3 g) for the chermoula, the rest for the fish

mise: Toast the cumin seeds in a small dry pan over medium heat for 60 to 90 seconds, shaking, until they darken a shade and smell nutty. Grind them.

Blend the coriander, parsley, garlic, cumin, paprika, cayenne, preserved lemon, lemon juice, olive oil and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt to a loose, bright green sauce with some texture. Taste: it should be punchy.
Pat the fish fillets very dry, especially the skin. Run the back of a knife along the skin, from tail to head, to squeeze out moisture, then dry again.
Score the skin with three shallow diagonal cuts, just through the skin, about 1/16 inch (2 mm) deep, so it does not curl in the pan.
Spread one third of the chermoula over the flesh side only. Keep the skin side clean and dry. Refrigerate 20 minutes, no longer.
Keep the remaining chermoula aside for the table.

timeline.do: Toast cumin and blend the chermoula.
Dry, score and marinate the fish flesh side only.
Prepare sides; take the fish out of the fridge.
Heat the pan. Salt the skin. Fry skin side down.
Turn for the last minute; check temperature.
Plate skin side up with fresh chermoula and lemon.

steps.do: Take the fish from the fridge, scrape off any chermoula that has strayed onto the skin and pat the skin dry once more. Season the skin with salt just before cooking.
steps.look: The skin looks matte and dry, like paper, not shiny or wet.
steps.mistake: Leaving marinade or water on the skin, which steams it and makes it stick.
steps.fix: Dry the skin again with a fresh paper towel; moisture is the enemy of crisp skin.

steps.do: Heat the neutral oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers but does not smoke, about 2 minutes.
steps.look: The oil moves freely and ripples when the pan is tilted.
steps.mistake: Adding fish to a cold pan, which glues the skin down.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer, then test with the tip of a fillet: it should sizzle immediately.

steps.do: Lay each fillet skin side down, placing it away from you. Immediately press the top gently with the fish spatula for 15 to 20 seconds so the whole skin makes contact as it tightens.
steps.look: A steady, crackling sizzle, and the fillet lies flat instead of curling.
steps.mistake: Not pressing, so the fillet curls up and the skin browns only at the edges.
steps.fix: If a fillet curls, press again for a few seconds until it relaxes.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium and cook without moving for 4 to 5 minutes, depending on thickness, until the flesh has turned opaque about three quarters of the way up the side.
steps.look: The opaque line climbs the side of the fillet. The sizzle settles to a steady crackle. The edges of the skin look golden.
steps.mistake: Peeking and moving the fish too early, which tears the skin.
steps.fix: When the skin is crisp it releases by itself; if it sticks, give it another 30 seconds.

steps.do: Slide the spatula under each fillet and turn it. Cook flesh side down for 30 to 60 seconds only, just to finish the top.
steps.look: The skin is deep golden and crackles when tapped. The flesh side takes a light golden colour from the chermoula.
steps.mistake: Cooking a long time on the flesh side, which burns the herbs and dries the fish.
steps.fix: One minute at most; the fish should be nearly cooked before you turn it.

steps.do: Check the thickest fillet with the thermometer. Pull the fish at 140°F (60°C); resting carries it to the safe 145°F (63°C). The flesh should be opaque and part into large flakes when nudged with a fork.
steps.look: Opaque, moist, pearly flakes that separate easily.
steps.mistake: Cooking until the flakes look dry and fall apart.
steps.fix: If it is short of temperature, cover the pan off the heat for 1 minute.

steps.do: Transfer the fillets skin side up to warm plates or a rack. Rest 1 minute. Never put sauce over the skin.
steps.look: The skin stays crisp and glassy.
steps.mistake: Resting skin side down on a plate, which steams the skin soft.
steps.fix: Always rest and serve skin side up.

steps.do: Spoon the fresh chermoula onto the plate beside or under the fish, not on top of the skin. Add a lemon wedge.
steps.look: A vivid green pool against golden skin.
steps.mistake: Drowning the fish in sauce so the skin turns soggy.
steps.fix: Serve extra chermoula in a small bowl at the table instead.

dishes.science: Fish skin is mostly collagen and water with a thin layer of fat beneath. To crisp, the water must be driven off and the collagen must shrink and dry, which only happens on a hot, dry surface. That is why the skin is scraped, dried and salted just before it meets the pan, and why it cooks most of the way skin side down: the skin insulates the delicate flesh while the heat climbs. Scoring prevents curling, because collagen contracts sharply when heated. The chermoula marinade stays on the flesh side and only for 20 minutes, because lemon juice is acidic: left longer, acid begins to denature the surface proteins, turning the fish chalky before it is cooked.
dishes.plating: Spoon a generous swoosh of chermoula across the plate with the back of a spoon. Set the fillet skin side up across it at an angle so the sauce shows on both sides. Add a neat pile of herbed couscous or roasted potatoes to one side and a lemon wedge. Finish with a few whole coriander leaves and a pinch of flaky salt on the skin.

pairing.drink: A crisp Loire Sauvignon Blanc. Its green, herbal character echoes the coriander and parsley and its acidity matches the lemon.
pairing.brennans: Famille Durand Val de Loire Sauvignon Blanc 2024: the Loire Sauvignon Blanc on the list, herbal enough for the chermoula

variations: The library’s roast version: layer sliced potatoes, peppers and tomatoes with chermoula, roast at 410°F (210°C) for 20 minutes, set the fish on top and roast 12 to 15 minutes more.
Chermoula shrimp: marinate peeled shrimp for 15 minutes and sear 1 minute a side.
Grilled whole fish: stuff the cavity with chermoula and lemon slices and grill over medium coals.
safety: Fish is safe at 145°F (63°C), when it is opaque and flakes easily.
Keep fish refrigerated until 10 minutes before cooking and marinate it in the fridge.
Lay fish into hot oil away from you to avoid splashes.

dishes.title: Wiener Schnitzel
dishes.summary: A thin veal or pork cutlet passed through flour, egg and fine crumbs and shallow-fried in swirling fat until the crust puffs away from the meat in golden ripples. The breading station is a fundamental of every kitchen, and that rippled, loose crust is its test.
skills: swirling in fat so the crumb puffs
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet with sides at least 2 inches (5 cm) deep
Meat mallet or a heavy small pan
Plastic wrap or a large zip-top bag
Three shallow dishes or plates for the breading station
Wire rack set over a sheet pan
Wide fish slice or slotted spatula

ingredients.item: Veal cutlets (top round) or boneless pork loin cutlets
ingredients.note: about 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thick before pounding
unseasoned, from white bread or rolls; not panko
enough for 3/4 inch (2 cm) depth in a 12 inch (30 cm) skillet

mise: Lay each cutlet between sheets of plastic wrap and pound from the centre outwards with even, glancing blows to 1/8 inch (3 mm), keeping it in one piece. It will roughly double in size.
Make the breading station left to right: flour on the first plate; eggs beaten with the cream until no streaks of white remain on the second; breadcrumbs on the third. Then the rack and sheet pan.
Season the cutlets on both sides with salt and pepper just before breading.
Keep one hand for dry (flour and crumbs) and one for wet (egg) so your fingers do not become clubbed with breading.
Line a sheet pan with a wire rack for draining. Set lemon and parsley ready.

timeline.do: Pound the cutlets. Set up the breading station.
Heat the fat slowly towards 330°F (165°C).
Bread the first two cutlets, right before frying.
Fry two at a time, about 2 minutes a side, swirling.
Bread and fry the second pair.
Plate at once with lemon.

steps.do: Pour the oil into the skillet and add the clarified butter. Heat over medium heat to 330 to 340°F (165 to 170°C), checking with the thermometer.
steps.look: The fat ripples, and a breadcrumb dropped in sizzles and turns golden in about 30 seconds.
steps.mistake: Fat too cool, so the crumb soaks up grease; fat too hot, so the crust browns before the meat cooks.
steps.fix: Adjust the heat and wait for the thermometer. Keep it steady between batches.

steps.do: Dredge a seasoned cutlet in flour on both sides and shake off all the excess. A thin, even film is all you want.
steps.look: The meat looks dusty and dry with no thick patches.
steps.mistake: Leaving thick flour, which forms a pasty layer between meat and crumb.
steps.fix: Tap firmly and pat off excess with your dry hand.

steps.do: Lay it in the egg, turn to coat, then lift and let the excess drip off for a few seconds.
steps.look: A thin, glossy coat of egg with no bare flour showing.
steps.mistake: Leaving too much egg, which makes a thick, heavy crust.
steps.fix: Let it drip longer, or run the cutlet against the rim of the dish.

steps.do: Lay the cutlet in the breadcrumbs and scatter crumbs over the top. Turn once and lift. Do not press: the crumbs should barely cling, loose and fluffy.
steps.look: An even, loose coating with no bare spots, slightly shaggy rather than packed flat.
steps.mistake: Pressing the crumbs on hard, which glues them to the meat and stops the crust from puffing.
steps.fix: If you pressed, the schnitzel will still be good; next time simply turn it in the crumbs.

steps.do: Lower the cutlet into the fat, laying it away from you. Immediately start swirling the pan gently in a circular motion so waves of hot fat wash over the top of the cutlet.
steps.look: Vigorous bubbling all around the cutlet. Within 30 seconds the crust begins to lift and form ripples and bubbles.
steps.mistake: Leaving the pan still, so the top stays flat and the crust clings.
steps.fix: Keep the pan moving. You can also spoon fat over the top continuously.

steps.do: Fry 1 1/2 to 2 minutes until the underside is deep golden, then turn with the fish slice and fry 1 to 1 1/2 minutes more, still swirling.
steps.look: Both sides deep golden, the crust billowed and wrinkled, separated from the meat like a loose jacket.
steps.mistake: Turning several times, which breaks the delicate puffed crust.
steps.fix: Turn once only.

steps.do: Lift the schnitzel out, let the fat drip off for a few seconds, and lay it on the rack. Pork must reach 145°F (63°C); a cutlet this thin passes it in the pan. Check the first one if unsure.
steps.look: The crust stays crisp and the meat is moist and just white or pale pink at the centre with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Draining on paper towels, which steam the underside soft.
steps.fix: Use the rack. If the second batch must wait, hold the first in a 200°F (95°C) oven for no more than 10 minutes.

steps.do: Bread and fry the remaining cutlets, letting the fat come back to temperature between batches. Serve immediately with lemon wedges, parsley and lingonberry jam.
steps.look: Each schnitzel as puffed and golden as the first.
steps.mistake: Frying the second batch in fat that has cooled, which gives a greasy crust.
steps.fix: Check the thermometer before each batch; wait for 330°F (165°C).

dishes.science: The puffed crust, called soufflieren in Vienna, comes from steam. As the cutlet hits hot fat, water in the egg layer turns to steam, and because the crumbs are loose rather than pressed, that steam can lift the egg and crumb layer away from the meat into a bubbled shell. Swirling the fat over the top keeps the upper surface hot so the coating sets in its raised shape. Flour gives the egg something to grip; egg glues the crumbs; fine crumbs brown evenly. Pounding the meat thin lets it cook through in the same 3 to 4 minutes the crust needs to turn golden. Clarified butter adds a nutty taste without milk solids, which would burn at frying temperature.
dishes.plating: Lay the schnitzel across a large warm plate so it nearly reaches the rim, which is the Viennese style. Set a lemon wedge and a small mound of lingonberry jam beside it and a scattering of parsley. Serve potato and cucumber salad or parsley potatoes in a separate dish so nothing sits against the crust and softens it.

pairing.drink: Austrian Grüner Veltliner, dry and peppery with bright acidity. It is the wine of Vienna’s own vineyards and cuts the fried crust cleanly.
pairing.brennans: Bründlmayer ‘Terrassen’ Grüner Veltliner 2023 (375 ml): the Grüner Veltliner on the list, the wine of Vienna for its most famous dish

variations: Schnitzel Wiener Art: pork loin in place of veal, the everyday Austrian version.
Chicken schnitzel: butterflied breast pounded to 1/4 inch (6 mm), fried to 165°F (74°C).
Holstein schnitzel: topped with a fried egg, anchovies and capers.
safety: Never fill a skillet more than half full with fat, and never leave hot fat unattended.
Keep a lid or sheet pan beside the stove to smother a fat fire. Never use water.
Pork and veal cutlets must reach 145°F (63°C).
Throw away leftover flour, egg and crumbs that touched raw meat.
Let the fat cool completely before straining or discarding it.

dishes.title: Kofta Kebabs with Yoghurt Sauce
dishes.summary: Spiced minced lamb kneaded with grated onion and herbs, shaped onto flat skewers and cooked under a fierce overhead grill (broiler), served with a garlicky yoghurt sauce and flatbread. Shaping and cooking mince evenly teaches seasoning by test patty and the safe internal temperature for ground meat.
skills: cooking under a hot grill or over coals
equipment: 8 flat metal skewers, or wooden skewers soaked in water for 30 minutes
Box grater and a clean kitchen towel for squeezing the onion
Sheet pan lined with foil, with a rack if you have one
Overhead grill or a charcoal or gas grill
Small frying pan for the test patty

ingredients.item: Minced lamb or beef, about 20 percent fat

mise: Grate the onion on the fine side of the grater, tip it into a clean towel and twist hard over the sink until no more juice drips. You should have about 1/3 cup (60 g) of dry pulp.
Chop the parsley and mint finely. Mix all the dry spices with the salt and pepper in a small bowl.
Make the yoghurt sauce: stir the yoghurt with the garlic paste, lemon juice, 1 tbsp (15 ml) olive oil and a pinch of salt. Refrigerate.
Toss the sliced red onion with the sumac and a pinch of salt; leave to soften.
If using wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes so they do not burn.

timeline.do: Grate and squeeze the onion; make the yoghurt sauce and sumac onions.
Knead the meat mixture; fry a test patty and adjust seasoning.
Chill the mixture 30 minutes.
Shape onto skewers. Preheat the grill to high.
Grill 3 to 4 minutes a side.
Rest 2 minutes; serve on flatbread with sauce.

steps.do: Put the mince, squeezed onion, garlic, herbs and spice mix into the bowl. Knead firmly with one hand for 2 to 3 minutes, squeezing the mixture through your fingers.
steps.look: The mixture changes from loose and crumbly to sticky and tacky; it clings to your palm and holds together when you press a lump.
steps.mistake: Mixing briefly with a fork, so the kofta crumbles and falls off the skewer.
steps.fix: Keep kneading. If your hand gets warm, rinse it under cold water and continue.

steps.do: Pinch off a walnut-sized piece, flatten it, and fry it in the small pan over medium heat for 2 minutes a side until cooked through. Taste it.
steps.look: A cooked patty that tastes well seasoned, warm with spice, with no bland finish.
steps.mistake: Tasting raw mince, which is unsafe, or skipping the test and serving bland kofta.
steps.fix: Add salt in 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) steps or more spice, knead again, and fry another test patty.

steps.do: Cover and chill the mixture for at least 30 minutes.
steps.look: Firm, cold meat that is easier to shape and holds onto the skewer.
steps.mistake: Shaping warm mixture, which is sticky and slumps.
steps.fix: If you are short of time, chill for 15 minutes in the freezer.

steps.do: Divide the mixture into 8 equal portions of about 3 oz (85 g). With wet hands, squeeze each around a skewer into a sausage about 5 inches (13 cm) long and 1 inch (2.5 cm) thick, pressing your fingertips along it to make shallow dents.
steps.look: Even cylinders of the same thickness, tight against the skewer, with finger dents along the length.
steps.mistake: Making uneven thickness, so the thin end overcooks before the thick end is done.
steps.fix: Roll gently on the board to even them out.

steps.do: Preheat the overhead grill on high for 10 minutes with the rack about 4 inches (10 cm) below the element. Lay the skewers on the foil-lined sheet pan, ideally on a rack, and brush lightly with oil.
steps.look: The element glows red; the oven is blazing hot.
steps.mistake: Putting the kofta under a grill that is not yet hot, so they stew grey in their fat.
steps.fix: Wait for the full preheat.

steps.do: Grill 3 to 4 minutes until the top is browned and sizzling, then turn each skewer with tongs and grill 3 to 4 minutes more.
steps.look: Deeply browned, sizzling surfaces with crisp edges at the dents; fat bubbles and drips.
steps.mistake: Turning too early, before a crust forms, so the meat tears and sticks.
steps.fix: Wait until the surface is browned; it releases more easily.

steps.do: Check the thickest kofta with the thermometer: minced lamb or beef must reach 160°F (71°C). Pull them when they reach it.
steps.look: Juices run clear; the centre is just cooked through, no pink.
steps.mistake: Judging by the outside, which can look done while the centre is raw.
steps.fix: Return any that are short for 1 to 2 minutes more.

steps.do: Rest 2 minutes. Slide the kofta off the skewers with a fork onto warm flatbread, spoon over the yoghurt sauce and top with sumac onions and a few mint leaves.
steps.look: Juicy, glossy kofta with the cool sauce melting around them.
steps.mistake: Sliding them off immediately, so the juices run out.
steps.fix: Give them the 2-minute rest.

dishes.science: Kneading mince with salt does the binding that egg or breadcrumbs do in other recipes. Salt dissolves a muscle protein called myosin, and working the meat draws it out as a sticky film that glues the particles together and holds the kofta onto the skewer. The onion is grated and squeezed because its water would loosen the mixture and make it slump and steam. Fat, about 20 percent, keeps the kofta moist and carries the spices, many of whose flavour compounds dissolve in fat. Ground meat needs to reach 160°F (71°C) because mincing spreads any surface bacteria right through the meat, unlike a whole steak where they sit only on the outside.
dishes.plating: Lay a warm flatbread on the plate and spoon a broad stripe of yoghurt sauce down the middle. Set two kofta side by side on the sauce. Pile sumac onions at one end, scatter chopped parsley and mint, and add a lemon wedge. A small chopped salad of tomato and cucumber on the side completes it.

pairing.drink: A Côtes du Rhône red, Grenache led, with warm spice and soft tannin that suits cumin, allspice and lamb.
pairing.brennans: Domaine de Châteaumar ‘Cuvée Vincent’ Côtes du Rhône 2023: the Grenache-led Côtes du Rhône on the list, warm with spice for lamb

variations: Kofta in a pan: shape into small patties and fry 3 minutes a side over medium-high heat.
Kofta with tahini: bake the kofta on a bed of sliced potatoes and tomatoes, covered with tahini sauce, at 400°F (200°C) for 25 minutes.
Chicken kofta with minced thigh, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
safety: Minced lamb and beef must reach 160°F (71°C); minced chicken or turkey 165°F (74°C).
Never taste raw mince: fry a test patty instead.
Wash hands well after kneading raw meat, and keep it cold until shaping.

dishes.title: Swedish Meatballs with Cream Sauce
dishes.summary: Small, tender meatballs of beef and pork seasoned with allspice and nutmeg, browned in butter and finished in a cream gravy built in the same pan. The panade of soaked breadcrumbs explains why some meatballs stay soft, and the gravy carries the pan sauce lesson into a roux and cream.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet, stainless or cast iron
Tongs or a spoon for turning
Sheet pan to hold shaped meatballs
mise: Make the panade: stir the breadcrumbs into the milk and leave 10 minutes until soft and pasty.
Soften the onion in 1 tbsp (14 g) butter over low heat for 5 minutes without colour, then cool it completely.
Warm the stock. Measure the cream and soy.
Set a sheet pan beside you and a bowl of cold water for wetting your hands.

timeline.do: Panade soaking; soften and cool the onion.
Mix the meat, test a small patty, adjust seasoning.
Roll the meatballs and chill briefly.
Brown in two batches.
Make the roux and gravy in the same pan.
Simmer the meatballs in the gravy until cooked through.

steps.do: Mash the panade with a fork until smooth. Add both minces, the cooled onion, egg, allspice, nutmeg, salt and pepper. Mix with your hand for about 1 minute, just until evenly combined.
steps.look: A soft, moist, evenly mixed mass that holds together when pressed.
steps.mistake: Kneading hard as you would for kofta, which makes these meatballs dense and springy.
steps.fix: Mix only until you see no streaks; tender is the goal here.

steps.do: Fry a teaspoon-sized test patty in a little butter for 1 minute a side, taste and adjust salt and spice.
steps.look: A warm, savoury taste with the allspice noticeable but not dominant.
steps.mistake: Seasoning by guesswork.
steps.fix: Adjust and test again; seasoning is fixed once rolled.

steps.do: With wet hands, roll the mixture into balls 1 inch (2.5 cm) across, about 1/2 oz (15 g) each. You should get about 28 to 30. Lay them on the sheet pan and chill 10 minutes.
steps.look: Smooth, round balls of equal size with no cracks.
steps.mistake: Making uneven sizes, which cook at different speeds.
steps.fix: Weigh the first few until your eye learns the size.

steps.do: Heat 1 tbsp (14 g) butter with the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat. When the foam subsides, add half the meatballs in one layer. Brown 5 to 6 minutes, shaking the pan and turning them so they colour on all sides. Lift onto a plate and repeat.
steps.look: Even deep brown all over, a steady sizzle, browned bits forming on the pan floor.
steps.mistake: Crowding the pan so the meatballs steam grey and stick.
steps.fix: Brown in batches with room around each ball.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Leave about 2 tbsp (30 ml) fat in the pan (add butter if needed). Sprinkle in the flour and whisk 1 to 2 minutes into a smooth paste, scraping the browned bits.
steps.look: A bubbling paste the colour of peanut butter that smells toasty.
steps.mistake: Burning the roux on a pan still too hot.
steps.fix: If it smells scorched or goes dark brown, wipe out and start the roux with fresh butter.

steps.do: Pour in the warm stock gradually, whisking constantly to keep it smooth. Bring to a simmer and cook 2 to 3 minutes until it thickens. Whisk in the cream and soy sauce.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, light brown gravy that coats the back of a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding cold stock all at once, which causes lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk out lumps, or strain the gravy through a sieve before the meatballs go back.

steps.do: Return the meatballs and their juices to the gravy. Simmer gently 5 to 8 minutes, turning, until cooked through. Check one with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C).
steps.look: The gravy bubbles lazily and thickens further; the meatballs are firm but springy.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which can split the cream and toughen the meat.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer. Thin the gravy with a splash of stock if it gets too thick.

steps.do: Taste the gravy and adjust salt and pepper. Scatter parsley or dill and serve with mashed potatoes, lingonberry jam and quick-pickled cucumber.
steps.look: Silky gravy, tender meatballs, a sweet-tart jam beside them.
steps.mistake: Underseasoning the gravy, which tastes flat against the jam.
steps.fix: Add salt a pinch at a time; a few drops of soy also deepen it.

dishes.science: A panade is starch soaked in liquid. When minced meat cooks, its proteins tighten and squeeze out juice, which is why plain meatballs can turn dry and bouncy. The soaked breadcrumbs sit between the meat particles, physically stopping the proteins from bonding too tightly, and the gelatinised starch holds onto moisture as the meat firms. Light mixing matters for the same reason: vigorous kneading draws out the sticky myosin that binds kofta, giving a springy texture these meatballs avoid. The gravy is thickened by a roux, flour cooked in fat, which coats each starch granule in fat so it can swell in hot liquid without clumping.
dishes.plating: Spoon a smooth mound of mashed potato slightly off centre in a warm shallow bowl and make a hollow with the back of the spoon. Arrange seven meatballs alongside, ladle the gravy over the meatballs and into the hollow, and place a neat spoon of lingonberry jam and a few slices of pickled cucumber on the side. Finish with chopped dill.

pairing.drink: A light, juicy red such as Beaujolais-Villages, low in tannin, with bright berry fruit that echoes the lingonberry and cuts the cream.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): the Beaujolais-Villages on the list, light and berry-bright against the cream gravy

variations: Minnesota style from the library: a larger batch with more gravy, served over egg noodles.
Köttbullar for a buffet: roll smaller, 3/4 inch (2 cm), and serve on picks with the gravy as a dip.
Mushroom gravy: add 4 oz (115 g) sliced mushrooms to the pan before the roux.
safety: Mixed minced beef and pork must reach 160°F (71°C).
Taste the cooked test patty, never the raw mixture.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours; reheat to 165°F (74°C).

dishes.title: Bangers and Mash with Onion Gravy
dishes.summary: Pork sausages cooked low and slow until taut and glossy, a smooth buttery mash and a deep onion gravy. A pub dinner that teaches three separate disciplines: gentle sausage cookery, the right potato and method for mash, and a gravy built on properly browned onions.
equipment: Large heavy skillet for the sausages
Potato ricer, food mill or hand masher (never a food processor)

ingredients.item: Good pork sausages, high meat content
ingredients.note: Cumberland, Lincolnshire or a butcher’s pork sausage

mise: Take the sausages out of the fridge 15 minutes before cooking. Do not prick them.
Peel the potatoes and cut into even 2 inch (5 cm) chunks. Rinse and put them in the large pan with cold water to cover by 1 inch (2.5 cm) and 1 tsp (6 g) salt.
Slice the onions thinly and evenly. Strip the thyme leaves.
Heat the stock and the milk in separate small pans or jugs.

timeline.do: Start the onions on low for the gravy.
Potatoes on, from cold water. Sausages into a cold pan on low.
Flour and stock into the onions; simmer the gravy.
Drain and steam-dry the potatoes; mash with butter, then milk.
Check the sausages; cook the peas.
Mash, sausages, gravy over.

steps.do: Melt the gravy butter in the saucepan over medium-low heat. Add the onions with a pinch of salt and the thyme. Cook 25 to 30 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until soft, sweet and deep golden brown.
steps.look: The onions collapse, turn jammy and take a rich amber colour. They smell sweet, not sharp.
steps.mistake: Turning up the heat to hurry them, so they scorch at the edges while staying pale in the middle.
steps.fix: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water whenever they stick or brown too fast, and scrape; patience gives the colour.

steps.do: Bring the potatoes to the boil from cold, then lower to a steady simmer and cook 15 to 20 minutes.
steps.look: A knife slides into the largest chunk with no resistance and the edges are just starting to crumble.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which breaks the outside to mush while the centre stays raw.
steps.fix: Simmer gently; test the largest piece, not the smallest.

steps.do: Meanwhile, put the oil and sausages in the cold skillet, then set it over low to medium-low heat. Cook 20 to 25 minutes, turning every few minutes so they brown evenly.
steps.look: A gentle, steady sizzle, never violent. The sausages swell, turn evenly golden brown and glossy, and the skins stay intact.
steps.mistake: High heat, which splits the skins and leaves the outside burnt and the inside raw. Pricking them, which lets the juices escape.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down at the first sign of spitting or splitting. A split sausage still eats well; just lower the heat.

steps.do: Stir the flour into the onions and cook 1 minute. Add the hot stock gradually, stirring, then the Worcestershire and mustard. Simmer 8 to 10 minutes until glossy and thick enough to coat a spoon. Season to taste.
steps.look: A shiny, dark gravy with soft onion strands, thick enough to leave a trail when you draw a finger across the coated spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding all the stock at once to raw flour, giving lumps.
steps.fix: Stir hard; small lumps dissolve as it simmers. Add a splash of water if it gets too thick.

steps.do: Drain the potatoes in the colander, return them to the hot empty pan over low heat and shake for 1 to 2 minutes to steam off excess water.
steps.look: The surfaces turn dry and floury and steam rises.
steps.mistake: Mashing wet potatoes, which gives a watery, heavy mash.
steps.fix: Let them steam-dry; it makes the mash fluffy.

steps.do: Press the potatoes through the ricer back into the pan (or mash thoroughly). Beat in the butter first, a few cubes at a time, then add the hot milk gradually, beating with a wooden spoon until smooth and soft. Season with salt and white pepper.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, fluffy mash that holds soft peaks on the spoon.
steps.mistake: Using a food processor or blender, which ruptures the starch cells and turns mash into glue. Adding cold milk.
steps.fix: If the mash is stiff, add more hot milk a tablespoon at a time. Gluey mash cannot be repaired; next time use a ricer.

steps.do: Check the largest sausage with the thermometer: pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C). Rest them 2 minutes.
steps.look: Firm, plump sausages with clear juices and no pink at the centre.
steps.mistake: Serving by colour alone; browned outsides can hide raw middles.
steps.fix: Cover the pan and cook on low a few minutes more if short.

steps.do: Cook the peas in boiling salted water for 2 minutes and drain. Plate the mash, rest two sausages against it and pour the gravy over everything.
steps.look: A pillow of mash, glossy sausages, gravy flowing over both.
steps.mistake: Letting the mash sit, which forms a skin.
steps.fix: Keep the mash covered over very low heat with a little extra milk until plating.

dishes.science: Floury potatoes have large starch granules and little moisture, so they break into a light, fluffy mash; waxy potatoes hold together and turn pasty. Overworking any cooked potato ruptures the swollen starch cells, releasing free starch that makes mash gluey, which is why a ricer beats a blender. Adding butter before milk lets the fat coat the starch first, keeping the texture silky. Sausages cook gently because the casing traps juice and fat: high heat makes the filling expand faster than the skin can stretch, so it splits. Onions turn sweet and brown slowly as their sugars caramelise and react with amino acids, which takes time at low heat.
dishes.plating: Spoon a generous mound of mash into a warm shallow bowl and make a wide well with the back of the spoon. Lean two sausages against the mash at an angle, crossed if you like. Pour the onion gravy into the well and over the sausages, letting it pool. Spoon the peas to one side and finish with a few thyme leaves.

pairing.drink: A pint of English bitter or a light, fruity red such as Côtes du Rhône. Both have enough body for the sausages without overpowering the gravy.

variations: Colcannon mash: fold in 2 cups (150 g) shredded cabbage or kale softened in butter, with chopped spring onions.
Oven method for sausages: roast on a sheet pan at 375°F (190°C) for 25 minutes, turning once.
Toad in the hole: brown the sausages, then bake them in a Yorkshire pudding batter.
safety: Pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C).
Drain potatoes by pouring away from you; steam scalds.
Never leave a pan of sizzling fat unattended.

dishes.title: Dublin Coddle
dishes.summary: A pale, gentle stew of pork sausages, bacon, sliced potatoes and onions simmered slowly in stock under a lid. It is here to show that a low, covered simmer builds deep flavour without any browning, and that a pale stew must be seasoned with care.
equipment: Heavy pot or Dutch oven with a tight lid, about 5 quarts (5 litres)

ingredients.note: Irish style breakfast sausages if available
peeled and sliced 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thick
taste at the end; bacon and stock are salty

mise: Peel and slice the potatoes into even 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) rounds; keep them in cold water so they do not brown.
Slice the onions. Cut the bacon into pieces.
Bring a medium pan of water to the boil for blanching.
Warm the stock. Chop the parsley.

timeline.do: Slice potatoes and onions; boil water.
Blanch the sausages and bacon 2 minutes.
Layer the pot and add the stock.
Lid on, the barest simmer or a 300°F (150°C) oven, for about 1 1/2 hours.
Check the sausages and potatoes, taste and season.
Ladle into warm bowls with parsley and bread.

steps.do: Drop the sausages and bacon into the boiling water and simmer 2 minutes. Lift out with the slotted spoon and drain. If you prefer, cut each sausage in half.
steps.look: The sausages firm and turn pale, and a little grey foam rises on the water.
steps.mistake: Boiling much longer, which drains flavour into water you will throw away.
steps.fix: Two minutes is enough; the job is to firm the sausages and rinse off excess salt.

steps.do: In the pot, make a layer of half the onions, then half the potatoes, then all the sausages and bacon. Season each layer with pepper and a scatter of parsley. Finish with the remaining onions, then the remaining potatoes on top.
steps.look: Neat layers, with potatoes forming a lid over the meat.
steps.mistake: Dumping everything in at random, so the top potatoes stay dry and the meat sits exposed.
steps.fix: Rearrange so the potatoes are on top and the meat is in the middle.

steps.do: Tuck the bay leaf and thyme sprigs in at the side. Pour the warm stock down the side of the pot until it comes about two thirds of the way up; the top layer of potatoes should sit just above the liquid to steam.
steps.look: Liquid visible just below the top potatoes.
steps.mistake: Drowning everything so it boils into a thin soup.
steps.fix: Ladle some stock out if you added too much; you can add it back later if needed.

steps.do: Bring to a simmer over medium heat, then cover tightly and turn the heat to the lowest setting, or move the pot to a 300°F (150°C) oven. Cook 1 1/2 hours without stirring.
steps.look: Under the lid, only a few slow bubbles rise at a time. A gentle, savoury steam.
steps.mistake: A rolling boil, which breaks the potatoes into mush and makes the sausages split.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down, or set the pot slightly off the burner, until the bubbles barely move.

steps.do: After 1 hour, lift the lid and check the liquid level. Add a splash of stock if it has dropped below halfway.
steps.look: Bottom potatoes soft and beginning to thicken the broth; top potatoes steamed and tender.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil dry and catch on the base.
steps.fix: Add hot stock or water and lower the heat.

steps.do: At 1 1/2 hours, check a sausage with the thermometer: 160°F (71°C). The potatoes should be completely tender and the broth slightly thickened by their starch.
steps.look: A knife slides through the top potatoes; the broth is milky and savoury.
steps.mistake: Serving with firm potatoes.
steps.fix: Cover and cook 15 minutes more.

steps.do: Taste the broth and season with salt only if needed, plus more black pepper. Remove the bay leaf and thyme stalks.
steps.look: A savoury, porky, peppery broth.
steps.mistake: Salting at the start, which can leave the finished stew far too salty after the bacon gives up its salt.
steps.fix: If over salted, add a few slices of raw potato and simmer 10 minutes, or add unsalted stock.

steps.do: Ladle into warm, deep bowls, giving everyone potatoes, sausages, bacon and plenty of broth. Shower with the remaining parsley and serve with buttered soda bread.
steps.look: A pale, steaming bowl with bright green parsley on top.
steps.mistake: Serving in shallow plates, which lose the broth.
steps.fix: Use deep bowls; the broth is half the dish.

dishes.science: Most stews start by browning meat for flavour, but coddle takes a different route: a long, gentle simmer below boiling extracts flavour into the liquid instead. As the sausages and bacon sit in hot stock, salt, fat and savoury compounds migrate out into the broth and the potatoes absorb them. Keeping the liquid just under boiling, around 185 to 195°F (85 to 90°C), stops the sausage casings from bursting and keeps the potatoes in whole slices while their outer starch slowly thickens the broth. Because there are no browned flavours to lean on, seasoning carries more weight, and pepper and parsley are doing real work.
dishes.plating: Use deep, warm bowls. Ladle in potatoes first, then lay a sausage and two pieces of bacon on top, pour broth around to half fill the bowl and scatter a generous handful of parsley over the top. Put a thick slice of soda bread with butter on the side plate.

pairing.drink: A dry Irish stout, roasted and bitter, which cuts the pork fat and suits the plain, savoury broth.

variations: Browned coddle: brown the sausages and bacon lightly before layering, for a deeper, darker stew.
Oven coddle: assemble in a casserole and bake covered at 300°F (150°C) for 2 hours.
With barley: add 1/4 cup (50 g) pearl barley with the stock for a thicker stew.
safety: Pork sausages must reach 160°F (71°C).
Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F (74°C).
Lift lids away from you so steam goes the other way.

dishes.title: Chicken Teriyaki
dishes.summary: Boneless chicken thighs with skin rendered crisp in a pan, then lacquered in a reduction of soy, mirin, sake and sugar. Real teriyaki is a pan glaze, not a marinade, and it teaches reduction as a glaze: thick enough to coat, stopped before the sugar burns.
skills: a soy, mirin and sake glaze
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet, stainless, cast iron or non-stick
A smaller pan or a pot lid to press the thighs flat

ingredients.note: ask your butcher to bone them, or bone them yourself
a light seasoning; the sauce is salty

mise: Pat the thighs dry. Trim any loose flaps of fat or skin hanging beyond the meat. With the tip of a knife, make two shallow cuts in the thickest part of the flesh side so the thighs cook evenly.
Prick the skin all over with a fork or the tip of a knife, about 10 times, so fat can escape. Season lightly with salt on both sides.
Stir the soy, mirin, sake, sugar and ginger in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves.
Start the rice. Slice the spring onions. Prepare the vegetables.

timeline.do: Rice on. Trim and prick the thighs; mix the sauce.
Thighs skin side down into the pan; render 8 to 10 minutes.
Turn, cook 3 to 4 minutes; check temperature.
Pour off the fat, wipe the pan, add the sauce and glaze.
Rest and slice.
Serve over rice with the glaze.

steps.do: Put the oil in the cold skillet and lay the thighs in skin side down, flattening them so all the skin touches the pan. Set over medium heat.
steps.look: Within a minute the thighs begin to sizzle quietly as the pan heats.
steps.mistake: Starting in a very hot pan, which shrinks the skin into tight, uneven ridges before the fat renders.
steps.fix: If the skin seizes, press it flat with a smaller pan set on top.

steps.do: Cook 8 to 10 minutes without turning, pressing the thighs flat with a smaller pan or a lid for the first few minutes. Adjust the heat to keep a steady, moderate sizzle.
steps.look: Fat renders out and pools in the pan; the skin turns deep golden brown, flat and crisp, and the flesh goes opaque two thirds of the way up the side.
steps.mistake: Turning early, before the fat has rendered, leaving flabby skin.
steps.fix: Be patient. If the skin is browning too fast before the fat renders, lower the heat.

steps.do: Turn the thighs and cook 3 to 4 minutes on the flesh side. Check the thickest part with the thermometer: at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are juiciest at 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Firm, springy meat with clear juices.
steps.mistake: Pulling at the first sign of colour on the second side.
steps.fix: Keep cooking in 1 minute bursts until the thermometer agrees.

steps.do: Lift the thighs onto a plate. Pour all the fat out of the pan into a heatproof bowl and wipe the pan with a wad of paper towel held in tongs, leaving the browned bits.
steps.look: A nearly dry pan with a little fond on the base.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fat in, so the glaze slides off the chicken instead of clinging.
steps.fix: Wipe again. Fat and glaze do not mix.

steps.do: Return the pan to medium heat, pour in the sauce and let it bubble 30 seconds. Return the thighs skin side up.
steps.look: The sauce boils immediately with a sweet, savoury smell.
steps.mistake: Adding the sauce to a ripping hot pan, which can scorch the sugar instantly.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off the heat for 20 seconds before the sauce goes in.

steps.do: Simmer 2 to 3 minutes, spooning the sauce over the thighs and turning them twice, until the sauce reduces to a thick, shiny glaze. Finish skin side up.
steps.look: The bubbles grow large, slow and glossy; a drop on the spoon stretches before it falls. The thighs look lacquered.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so the sugar burns and turns bitter and sticky.
steps.fix: Pull the pan off as soon as it coats a spoon; it thickens more as it cools. If it went too far, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) water and swirl.

steps.do: Rest the thighs 2 minutes on a board, then slice across the grain into 3/4 inch (2 cm) strips, keeping the shape of each thigh.
steps.look: Moist, opaque slices with the glossy skin intact on top.
steps.mistake: Slicing straight away, so juice floods the board.
steps.fix: Give them the short rest.

steps.do: Spoon rice into bowls, fan a sliced thigh over the top, drizzle the remaining glaze over the meat and finish with spring onions and sesame seeds.
steps.look: Mahogany, glossy skin and a thin drizzle of glaze, not a puddle.
steps.mistake: Pouring glaze all over the rice so it turns syrupy.
steps.fix: Use a spoon to place the glaze on the chicken.

dishes.science: Teriyaki means lustre and grilling, and the shine comes from reduction. As the soy, mirin, sake and sugar boil, water evaporates and the sugars concentrate into a syrup that sets into a glossy film on cooling. Sugar also browns fast above about 320°F (160°C), which is why the sauce goes in only after the cooking is done: marinate first and the sugars burn before the skin has rendered. Rendering skin is slow because the fat beneath it must melt and escape before the skin itself can dry and crisp, so a moderate heat and a flat, pressed thigh give the best result. Draining the fat lets the water-based glaze grip the skin instead of sliding off on an oily layer.
dishes.plating: Fill a warm bowl two thirds with rice and flatten the top. Fan the sliced thigh across the rice, keeping the skin uppermost and the slices slightly overlapping. Spoon a ribbon of glaze along the slices, scatter spring onions and sesame seeds, and set the green vegetables in a neat pile at one side.

pairing.drink: A chilled junmai sake, or an off-dry Riesling whose sweetness meets the glaze and whose acidity cuts the rendered skin.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Riesling Réserve 2020: the Alsace Riesling on the list, crisp against the sweet glaze

variations: Salmon teriyaki: sear skin-on fillets 4 minutes skin side, 1 minute flesh side, then glaze.
Tofu teriyaki: press and slice firm tofu, dust with cornstarch, fry until crisp, then glaze.
Yakitori style: thread thigh pieces on skewers, grill, and brush with the reduced sauce.
safety: Chicken thighs must reach at least 165°F (74°C).
Pour hot fat into a heatproof container and let it cool before throwing it away; never pour fat down the sink.
Wash boards and knives after trimming raw chicken.

dishes.title: Kung Pao Chicken
dishes.summary: Diced, velveted chicken stir-fried in a wok with dried chillies, Sichuan peppercorns, aromatics and peanuts, finished in a glossy sauce that is sweet, sour and gently numbing. A classic stir-fry teaches mise en place, because nothing can be cut once the wok is hot.
skills: frying dried chillies and Sichuan pepper
a balanced sweet and sour sauce
equipment: Wok, 14 inch (35 cm) carbon steel, or a 12 inch (30 cm) heavy skillet
Wok spatula or wide metal spatula
Small bowls for each prepared ingredient (the mise en place)
Strong extractor fan or an open window

ingredients.note: plus 1 tsp (5 ml) for the marinade
snipped in half, seeds shaken out

ingredients.item: Spring onions, white and pale green parts

mise: Dice the chicken into even 3/4 inch (2 cm) cubes. Toss with 2 tsp (10 ml) light soy, 1 tsp (5 ml) Shaoxing and 2 tsp (6 g) cornstarch until coated, then stir in 1 tsp (5 ml) oil. Marinate 15 to 30 minutes in the fridge. This is velveting.

Whisk the sauce ingredients (light and dark soy, vinegar, sugar, cornstarch, stock, Shaoxing) in a small bowl until the sugar dissolves. Taste it: sweet and sour should balance, with salt behind. Adjust now, because you cannot adjust once it is in the wok.
Snip the chillies in half crossways with scissors and shake out most of the seeds.

Slice the garlic and ginger, cut the spring onions. Put every ingredient in its own bowl, lined up beside the stove in the order it goes in: chillies and peppercorns, chicken, aromatics, sauce, peanuts.
Turn on the extractor fan; frying chillies gives off pungent fumes.

timeline.do: Rice on. Dice and velvet the chicken.
Mix and taste the sauce. Prepare every aromatic into bowls.
Heat the wok until it smokes faintly.
Chillies and peppercorns, then the chicken.
Aromatics, sauce, peanuts.
Into a warm dish and to the table.

steps.do: Heat the empty wok over high heat until a wisp of smoke rises, about 1 to 2 minutes. Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) oil and swirl to coat the sides.
steps.look: The oil shimmers instantly and streaks across the hot surface.
steps.mistake: Adding oil to a cold wok, so food sticks.
steps.fix: Heat the wok first, then the oil. Hot wok, cool oil, as the saying goes.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the dried chillies and Sichuan peppercorns and stir 20 to 30 seconds until the chillies darken to deep red and smell toasty.
steps.look: Chillies turn a shade darker, puff slightly and smell fragrant and smoky. The oil takes on a red tint.
steps.mistake: Cooking on high heat so the chillies blacken and turn the dish acrid and bitter.
steps.fix: If any chilli goes black, scoop them all out, wipe the wok and start again; burnt chillies ruin the dish.

steps.do: Turn the heat to high, add the chicken and spread it in a single layer. Leave it for 1 minute to sear, then stir-fry 2 to 3 minutes, tossing, until the pieces are white all over with golden edges.
steps.look: A loud sizzle, chicken pieces separating and turning opaque, golden spots on the edges.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly from the start, so the chicken never browns and the wok cools.
steps.fix: Let it sit for that first minute. If the wok is small, cook the chicken in two batches.

steps.do: Push the chicken up the side of the wok, add the remaining 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil to the centre, and stir-fry the garlic, ginger and spring onions for 30 seconds until fragrant. Toss everything together.
steps.look: A burst of fragrance, the garlic softening without browning.
steps.mistake: Adding the aromatics too early, so they burn while the chicken cooks.
steps.fix: They go in only for the last minute.

steps.do: Stir the sauce again (the cornstarch settles) and pour it around the edge of the wok. Toss for 20 to 30 seconds until it thickens and turns glossy.
steps.look: The sauce bubbles, thickens in seconds and coats every piece with a shine.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to restir, so lumps of cornstarch form.
steps.fix: If it thickens too much, add a splash of water and toss.

steps.do: Check a large piece of chicken: 165°F (74°C), opaque through.
steps.look: Juicy, opaque meat.
steps.mistake: Overcooking while you check, so the sauce reduces to stickiness.
steps.fix: Pull the wok off the heat while you check.

steps.do: Off the heat, toss in the peanuts. Taste and add a few drops of vinegar if it needs brightness.
steps.look: The peanuts are coated but still crunchy.
steps.mistake: Adding the peanuts early, so they soften.
steps.fix: Peanuts last, off the heat.

steps.do: Tip into a warm serving dish at once and serve with rice. Warn diners that the whole chillies are for flavour, not for eating.
steps.look: Glossy chicken studded with red chillies, green onions and golden peanuts.
steps.mistake: Leaving it in the hot wok, where it keeps cooking.
steps.fix: Transfer immediately.

dishes.science: Velveting coats the chicken in a thin film of cornstarch and soy. In the wok, the starch gelatinises into a protective layer that slows moisture loss and gives the meat its silky surface, while also helping the sauce cling. The numbing tingle of Sichuan peppercorns comes from a compound called hydroxy-alpha-sanshool, which stimulates touch receptors in the mouth rather than heat receptors. Frying dried chillies in oil releases their flavour compounds into the fat, but chillies are thin and dry and burn quickly, so the heat is lowered for that step. A stir-fry happens in under five minutes at very high heat, so every ingredient must be ready before cooking starts.
dishes.plating: Serve family style in a warm shallow bowl or on a platter, piled high in the centre so the red chillies and green onions show on top. Scatter a few extra peanuts and sliced green onion tops. Rice goes in separate bowls.

pairing.drink: An off-dry German Riesling Spätlese-style or a Kabinett: the touch of sugar soothes the chilli and the acidity matches the black vinegar.
pairing.brennans: J.J. Prüm ‘Wehlener Sonnenuhr’ Riesling Kabinett 2020: the Mosel Kabinett on the list, its touch of sweetness for the chillies

variations: Kung pao shrimp: peeled shrimp, velveted the same way, stir-fried for 1 1/2 minutes.
Kung pao tofu: extra-firm tofu cubes fried crisp before the chillies.
With vegetables: add diced celery or red pepper with the aromatics.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Frying chillies releases fumes that sting eyes and throat: run the fan and do not lean over the wok.
Peanuts are a common, serious allergen: tell anyone you are cooking for that the dish contains them.
Wash hands after handling chillies before touching your eyes.

dishes.title: Jeyuk Bokkeum (Spicy Stir-Fried Pork)
dishes.summary: Thinly sliced pork shoulder marinated in gochujang, chilli flakes, garlic and ginger, then stir-fried with onion until the edges caramelise. Korean spicy pork introduces fermented chilli paste and the danger that sugar brings to high heat.
skills: stir-frying to caramelise without burning sugar
equipment: Large wok or 12 inch (30 cm) skillet

ingredients.item: Pork shoulder (butt) or pork belly, boneless

ingredients.note: grated, optional; it adds sweetness and tenderises

mise: If the pork is not pre-sliced, wrap it and freeze for 30 to 45 minutes until firm but not hard, then slice across the grain into 1/8 inch (3 mm) slices, about 2 inches (5 cm) long.
In the bowl, stir the gochujang, gochugaru, soy, sugar, mirin, garlic, ginger, grated pear, half the sesame oil and the pepper into a thick red paste.
Add the pork and massage the marinade in with your hand (wear a glove if you like) until every slice is coated. Cover and refrigerate at least 30 minutes, or up to overnight.
Slice the onion, cut the spring onions and chilli. Wash and dry the lettuce leaves.
Start the rice.

timeline.do: Freeze and slice the pork if needed.
Make the marinade and coat the pork; refrigerate.
Rice on if not already. Slice the vegetables.
Heat the pan; stir-fry the pork.
Onions in; then spring onions and chilli.
Sesame oil and seeds; serve with rice and lettuce.

steps.do: Heat the neutral oil in the wok or skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers.
steps.look: Rippling oil, a faint haze.
steps.mistake: Starting cold, so the pork stews in its marinade.
steps.fix: Wait for the shimmer.

steps.do: Add the pork, spreading it out in as even a layer as you can. Leave it for 1 minute to sear.
steps.look: A loud sizzle; the marinade begins to bubble and darken at the edges.
steps.mistake: Piling all the pork in a heap, which steams it grey.
steps.fix: If your pan is small, cook in two batches.

steps.do: Stir-fry for 4 to 5 minutes, turning and spreading the meat, until the pork is cooked through and the edges begin to caramelise. Lower the heat a notch if the marinade on the pan starts to blacken.
steps.look: Pork opaque with dark red, slightly charred edges and a sweet, smoky, spicy smell.
steps.mistake: High heat throughout, so the sugar in the marinade burns black and bitter before the pork cooks.
steps.fix: Add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and scrape; it releases the stuck marinade and cools the pan. Lower the heat.

steps.do: Add the sliced onion and stir-fry 2 minutes until it softens but keeps some bite.
steps.look: The onion turns glossy and translucent at the edges, coated in red sauce.
steps.mistake: Adding the onion at the start, so it releases water and the pork boils.
steps.fix: Onion goes in once the pork has browned.

steps.do: Check a thick slice of pork with the thermometer: 145°F (63°C) minimum; thin slices pass this quickly. Then add the spring onions and chilli and toss 30 seconds.
steps.look: Spring onions bright green and just wilted.
steps.mistake: Cooking the spring onions until limp.
steps.fix: They need only 30 seconds.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Drizzle with the remaining sesame oil and scatter the sesame seeds. Taste and add a pinch of sugar or a splash of soy if needed.
steps.look: A glossy, deep red stir-fry smelling of toasted sesame.
steps.mistake: Adding sesame oil over high heat, which burns off its aroma.
steps.fix: Sesame oil is a finishing oil; add it off the heat.

steps.do: Serve with rice and lettuce leaves. To eat as a wrap (ssam), lay a lettuce leaf in your palm, add a spoon of rice and a piece of pork, fold and eat in one bite.
steps.look: Hot, spicy pork against cool, crisp lettuce.
steps.mistake: Serving without anything to temper the heat.
steps.fix: Rice, lettuce and a side of kimchi or cucumber balance the spice.

dishes.science: Gochujang is a fermented paste of chilli, glutinous rice, soybeans and salt. Fermentation breaks starches into sugars and proteins into savoury amino acids, so the paste brings sweetness, heat and deep umami at once. That sugar is what caramelises on the pork edges, but sugars burn fast above about 350°F (175°C), so marinated meat demands a slightly lower heat than plain stir-fries and an eye on the pan floor. Slicing the pork thin and across the grain shortens the muscle fibres, making each bite tender and letting it cook through in minutes. Grated pear contains enzymes that soften surface proteins and adds natural sugar.
dishes.plating: Pile the pork in the centre of a warm platter, mounded high with the onions woven through. Scatter sesame seeds and a few fine rings of spring onion on top. Serve rice in individual bowls and stack the lettuce leaves beside the platter with small dishes of kimchi.

pairing.drink: An off-dry German Riesling. Its touch of sweetness cools the gochujang heat and its acidity cuts the pork fat. A cold lager also works.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023: the off-dry Riesling on the list, cooling against gochujang heat

variations: Ojingeo bokkeum: the same marinade with squid, cooked for only 2 minutes.
Dak galbi style: boneless chicken thighs with cabbage and sweet potato, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Milder version: halve the gochugaru and add an extra tbsp of soy and sugar.
safety: Pork must reach at least 145°F (63°C).
Marinate in the fridge, never on the counter, and throw away leftover marinade that touched raw meat.
Partly frozen meat slices more safely; keep your fingers curled under on the guiding hand.

dishes.title: Gà Kho Gừng (Caramel Ginger Chicken)
dishes.summary: Vietnamese caramel ginger chicken: bone-in chicken braised in a dark caramel with fish sauce, shallots and two additions of ginger, reduced until the sauce turns to a sticky glaze. Kho cooking uses a caramel taken nearly to bitter, which makes this the first meeting with sugar stages.
skills: a dark caramel as a savoury base
equipment: Heavy medium pot or deep skillet, about 3 quarts (3 litres), light coloured inside if possible so you can judge the caramel
Cleaver or heavy knife if chopping bone-in chicken
Small bowl of cold water and a pastry brush

ingredients.note: chopped into 2 inch (5 cm) pieces through the bone, or boneless thighs halved
half smashed, half cut into fine matchsticks

mise: Pat the chicken dry and toss with 1 tbsp (15 ml) of the fish sauce. Leave 15 minutes.
Peel the ginger. Cut half into 1/4 inch (6 mm) coins and smash them with the flat of the knife; cut the other half into fine matchsticks.
Slice the shallots, mince the garlic, slice the spring onions and chilli.
Measure everything and set it by the stove. Caramel moves fast, so the fish sauce, shallots and chicken must be within reach before the sugar goes in.

timeline.do: Toss chicken with fish sauce; prepare ginger and aromatics.
Make the dark caramel.
Shallots, fish sauce, chicken and smashed ginger in.
Simmer uncovered, turning, about 25 minutes.
Julienned ginger and black pepper in.
Spring onions on; serve with rice.

steps.do: Put the sugar and 1 tbsp (15 ml) water in the dry pot and set it over medium heat. Swirl the pot gently to dissolve the sugar; do not stir with a spoon. If crystals form on the sides, brush them down with a wet pastry brush.
steps.look: The sugar dissolves into a clear syrup and starts to bubble.
steps.mistake: Stirring, which can make the syrup crystallise into grainy sugar.
steps.fix: If it crystallises, add 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and heat gently to redissolve.

steps.do: Keep cooking, swirling, until the caramel turns from pale gold to amber and then to a deep mahogany, like strong tea or dark maple syrup. This takes 4 to 6 minutes; the last stage happens in seconds.
steps.look: Thin wisps of smoke and a smell that is rich and slightly bitter, like the edge of burnt sugar, but not acrid.
steps.mistake: Pulling it at light gold, which makes a sweet sauce without the bitter depth kho needs. Or letting it go black and acrid.
steps.fix: If it smells sharp and burnt and looks black, discard it once cool and start again. Never taste hot caramel.

steps.do: Immediately add the oil and shallots and stir 30 seconds. Then stand back and pour in the remaining 2 tbsp (30 ml) fish sauce; it will hiss and steam.
steps.look: The caramel loosens into a dark sauce; the shallots soften. A savoury, salty-sweet steam.
steps.mistake: Pouring the fish sauce in while leaning over the pot.
steps.fix: Pour at arm’s length and turn your face away. If the caramel seizes into lumps, keep stirring over the heat; it melts back.

steps.do: Add the chicken, smashed ginger and garlic. Turn the pieces to coat them in the caramel for 2 minutes.
steps.look: The chicken takes on a deep amber coat.
steps.mistake: Leaving the chicken still, so the caramel burns on the base.
steps.fix: Keep turning until coated.

steps.do: Add the water or coconut water, bring to a simmer and cook uncovered over medium-low heat for 20 to 25 minutes, turning the pieces every 5 minutes.
steps.look: The liquid bubbles steadily and reduces slowly; the chicken turns a rich brown.
steps.mistake: Covering the pot, which stops the reduction.
steps.fix: Leave it uncovered; reduction is the method.

steps.do: When the sauce has reduced to a few spoonfuls of dark, sticky glaze, add the julienned ginger and black pepper. Cook 3 to 5 minutes more, turning to coat.
steps.look: Large, slow bubbles; the sauce coats the chicken glossily. The fresh ginger smells sharp and bright.
steps.mistake: Reducing until the pan is dry and the sauce burns.
steps.fix: Add 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) water and scrape; you want a glaze, not a crust.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece: 165°F (74°C) minimum, near but not touching the bone; thighs are best at 175°F (79°C).
steps.look: Meat pulls from the bone; juices run clear.
steps.mistake: Undercooking bone-in pieces that look brown outside.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water, cover, and simmer 5 minutes more.

steps.do: Taste the sauce: it should be salty, sweet and faintly bitter, with ginger heat. Adjust with fish sauce or a pinch of sugar. Scatter spring onions and chilli and serve with plenty of rice.
steps.look: Glossy, dark chicken with a sharp ginger finish.
steps.mistake: Serving with too little rice; kho is meant to be salty and eaten with rice.
steps.fix: Serve generous rice and a plain green vegetable.

dishes.science: Sugar passes through stages as it heats. Above about 340°F (170°C) the molecules break apart and recombine into hundreds of new compounds: first buttery and sweet, then, as it darkens towards 375°F (190°C), increasingly bitter and roasted. Vietnamese kho deliberately takes the caramel to the dark end because the bitterness balances the salty fish sauce and gives depth and colour without soy. Fish sauce is fermented anchovy and salt, packed with glutamates that taste deeply savoury. The two ginger additions work differently: smashed ginger simmered long mellows and sweetens, while ginger added at the end keeps its sharp heat because its pungent compounds have not had time to break down.
dishes.plating: Serve in the pot or a warm clay pot on a board, with the pieces piled and glazed and the fresh ginger matchsticks visible on top. Scatter spring onions and chilli. Rice goes in individual bowls; spoon a little glaze over each person’s rice.

pairing.drink: An aromatic, off-dry Alsace Pinot Gris, with enough weight and sweetness for caramel and fish sauce, or a crisp lager.
pairing.brennans: Albert Boxler Pinot Gris 2020: the Alsace Pinot Gris on the list, weighty enough for caramel and fish sauce

variations: Cá kho: the same caramel method with thick catfish steaks, cooked gently 30 minutes.
Thịt kho: pork belly and boiled eggs in caramel and coconut water, simmered 1 1/2 hours.
Boneless version: halved boneless thighs simmered 15 minutes.
safety: Caramel is far hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Never touch or taste it hot, and keep children away from the stove.
Pour fish sauce into hot caramel at arm’s length; it spits violently.
Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).

dishes.title: Chicken Adobo
dishes.summary: The Philippine classic: chicken simmered in vinegar, soy, garlic, bay and black pepper, then browned and returned to its reduced, glossy sauce. Adobo reverses the usual order, simmer first and sear last, and teaches how cooked vinegar softens from sharp to rounded.
equipment: Heavy pot or deep skillet with a lid, about 4 quarts (4 litres), stainless or enamel (not bare aluminium or cast iron, which react with vinegar)
Separate skillet for browning, or a sheet pan under the overhead grill (broiler)

ingredients.item: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks

ingredients.note: Filipino soy if you can find it

mise: Put the chicken in a bowl with the soy, vinegar, garlic, bay and pepper. Turn to coat, cover and refrigerate 30 minutes (or up to overnight).
Crack the peppercorns under a heavy pan or in a mortar so they split but are not powdered.
Start the rice when the chicken goes on to simmer.

timeline.do: Marinate the chicken in the fridge.
Everything into the pot with water; simmer uncovered 10 minutes without stirring.
Cover and simmer 30 minutes, turning once.
Lift out the chicken and brown it. Reduce the sauce.
Chicken back into the glaze.
Serve over rice.

steps.do: Tip the chicken and all of its marinade into the pot, arrange the pieces skin side down in one layer, and add the water. Bring to a boil over medium-high heat.
steps.look: The liquid comes to a lively boil and the sharp smell of vinegar rises.
steps.mistake: Using a reactive pan, which gives a metallic taste.
steps.fix: Use stainless steel or enamel.

steps.do: Lower to a steady simmer and cook uncovered for 10 minutes without stirring.
steps.look: The harsh vinegar smell softens noticeably over the 10 minutes.
steps.mistake: Stirring or covering straight away, which, by Filipino kitchen tradition, traps the raw vinegar taste.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; let the sharpest acidity cook off in the open first.

steps.do: Turn the pieces skin side up, cover with the lid and simmer gently 25 to 30 minutes until tender.
steps.look: The meat is tender and beginning to pull back from the ends of the drumstick bones.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which toughens the chicken.
steps.fix: Keep it at a gentle simmer with small, steady bubbles.

steps.do: Check the thickest piece with the thermometer: at least 165°F (74°C); 175 to 185°F (79 to 85°C) is best for thighs and legs. Lift the chicken onto a plate and pat the skin dry with paper towels.
steps.look: Tender, cooked chicken with pale, soft skin.
steps.mistake: Trying to brown wet skin, which spits and will not crisp.
steps.fix: Pat thoroughly dry.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the skillet over medium-high heat. Brown the chicken skin side down for 3 to 4 minutes until golden and crisp, then 1 minute on the other side. (Or cook skin side up under a hot overhead grill for 4 to 5 minutes.)
steps.look: Deep golden, blistered skin with a loud sizzle. The soy in the skin browns fast.
steps.mistake: Walking away; the soy-soaked skin can burn quickly.
steps.fix: Watch it closely and lower the heat if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: While the chicken browns, raise the heat under the pot and boil the sauce hard for 8 to 10 minutes until reduced by about two thirds. Stir in the brown sugar if using, and taste.
steps.look: The sauce darkens and turns glossy, coating a spoon. It tastes salty, tangy and rounded, with no raw vinegar sting.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so it becomes intensely salty.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water to bring it back.

steps.do: Return the browned chicken to the pot and turn it in the glaze for 1 minute. Fish out the bay leaves.
steps.look: Glossy, dark chicken with crisp edges.
steps.mistake: Simmering again for long, which softens the crisp skin.
steps.fix: One minute is enough to coat.

steps.do: Serve over plenty of rice with the soft garlic cloves and a spoon of sauce, scattered with spring onions.
steps.look: Rice soaking up the dark sauce.
steps.mistake: Too little rice; adobo sauce is meant for rice.
steps.fix: Serve generous rice.

dishes.science: Vinegar is acetic acid in water. When it simmers uncovered, some of the acid and its sharpest volatile compounds evaporate, and the remainder mellows as it combines with the soy and the juices from the chicken. That is why the smell changes so clearly in the first ten minutes. The acid also slightly firms the outside of the meat and helps the dish keep well, which suits a hot kitchen. Simmering first and browning last works because the skin, once rendered by the gentle braise, crisps very quickly in a hot pan, and the soy that soaked into it browns fast through the Maillard reaction.
dishes.plating: Mound rice in a warm shallow bowl and set two pieces of chicken against it, crisp skin up. Spoon the glaze over the chicken and let some run into the rice. Add three or four soft garlic cloves on top and scatter spring onions.

pairing.drink: A Beaujolais cru such as Morgon: juicy acidity to match the vinegar and soft tannins that suit soy and chicken.
pairing.brennans: Marcel Lapierre Morgon 2023: the Morgon on the list, juicy acidity for a vinegar braise

variations: Adobo sa gata: stir in 1/2 cup (120 ml) coconut milk at the end for a creamy, mellower sauce.
Pork adobo: 2 lb (900 g) pork belly or shoulder in 2 inch (5 cm) chunks, simmered 1 hour.
Adobong puti: leave out the soy and use salt, for a pale, sharp adobo.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Marinate in the fridge. The marinade is boiled with the chicken, so it is safe to use as the sauce here.
Browning soy-soaked skin spits: lay pieces away from you.
