dishes.title: Chana Masala
dishes.summary: Chickpeas simmered in a North Indian masala of slowly browned onion, ginger, garlic, tomato and ground spices, cooked until the oil separates from the sauce. That masala base, fried until it releases its oil, is the foundation of a great deal of North Indian cooking.
skills: an onion, ginger and tomato masala cooked until the oil separates
equipment: Heavy pot or deep sauté pan, about 4 quarts (4 litres)
Microplane or mortar for ginger and garlic paste

ingredients.note: drained and rinsed; or 1 1/4 cups (250 g) dried, soaked and cooked
for colour; or 1/2 tsp (1 g) cayenne
finely chopped or grated; or one 14 oz (400 g) can crushed

mise: Chop the onions finely and evenly; uneven pieces brown unevenly.
Grate the ginger and garlic to a paste. Slit the chilli.
Measure the ground coriander, cumin, turmeric and chilli powder into one small bowl, and the garam masala and amchur into another.
Grate the tomatoes on a box grater, discarding the skins, or open the can.
Drain and rinse the chickpeas. Chop the coriander. Start the rice.

timeline.do: Chop, grate and measure everything.
Bloom cumin seeds; brown the onions 12 to 15 minutes.
Ginger, garlic and ground spices; then tomatoes until the oil separates.
Chickpeas and water; simmer 15 minutes, mashing a few.
Garam masala and amchur off the heat.
Coriander on; serve with rice or naan.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium heat. Add the cumin seeds and bay leaf and fry 20 to 30 seconds until the seeds crackle and darken one shade. This is the tadka.
steps.look: The seeds sizzle, pop and smell toasty and nutty.
steps.mistake: Burning the seeds black, which makes the whole dish bitter.
steps.fix: If they go black, wipe out the pot and start again; it costs only 30 seconds.

steps.do: Add the onions and a pinch of the salt. Cook 12 to 15 minutes, stirring every minute or so, until deep golden brown.
steps.look: The onions go from white to translucent to light gold to an even deep gold, and smell sweet and caramel-like.
steps.mistake: Rushing the onions on high heat or stopping at pale; under-browned onions give a thin, sharp masala.
steps.fix: Lower the heat if edges darken before the centres; add a splash of water if they stick.

steps.do: Add the ginger, garlic and green chilli and stir 1 minute until the raw smell disappears.
steps.look: A fragrant steam; the paste turns from bright to pale.
steps.mistake: Burning the garlic paste on the hot base.
steps.fix: Lower the heat slightly before adding.

steps.do: Add the ground spices with 2 tbsp (30 ml) water and stir constantly for 30 to 45 seconds.
steps.look: The spices darken slightly and smell toasted; the water stops them scorching.
steps.mistake: Frying dry ground spices too long, which burns them in seconds.
steps.fix: The splash of water is your insurance; add more if they stick.

steps.do: Add the tomatoes and the rest of the salt. Cook 8 to 12 minutes, stirring and scraping often, until the mixture thickens to a paste, pulls away from the sides of the pan, and the oil separates and glistens at the edges.
steps.look: A thick, glossy, brick red masala with small beads of red oil around the rim and on the surface. It no longer tastes of raw tomato.
steps.mistake: Adding the chickpeas while the tomatoes are still watery; the masala then tastes stewed, not fried.
steps.fix: Keep cooking and stirring. The oil separating is the sign that the water has gone and the masala has fried.

steps.do: Add the chickpeas and water, stir and bring to a simmer. Cook 15 minutes over medium-low heat, stirring now and then. Mash about a quarter of the chickpeas against the side of the pan.
steps.look: The sauce thickens and turns creamy as the mashed chickpeas dissolve into it.
steps.mistake: Adding too much water, giving a thin soup.
steps.fix: Simmer uncovered a little longer to reduce, or mash more chickpeas.

steps.do: Take the pot off the heat. Stir in the garam masala and amchur. Taste and adjust the salt; it should be tangy, warm and savoury.
steps.look: A bright, sour lift in the finish and a warm, aromatic smell.
steps.mistake: Adding garam masala early and cooking out its fragrance.
steps.fix: Always add it at the end.

steps.do: Scatter the coriander, set lemon wedges alongside and serve with rice or warm naan.
steps.look: A thick, glossy curry clinging to the chickpeas.
steps.mistake: Serving it too thin.
steps.fix: Let it stand 5 minutes; it thickens as it sits.

dishes.science: Many flavour compounds in spices are fat soluble, so blooming whole cumin in hot oil, a tadka, releases them into the fat that then carries them through the dish. Browning onions slowly converts their sugars and amino acids into sweet, deep flavours through caramelisation and the Maillard reaction. The masala is ready when the oil separates because, once the water from the tomatoes and onions has evaporated, there is nothing left to hold the fat in suspension; it pools at the edges, and the remaining solids can then fry rather than boil, deepening in flavour. Mashing some chickpeas releases starch that thickens the sauce from within.
dishes.plating: Ladle into a warm bowl, smoothing the top with the back of the ladle. Scatter coriander and a few fine rings of onion or slivers of ginger across one side, and set a lemon wedge on the rim. Serve rice in a separate bowl or naan folded in a basket.

pairing.drink: An aromatic, off-dry white such as Alsace Gewurztraminer or Riesling, or a mango lassi. Sweetness and spice notes in the wine suit garam masala.

variations: Pindi chole: add a tea bag while simmering the chickpeas for a dark colour, and finish with a tadka of ghee and green chilli.
Chana saag: stir in 5 oz (140 g) baby spinach in the last 3 minutes.
Rajma masala: the same base with kidney beans, simmered 25 minutes.
safety: Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat until steaming throughout, 165°F (74°C).
If cooking dried kidney beans for the variation, boil them hard for 10 minutes first to destroy a natural toxin; chickpeas do not need this.

dishes.title: Thai Green Curry with Chicken
dishes.summary: Chicken simmered in a green curry made by frying the paste in cracked coconut cream until the oil separates, then balanced with fish sauce, palm sugar and Thai basil. Frying paste in coconut cream until it splits is the Thai cousin of the Indian masala, and the balance of salty, sweet and hot is a seasoning lesson in itself.
skills: frying curry paste in cracked coconut cream
balancing fish sauce, palm sugar and lime
equipment: Wok or heavy 3 quart (3 litre) saucepan
Can opener and a spoon to scoop the cream

ingredients.note: choose one without stabilisers if you can; it cracks more easily
Thai brands such as Maesri or Mae Ploy; use 3 tbsp (45 g) for milder
sliced 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick, bite sized

ingredients.item: Thai aubergines or 1 small Japanese aubergine
ingredients.note: Thai aubergines quartered, or 1 inch (2.5 cm) pieces

ingredients.item: Palm sugar or light brown sugar

ingredients.note: only if your coconut cream will not split

mise: Open the coconut milk without shaking it. Spoon the thick cream from the top, about 1/2 cup (120 ml), into one bowl and leave the thin milk in the can.
Slice the chicken thin across the grain. Cut the aubergines. Drain the bamboo shoots.
Tear the lime leaves and remove the tough centre rib.
Shave or chop the palm sugar. Pick the basil leaves. Slice the chilli.
Start the rice.

timeline.do: Rice on. Separate the coconut cream; prepare chicken and vegetables.
Crack the coconut cream and fry the paste.
Chicken in, then thin coconut milk, stock, lime leaves, aubergine.
Simmer until chicken and aubergine are tender.
Season with fish sauce and palm sugar; taste and balance.
Basil in off the heat; serve with rice.

steps.do: Put the thick coconut cream in the wok over medium heat. Bring it to a bubble and cook, stirring often, for 3 to 5 minutes until it reduces, turns thick and the oil separates out in clear, shiny pools. This is cracking the cream.
steps.look: The cream bubbles, thickens, then breaks: you see clear oil around white curds and hear a light frying sound instead of a bubble.
steps.mistake: Stopping before it splits, so the paste simmers rather than fries.
steps.fix: Some brands contain stabilisers that stop the oil separating. After 5 minutes, add 1 tbsp (15 ml) neutral oil and carry on.

steps.do: Add the curry paste and fry it in the separated oil for 2 to 3 minutes, stirring and pressing it into the fat.
steps.look: The paste darkens a shade, smells intensely fragrant of lemongrass and chilli, and the oil turns green tinged.
steps.mistake: Rushing this step; raw paste tastes harsh and grassy.
steps.fix: Keep frying until the smell changes from raw to rounded and toasty; lower the heat if it sticks.

steps.do: Add the chicken and stir for 2 minutes until every piece is coated in paste and has turned opaque on the outside.
steps.look: Chicken pieces turning white at the edges, glossy with green paste.
steps.mistake: Adding all the liquid first and poaching the chicken in a bland broth.
steps.fix: Coat the meat in paste first; it seasons the surface.

steps.do: Pour in the thin coconut milk from the can and the stock. Add the lime leaves, aubergine and bamboo shoots. Bring to a gentle simmer.
steps.look: A pale green, oil-flecked curry bubbling gently, the lime leaves giving off a citrus scent.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which can make coconut milk grainy.
steps.fix: Keep a gentle simmer with small bubbles.

steps.do: Simmer 8 to 10 minutes until the aubergine is tender and the chicken is cooked. Check a piece of chicken: 165°F (74°C).
steps.look: Aubergine soft and translucent at the edges; chicken opaque through.
steps.mistake: Overcooking the aubergine into mush.
steps.fix: Thai aubergines need about 8 minutes; check one with a knife.

steps.do: Season with 1 1/2 tbsp (22 ml) fish sauce and the palm sugar. Taste. Green curry should lead with heat and salt, with sweetness behind. Add fish sauce for salt, sugar to round, a few drops at a time.
steps.look: A curry that tastes hot, salty and fragrant with a soft sweet finish.
steps.mistake: Seasoning by measurement alone, without tasting.
steps.fix: Adjust in small amounts and taste between each addition.

steps.do: Take the wok off the heat. Stir in the Thai basil and red chilli; the basil should wilt in the residual heat.
steps.look: Bright green basil just collapsing, with a sweet anise perfume rising.
steps.mistake: Adding basil over the heat and cooking it to a black, limp tangle.
steps.fix: Basil goes in off the heat, at the last moment.

steps.do: Ladle into bowls and serve with jasmine rice on the side.
steps.look: A loose, oil-flecked curry: it should be soupy, not thick.
steps.mistake: Reducing it to a thick gravy.
steps.fix: Thai curries are meant to be spooned over rice; add a splash of stock if it has thickened.

dishes.science: Coconut milk is an emulsion of coconut fat droplets in water, held together by proteins. Heating the thick cream drives off water until those proteins can no longer keep the fat dispersed, and it separates into clear oil and solids, which is the cracking. That oil is what fries the paste. Frying matters because many aromatic compounds in chilli, lemongrass, galangal and shrimp paste dissolve in fat and only develop their full, rounded flavour at frying temperatures well above boiling. Simmer the paste in liquid alone and it stays near 212°F (100°C), tasting raw. Basil goes in last because its fragrant oils, especially the anise-scented ones in Thai basil, evaporate quickly with heat.
dishes.plating: Serve the curry in a deep bowl with a ladle, a few whole basil leaves and chilli slices floating on top and the green-tinged oil glistening on the surface. Rice goes in a separate bowl or moulded in a small cup and turned out on the plate beside a shallow bowl of curry.

pairing.drink: An off-dry Riesling or Gewurztraminer: a little sweetness calms the chilli, and aromatic grapes echo lime leaf and basil. A cold Thai lager also works.
pairing.brennans: Stein ‘Weihwasser’ Riesling Feinherb 2023: the off-dry Riesling on the list, a little sweetness to calm the chilli

variations: Red curry with duck: red paste, sliced roast duck breast, pineapple and cherry tomatoes.
Vegetable green curry: tofu, green beans and courgette, with soy sauce in place of fish sauce.
Green curry with fish balls or shrimp, added for the last 3 minutes only.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C).
Wash hands after slicing fresh chilli and keep them away from your eyes.
Some curry pastes contain shrimp paste: tell guests if they ask what is in the dish.

dishes.title: Maafe (Groundnut Stew)
dishes.summary: A Senegalese and West African stew of beef simmered in tomato and thickened with groundnut paste, with sweet potato, carrot and cabbage, cooked until the peanut oil rises and shines on top. It teaches slow simmering until meat is tender and how to read, and skim, the oil a finished stew releases.
equipment: Heavy pot or Dutch oven, about 5 quarts (5 litres), with a lid
Wooden spoon with a flat edge for scraping the base
Ladle and a shallow spoon for skimming

ingredients.note: cut into 1 1/2 inch (4 cm) cubes; or bone-in lamb shoulder
left whole and unbroken; pierce once for more heat

ingredients.item: Natural peanut butter, smooth and unsweetened

mise: Pat the beef dry and season with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and the pepper.
Chop the onion, mince the garlic and grate the ginger.
Peel and cut the carrots and sweet potato into large, even chunks so they hold their shape in the long simmer. Cut the cabbage into wedges, keeping a little core on each so they stay together.
Warm the stock.
Stir the peanut butter in its jar so the oil is mixed back in before measuring.

timeline.do: Season the beef; cut vegetables.
Brown the beef in batches; soften onion, garlic, ginger; fry the tomato paste.
Tomatoes, stock, bay and Scotch bonnet in; simmer 1 hour partly covered.
Whisk in the peanut butter; add carrots and sweet potato. Simmer uncovered.
Cabbage in. Rice on.
Skim some oil, remove the chilli, taste and serve.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium-high heat until shimmering. Brown the beef in two batches, 3 to 4 minutes per side, without crowding. Lift each batch onto a plate.
steps.look: Deep brown crust on at least two sides of each cube and brown fond on the pot base.
steps.mistake: Crowding all the beef in at once, which steams it grey.
steps.fix: Brown in batches; the colour is flavour for the whole stew.

steps.do: Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion with a pinch of salt and cook 6 to 8 minutes, scraping up the fond, until soft and lightly golden. Add the garlic and ginger and cook 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, golden onion; the fond dissolving into it.
steps.mistake: Leaving the fond to burn while the onions cook.
steps.fix: Add a splash of water to lift it if it darkens too fast.

steps.do: Stir in the tomato paste and fry 2 minutes, stirring constantly.
steps.look: The paste darkens from bright red to a deeper brick red and smells sweet.
steps.mistake: Adding liquid before the paste has fried, leaving a raw tomato taste.
steps.fix: Give it the full 2 minutes, scraping so it does not burn.

steps.do: Add the crushed tomatoes, stock, bay leaves and the whole Scotch bonnet. Return the beef and its juices. Bring to a boil, then lower to a gentle simmer, partly cover and cook 1 hour.
steps.look: Steady small bubbles; the beef starting to soften.
steps.mistake: Breaking the Scotch bonnet, which can make the stew fiercely hot.
steps.fix: Stir gently around the chilli. If it bursts, taste early and add more stock or tomato to dilute.

steps.do: Ladle about 1 cup (240 ml) of hot broth into a bowl with the peanut butter and whisk until smooth and pourable. Stir it back into the pot.
steps.look: A smooth, creamy orange broth with no lumps of peanut butter.
steps.mistake: Adding cold peanut butter straight to the pot, where it forms lumps that scorch on the base.
steps.fix: Whisk it loose first; any lumps left will melt as you stir.

steps.do: Add the carrots and sweet potato. Simmer uncovered over medium-low heat for 35 to 40 minutes, stirring and scraping the base every 5 minutes.
steps.look: The sauce thickens and darkens to a rich reddish brown; the vegetables become tender.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so the peanut sauce catches and burns on the base.
steps.fix: Scrape the bottom often. If it does catch, move the stew to a clean pot without scraping up the burnt layer.

steps.do: Nestle the cabbage wedges into the stew for the last 15 to 20 minutes, spooning sauce over them.
steps.look: Cabbage wedges wilted and tender, holding together.
steps.mistake: Adding cabbage too early, so it disintegrates.
steps.fix: Add it near the end.

steps.do: The stew is done when the beef is fork tender, the sauce clings to a spoon and a layer of reddish oil has risen and shines on the surface. Skim off some of that oil with a shallow spoon if you prefer it lighter, leaving a sheen. Remove the Scotch bonnet and bay leaves.
steps.look: A glossy, thick sauce with beads and a thin layer of red oil on top. The beef breaks apart with a fork.
steps.mistake: Stopping before the oil rises, when the peanut still tastes raw and pasty.
steps.fix: Simmer longer. The oil rising is the sign the peanut has cooked through.

steps.do: Taste and season with salt. Serve over rice with the vegetables arranged around the meat.
steps.look: Rich, savoury, gently hot, nutty but not sweet.
steps.mistake: Undersalting, which leaves peanut stews tasting flat and sweet.
steps.fix: Salt in small additions, tasting each time.

dishes.science: Beef chuck is full of collagen, the tough connective tissue that makes it chewy if cooked quickly. In a long simmer at 180 to 200°F (82 to 93°C), collagen slowly converts to gelatin, which makes the meat tender and gives the sauce body. Peanut butter is about half fat. As the stew simmers, water evaporates and the peanut proteins and starches cook and thicken, until the fat can no longer stay suspended and rises as a red-tinted oil, coloured by the tomato. That separation, like the oil in a finished masala, shows the raw paste has cooked into a sauce. Skimming some is a matter of taste.
dishes.plating: Spoon rice into a wide, shallow bowl, slightly to one side. Ladle the stew beside and over part of the rice, then arrange a piece of sweet potato, a carrot chunk and a cabbage wedge on top so each vegetable shows. Spoon a little of the glossy red oil over the meat. Add a few slices of fresh chilli for those who want it.

pairing.drink: A fruity, medium-bodied red with soft tannins, such as Barbera: its acidity cuts the peanut richness. A ginger beer also suits it.
pairing.brennans: La Miraja ‘Le Masche’ Barbera d’Asti 2023: the Barbera on the list, its acidity cutting the peanut

variations: Chicken maafe: bone-in thighs browned and simmered only 30 minutes before the peanut goes in.
Vegetable maafe: double the sweet potato, add chickpeas and okra, and use vegetable stock.
Lamb maafe: bone-in lamb shoulder, simmered 1 1/2 hours before the peanut.
safety: Peanuts are a common and serious allergen; tell anyone you cook for that the stew is built on them.
Wear gloves to handle cut Scotch bonnet, and never touch your eyes after handling it.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours and reheat to 165°F (74°C).

dishes.title: Beef Fajitas
dishes.summary: Skirt steak marinated in citrus, garlic and cumin, seared hard over the highest heat, rested and sliced thin across the grain, with charred onions and peppers and warm tortillas. Skirt steak teaches the single most important carving rule: always slice across the grain.
equipment: 12 inch (30 cm) cast-iron skillet, griddle or a very hot outdoor grill
Zip-top bag or shallow dish for marinating
Large board with a groove to catch juices
Clean kitchen towel or tortilla warmer
mise: Pull off any shiny silverskin from the steak with a knife tip and your fingers. Cut the steak into pieces about 6 inches (15 cm) long so it fits the pan. Look at the meat and notice the grain: the long fibres run across the width of the strip, not along it.

Whisk the lime and orange juice, 3 tbsp (45 ml) oil, garlic, cumin, chilli powder, soy, salt and pepper. Put the steak and marinade in the bag, press out the air and refrigerate 1 to 4 hours, no longer.
Slice the onion and peppers into strips of even width.
Prepare the pico de gallo, guacamole, sour cream, lime and coriander in small bowls.
Wrap the tortillas in a clean towel ready to warm.

timeline.do: Trim the steak; marinate in the fridge 1 to 4 hours.
Slice the vegetables; set out the toppings.
Heat the cast iron for 8 to 10 minutes. Pat the steak dry.
Sear the steak 2 to 4 minutes a side; rest it.
Char the onions and peppers; warm the tortillas.
Slice across the grain and serve everything at once.

steps.do: Take the steak out of the marinade, scrape off the garlic and pat it very dry with paper towels. Throw the marinade away.
steps.look: Dry, matte surfaces with no pooling liquid.
steps.mistake: Searing wet meat, which steams instead of browning.
steps.fix: Dry it again; the sear depends on it.

steps.do: Heat the cast iron over high heat for 8 to 10 minutes until it smokes faintly. Add 1 tbsp (15 ml) oil and swirl.
steps.look: The oil shimmers and smokes immediately.
steps.mistake: Cooking skirt on a medium pan, so it greys and toughens before it browns.
steps.fix: Wait for the smoke; skirt wants the hottest pan you can make.

steps.do: Lay the steak in, away from you, and sear without moving for 2 to 3 minutes until deeply browned, then turn and sear 2 to 3 minutes more.
steps.look: A loud sizzle, a dark brown crust with some charred spots, and a savoury, slightly smoky smell.
steps.mistake: Moving it around, which stops the crust forming.
steps.fix: Leave it alone; turn only once.

steps.do: Check the thickest part. The USDA safe minimum for whole cuts of beef is 145°F (63°C) followed by a 3 minute rest. Skirt is traditionally served medium-rare, pulled at 125 to 130°F (52 to 54°C) to finish near 135°F (57°C) after resting. Choose the 145°F (63°C) mark for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weakened immune system.
steps.look: The meat feels springy, like the flesh at the base of your thumb when you touch thumb to middle finger, for medium-rare.
steps.mistake: Cooking skirt well done, which makes it tough and chewy.
steps.fix: Pull it a few degrees early; it rises as it rests.

steps.do: Move the steak to the board and rest 5 to 10 minutes, loosely tented with foil.
steps.look: Juices settle; only a little pools on the board.
steps.mistake: Slicing immediately, so the juice floods out.
steps.fix: Use the rest time to cook the vegetables.

steps.do: Add the remaining oil to the hot pan. Add the onion and peppers in an even layer, season with a pinch of salt and cook over high heat for 6 to 8 minutes, tossing only every minute or two, until charred at the edges but still slightly crisp.
steps.look: Blackened edges, softened but not limp strips and a sweet, smoky smell. The browned juices from the steak coat them.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly, which stops them charring.
steps.fix: Let them sit between tosses; cook in two batches if the pan is crowded.

steps.do: Warm the tortillas one at a time in a dry pan over medium heat for 20 to 30 seconds a side until soft and lightly spotted. Stack them in the towel.
steps.look: Soft, pliable tortillas with a few golden spots.
steps.mistake: Serving cold tortillas, which crack when folded.
steps.fix: Keep them wrapped in the towel; they steam and stay soft.

steps.do: Slice the steak: first cut each piece into 5 inch (13 cm) lengths following the grain, then turn each length 90 degrees and slice it across the grain, on a slight angle, into 1/4 inch (6 mm) strips.
steps.look: Each slice shows short fibre ends on its cut face, and the meat is pink and tender.
steps.mistake: Slicing along the grain, which leaves long fibres and chewy strips however well it was cooked.
steps.fix: If a slice feels stringy, turn the knife 90 degrees; you are going with the grain.

steps.do: Serve the steak and vegetables on a hot platter or straight from the skillet with tortillas, pico de gallo, guacamole, sour cream, lime and coriander, and let everyone build their own.
steps.look: A sizzling platter of pink steak and charred vegetables.
steps.mistake: Letting it all go cold while you set the table.
steps.fix: Set the table and toppings before you slice.

dishes.science: Skirt steak comes from the diaphragm, a hard-working muscle with long, coarse fibres running across its width. Those fibres are strong and chewy if you bite along them, but slicing across the grain cuts them into short lengths that your teeth separate easily. The citrus marinade flavours the surface, but acid also begins to break down surface proteins, so beyond four hours the outside turns mushy and grey. Skirt is thin, so it needs extreme heat to brown before the centre overcooks. Resting lets the muscle fibres relax and the juices, which are pushed to the centre by heat, redistribute so they stay in the meat when you slice.
dishes.plating: Bring the cast iron to the table on a board, still sizzling: vegetables in a bed on one side, the sliced steak fanned across the top in overlapping rows so the pink centres show. Scatter coriander and set lime wedges at the edge. Put the toppings in small bowls around it and tortillas in a folded towel.

pairing.drink: A Paloma or a classic margarita, whose lime and salt mirror the marinade, or a juicy Zinfandel with enough fruit for the char.
pairing.brennans: Ridge Vineyards ‘Lytton Springs’ Dry Creek Valley 2021 (375 ml): the Zinfandel blend on the list, ripe fruit for charred steak

variations: Chicken fajitas: boneless thighs in the same marinade, cooked to 165°F (74°C).
Shrimp fajitas: marinate 20 minutes only and sear 1 minute a side.
Portobello fajitas: thick mushroom slices seared hard with the peppers.
safety: The USDA safe minimum for whole beef cuts is 145°F (63°C) with a 3 minute rest; medium-rare is a choice, not the safe standard, for vulnerable diners.
Never reuse marinade that touched raw meat as a sauce unless you boil it for at least 1 minute.
Cast iron stays dangerously hot for a long time; always use a mitt and warn diners if it goes to the table.

dishes.title: Picadillo Cubano
dishes.summary: Cuban picadillo: minced beef browned hard, simmered with a sofrito of onion, pepper and garlic, tomato and dry wine, then balanced with olives, capers, raisins and crisp potato. The sofrito and the balance of salty, sweet and sour make a quick weeknight dish into a lesson in seasoning.

ingredients.item: Minced beef chuck, about 20 percent fat

ingredients.note: peeled, cut in 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) dice

ingredients.item: Green cubanelle or green bell pepper

ingredients.note: mashed to a paste with a pinch of salt
grated, skin discarded; or 1/2 cup (120 ml) tomato sauce

ingredients.item: White rice, black beans and fried sweet plantains

mise: Dice the potato into even 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) cubes, rinse and pat completely dry.
Finely dice the onion and pepper to the same size, about 1/4 inch (6 mm). Mash the garlic.
Grate the tomato. Halve the olives, rinse the capers, measure the raisins.
Keep the beef cold until it goes in the pan, and do not salt it in advance.

timeline.do: Dice the potato and the sofrito vegetables. Rice on.
Fry the potato until golden; lift out.
Brown the beef as one layer; break it up and salt it.
Sofrito into the fat, then cumin and oregano.
Tomato, wine and bay; then olives, capers, raisins.
Vinegar and potatoes in; season and serve.

steps.do: Heat the olive oil in the skillet over medium-high heat until it shimmers. Fry the potato in one layer for 8 to 10 minutes, turning every couple of minutes, until golden on the edges and tender inside. Lift onto paper towels and salt lightly.
steps.look: Golden, crisp-edged cubes; a knife slides in easily.
steps.mistake: Stirring constantly, so they never brown, or crowding them.
steps.fix: Leave them for a minute between turns. Cook in batches if needed.

steps.do: Pour off all but 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the oil. Raise the heat to high. Add the beef and press it into one flat layer across the pan. Leave it completely still for 4 to 5 minutes.
steps.look: A loud sizzle; the underside forms a deep brown crust and releases from the pan on its own.
steps.mistake: Stirring and breaking it up immediately, so the meat greys and stews in its juice.
steps.fix: Resist touching it. If the pan is small, brown in two batches.

steps.do: Turn the beef over in large pieces, then break it into small crumbles with the spoon. Season it now with 1 tsp (6 g) salt and the pepper. Cook 2 minutes more.
steps.look: Brown crumbs with crisp edges, fat rendering out.
steps.mistake: Salting the raw mince in a bowl beforehand, which makes it bind into springy pellets.
steps.fix: Salt in the pan, after browning.

steps.do: Push the beef to one side. Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion and pepper to the cleared space in the rendered fat and cook 5 to 6 minutes until soft and slumped. Add the garlic for 1 minute.
steps.look: Soft, translucent onion and pepper; a sweet, fragrant smell.
steps.mistake: Browning the sofrito hard; it should be soft and sweet.
steps.fix: Lower the heat and stir often.

steps.do: Sprinkle the cumin and oregano over the vegetables and stir them into the fat for 30 seconds, then mix everything together.
steps.look: A toasty, warm smell as the spices bloom.
steps.mistake: Adding the spices with the liquid, where they taste raw.
steps.fix: Bloom them in fat first.

steps.do: Add the grated tomato, wine and bay leaves. Simmer 5 minutes until the liquid reduces and the fat rises and shines on top. Fold in the olives, capers and raisins and cook 8 to 10 minutes more.
steps.look: A thick, glossy mixture with no pool of liquid; raisins plumped.
steps.mistake: Leaving it watery, so it slides off the rice.
steps.fix: Simmer longer, uncovered.

steps.do: Check the temperature: minced beef must reach 160°F (71°C), which it will have passed long ago. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the vinegar and the potatoes.
steps.look: The potatoes stay crisp on the outside.
steps.mistake: Adding the potatoes early, so they turn soft.
steps.fix: Potatoes go in at the very end.

steps.do: Taste and balance: it should land savoury first, then sweet, then sour. Add salt for savoury, a few more raisins for sweet, a splash of vinegar or olive brine for sour. Remove the bay leaves.
steps.look: A lively mix where no single note shouts.
steps.mistake: Seasoning only with salt.
steps.fix: Balance with the brine, raisins and vinegar as well.

dishes.science: Browning minced meat follows the same rule as any sear: the surface must be dry and hot enough, above about 285°F (140°C), for the Maillard reaction. Spread in a still layer, the meat browns; stirred and crowded, it releases water and drops to boiling point, turning grey. Salting raw mince early dissolves the protein myosin, which then binds the meat into a firm, springy mass, perfect for kofta but wrong for loose picadillo. The sofrito sweats gently because onion and pepper turn sweet when their cell walls soften slowly. Balancing salty olives and capers against sweet raisins and sour vinegar works because each taste makes the others clearer.
dishes.plating: Mould white rice in a small bowl and turn it out to one side of a warm plate. Spoon the picadillo beside it in a generous mound, showing the olives and potatoes on top. Add a ladle of black beans in a small dish or on the plate and three slices of fried sweet plantain fanned at the edge.

pairing.drink: A Rioja Crianza, whose red fruit and soft oak suit the cumin and raisins, or a classic daiquiri.
pairing.brennans: López de Heredia ‘Viña Cubillo’ Rioja Crianza 2016: the Rioja Crianza on the list, red fruit for cumin and raisins

variations: Picadillo empanadas: cool the mixture and use it to fill pastry rounds, then bake at 400°F (200°C) for 20 minutes.
Pumpkin picadillo: add diced calabaza in place of potato and simmer until tender.
Mexican style: add chopped tomato, serrano chilli and diced carrot, without olives or raisins.
safety: Minced beef must reach 160°F (71°C).
Fry potatoes dry: water in hot oil spits.
Cool leftovers within 2 hours.

dishes.title: Arroz con Pollo
dishes.summary: Latin American chicken and rice: bone-in chicken browned, a sofrito cooked down with tomato and annatto, the rice toasted in the fat and steamed under a lid with stock, olives and peas. A one-pot rice teaches the liquid ratio and the discipline of leaving the lid alone.
skills: cooking rice with stock and saffron or achiote without stirring
equipment: Wide heavy pot or Dutch oven with a tight lid, about 5 quarts (5 litres) and 11 inches (28 cm) across

ingredients.item: Bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks

ingredients.us: 1 tsp annatto, or a large pinch saffron
ingredients.note: saffron crumbled into 2 tbsp (30 ml) warm stock
plus 2 tbsp (30 ml) of their brine

mise: Pat the chicken dry and season all over with 1 tsp (6 g) salt. Leave at room temperature 20 minutes.
Rinse the rice in the sieve under cold water, swirling, until the water runs nearly clear. Drain well for at least 10 minutes so it is not dripping.
Mince the onion, pepper and garlic finely; grate the tomato.
Heat the stock. If using saffron, crumble it into 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the warm stock.
Measure the wine, olives and brine. Leave the peas in the freezer.

timeline.do: Season the chicken; rinse and drain the rice.
Brown the chicken, skin side first.
Sofrito, tomato and annatto in the same fat until the oil runs orange.
Toast the rice 2 minutes; wine; hot stock and olives; chicken on top.
Lid on, lowest heat, 22 to 25 minutes. Do not lift the lid.
Peas on, lid back, off the heat 10 minutes. Check the chicken. Fluff and serve.

steps.do: Heat the oil in the pot over medium-high heat. Add the chicken skin side down and cook without moving for 7 to 8 minutes until the skin is deep brown and releases by itself. Turn and cook 2 minutes more. Lift onto a plate.
steps.look: Even deep golden skin and brown fond on the pot floor.
steps.mistake: Moving the chicken early, tearing the skin.
steps.fix: Wait until it releases on its own.

steps.do: Pour off all but about 3 tbsp (45 ml) of fat. Lower the heat to medium. Add the onion, pepper and garlic and cook 5 minutes until soft and sweet, scraping up the fond.
steps.look: Translucent, soft vegetables with no hard browning.
steps.mistake: Burning the fond while the vegetables cook.
steps.fix: Add a splash of stock to lift the fond if it darkens.

steps.do: Add the tomato, oregano, bay and annatto (if using saffron, it goes in with the stock). Cook 4 to 5 minutes, stirring, until the mixture darkens and the oil runs orange at the edges.
steps.look: A thick, jammy sofrito with orange oil pooling at the rim.
steps.mistake: Adding the rice to a watery sofrito, which changes the liquid ratio.
steps.fix: Cook until the tomato water has evaporated.

steps.do: Add the drained rice and stir 2 minutes until every grain is coated with fat and the edges turn slightly translucent.
steps.look: Glossy, orange grains; a faint toasty smell; some grains turning chalky white at the tips.
steps.mistake: Adding wet rice, which steams and clumps.
steps.fix: Drain the rice thoroughly; spread it on a towel if needed.

steps.do: Pour in the wine and stir until it boils away, about 1 minute. Add the hot stock (and saffron), olives and brine. Stir once, taste the liquid: it should taste a little saltier than you would like the rice. Add salt if needed.
steps.look: A lively boil; the liquid tastes well seasoned.
steps.mistake: Underseasoning the liquid; rice cannot be seasoned evenly afterwards.
steps.fix: Adjust now, before the lid goes on.

steps.do: Nestle the chicken pieces skin side up on top of the rice, pressing them in slightly, with any juices from the plate. Bring back to a boil, cover tightly and turn the heat to the lowest setting. Cook 22 to 25 minutes without lifting the lid.
steps.look: Steam escaping gently from under the lid; a quiet bubbling sound.
steps.mistake: Lifting the lid to check or stirring the rice, which lets out the steam and leaves the top layer hard and chalky.
steps.fix: Trust the time. If your lid is loose, put a sheet of foil under it.

steps.do: Take the pot off the heat. Lift the lid quickly, scatter the peas over, and replace the lid. Rest 10 minutes.
steps.look: The rice has absorbed all the liquid, with small steam holes on the surface.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, when the rice is wet at the bottom and firm on top.
steps.fix: The rest evens out the moisture; do not skip it.

steps.do: Check the thickest thigh near the bone: at least 165°F (74°C); thighs are best at 175°F (79°C). If a piece is short, put it on a sheet pan in a 375°F (190°C) oven for 5 to 10 minutes while the rice rests.
steps.look: Juices clear, meat pulling from the bone.
steps.mistake: Serving chicken that is pink at the bone.
steps.fix: Always check; the oven rescue costs only minutes.

steps.do: Fluff the rice gently with a fork from the edges inward, lifting rather than stirring. Remove the bay leaves. Garnish with red pepper strips and coriander.
steps.look: Separate, tender, golden grains, each one distinct.
steps.mistake: Stirring with a spoon, which mashes the grains.
steps.fix: Use a fork and a light hand.

dishes.science: Coating rice in hot fat before liquid arrives, the pilaf method, seals the outer starch so water enters more slowly and the grains stay separate instead of turning sticky. Rinsing first removes loose surface starch that would otherwise make the pot gluey. The liquid ratio, about 1 3/4 parts liquid to 1 part rice by volume here, accounts for the wine and tomato and the juice the chicken gives up. Rice cooks in steam as much as in water, so lifting the lid lets the steam escape and the top layer stays hard. During the rest off the heat, moisture moves from the wetter bottom to the drier top, evening out the texture.
dishes.plating: Bring the pot to the table and serve from it, chicken on top, peas and red pepper strips bright against the golden rice. For plates, spoon a mound of rice in the centre, set a thigh and a drumstick against it, and scatter coriander and a few olives.

pairing.drink: A Spanish white such as Albariño, or a light red Garnacha. Both have the freshness for saffron or annatto and enough body for chicken.
pairing.brennans: Pazo das Bruxas Albariño 2025: the Albariño on the list, fresh enough for saffron and chicken

variations: Puerto Rican style: add sofrito made with culantro and ají dulce, and a little sazón with annatto.
Arroz con pollo with beer, a Peruvian style: green rice coloured with puréed coriander and a splash of lager.
Oven method: after adding the stock, cover and bake at 350°F (175°C) for 30 minutes.
safety: Chicken must reach 165°F (74°C) at the thickest point near the bone.

Cooked rice must be cooled quickly and refrigerated within 1 hour of finishing if not eaten, because spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking and multiply at room temperature. Reheat until steaming hot.
Lift lids away from your face.

dishes.title: Shrimp and Grits
dishes.summary: Slow-cooked stone-ground grits enriched with butter and sharp cheddar, crowned with shrimp seared in bacon fat and finished in a quick pan sauce made from their own shells. Grits are a porridge for dinner, and the shrimp pan sauce pulls together the browning, deglazing and butter-mounting lessons of the whole level. It is also a dish your restaurant serves in its own New Orleans way.
equipment: Heavy medium saucepan with a lid, about 3 quarts (3 litres), for the grits
Small saucepan for the shell stock

ingredients.note: 3 tbsp (42 g) for the grits, 2 tbsp (28 g) cold for the sauce
cut into 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) pieces; or 4 oz (115 g) andouille, sliced

mise: Peel and devein the shrimp, keeping the shells. Simmer the shells in the 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) water for 15 minutes, then strain. You should have about 1 cup (240 ml) of stock.
Pat the shrimp dry, season with 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt and the Creole seasoning, and refrigerate.
Grate the cheese. Cut the bacon. Mince the shallot and garlic. Slice the spring onions. Cube the cold butter for the sauce and keep it chilled.
Put the grits in a bowl and cover with water; skim off any husks that float, then drain. This is optional but cleans stone-ground grits.

timeline.do: Peel the shrimp; simmer the shell stock.
Start the grits; stir every 5 minutes for 45 to 50 minutes.
Render the bacon until crisp.
Sear the shrimp in the drippings; lift out underdone.
Finish the grits with butter and cheese. Build the pan sauce.
Shrimp back for 30 seconds; spoon over the grits.

steps.do: Bring the milk, 2 cups (480 ml) water and 1 tsp (6 g) salt to a simmer in the saucepan over medium heat. Pour in the grits in a slow, steady stream, whisking constantly.
steps.look: The grits swirl evenly through the liquid with no clumps.
steps.mistake: Dumping the grits in at once, which forms lumps that stay raw inside.
steps.fix: Whisk hard; break any lumps against the side of the pan.

steps.do: Lower the heat to the lowest setting so the grits barely bubble. Cover and cook 45 to 50 minutes, stirring well every 5 minutes and scraping the bottom and corners. Add hot water 1/4 cup (60 ml) at a time whenever they get too thick.
steps.look: Slow, lazy bubbles that pop like a volcano; the grits thicken, swell and turn creamy.
steps.mistake: Cooking on higher heat to save time, which scorches the bottom and leaves the grains gritty.
steps.fix: Low and slow. If the bottom scorches, do not scrape it up; spoon the top into a clean pan.

steps.do: Taste a spoonful at 45 minutes: the grains should be soft and creamy with no hard bite. Hold the grits covered on the lowest heat.
steps.look: Creamy grits that slowly fall from a spoon, loose but not runny.
steps.mistake: Stopping when they are still sandy and firm.
steps.fix: Give them 10 more minutes and more water.

steps.do: Meanwhile, cook the bacon in the skillet over medium heat for 6 to 8 minutes, stirring, until crisp and the fat has rendered. Lift the bacon out with the slotted spoon onto paper towels, leaving about 2 tbsp (30 ml) fat in the pan.
steps.look: Crisp, golden brown bacon pieces and clear fat in the pan.
steps.mistake: High heat, which burns the bacon before the fat renders.
steps.fix: Lower the heat; rendering is gentle.

steps.do: Raise the heat to medium-high. Add the shrimp in one layer and sear 1 minute until pink underneath, turn and sear 30 seconds more. Lift them onto a plate while still slightly translucent in the centre.
steps.look: Pink, lightly golden shrimp in loose C shapes.
steps.mistake: Cooking them through now, so they turn rubbery in the sauce.
steps.fix: Pull them early; they finish later.

steps.do: Finish the grits: stir in 3 tbsp (42 g) butter and the cheddar until melted. Taste and season. Keep covered.
steps.look: Glossy, golden grits that hold a soft shape on a spoon.
steps.mistake: Adding cheese over high heat, which can make it stringy and oily.
steps.fix: Stir it in off the heat or on the lowest setting.

steps.do: Lower the heat under the skillet to medium. Add the shallot and garlic and stir 30 seconds. Pour in the shell stock and scrape up all the browned bits. Boil 3 to 4 minutes until reduced by half.
steps.look: The stock turns amber and smells richly of shrimp; about 1/2 cup (120 ml) remains.
steps.mistake: Not reducing, so the sauce is thin and weak.
steps.fix: Keep boiling until the volume halves.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Swirl in the cold butter a cube at a time until the sauce turns glossy and slightly thick. Add the lemon juice. Return the shrimp, bacon and any juices and toss over low heat for 30 seconds until the shrimp are just opaque.
steps.look: A glossy sauce coating loose C-shaped, opaque shrimp.
steps.mistake: Boiling after the butter goes in, which splits the sauce.
steps.fix: If it splits, add a spoon of hot grits liquid or water off the heat and swirl.

steps.do: Spoon the grits into warm, shallow bowls. Arrange the shrimp on top, pour the pan sauce over and scatter the spring onions. Pass hot sauce at the table.
steps.look: A golden pool of grits, pink shrimp, glossy sauce running into the grits.
steps.mistake: Letting the grits stand uncovered until a skin forms.
steps.fix: Stir in a splash of hot milk to loosen them just before plating.

dishes.science: Stone-ground grits are coarsely milled whole corn, including some of the germ and bran, so they need a long, slow cook for water to penetrate the hard grains and gelatinise their starch. As starch granules absorb liquid and swell, they release amylose into the liquid, turning it creamy; stirring helps that release and stops the heavy grains settling and scorching. Milk adds body and sweetness. The shell stock is the flavour secret: shrimp shells are full of savoury compounds and the pigment astaxanthin, which gives stock its colour and depth in a quarter of an hour. Mounting the reduced stock with cold butter creates an emulsion that coats the shrimp in a glossy sauce.
dishes.plating: Spoon a generous ladle of grits into a warm shallow bowl and tap the bowl so it settles into a smooth, even pool. Arrange five or six shrimp in a loose ring or a neat cluster in the centre, tails pointing up and in the same direction. Spoon the sauce and bacon over the shrimp so it runs into the grits, then scatter spring onions over the top.

pairing.drink: A rich Chardonnay with gentle oak, whose buttery body matches the grits, or a Brandy Milk Punch for a true New Orleans brunch.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans Shrimp & Grits: Brennan's own version of this dish, worth tasting against yours

variations: With andouille: smoked sausage in place of bacon, the older Lowcountry road.
Creole sauce: add 1 cup (240 ml) chopped tomato, celery and green pepper to the pan before the stock.
Grit cakes: chill leftover grits in a pan, cut into squares and pan-fry until crisp.
safety: Cook shrimp until opaque throughout, about 145°F (63°C).
Simmering grits spit and can burn: stir with a long spoon and keep the lid on between stirs.
Keep shrimp refrigerated until cooking and discard any that smell of ammonia.

dishes.title: Poires à la Beaujolaise
dishes.summary: Whole pears poached at a bare shiver in spiced Beaujolais until they turn deep ruby, then glazed with the poaching wine reduced to a syrup with cassis. Poaching fruit is the gentlest dessert technique, and it teaches the moment a skewer slides into the core with only slight resistance.
skills: reducing the liquor to a syrup
equipment: Saucepan just wide enough to hold 4 pears on their sides, about 3 quarts (3 litres)
Melon baller or small spoon for coring
Parchment paper for a cartouche, and a small plate to weigh it down
Thin metal skewer or cake tester
Small saucepan for reducing the syrup

ingredients.note: pared with a peeler, no white pith

ingredients.item: Crème fraîche or vanilla ice cream

mise: Peel the pears from stalk to base in long, smooth strokes, leaving the stalks on. Rub each one all over with a cut lemon half as you go so it does not brown.
Cut a thin slice off the base of each pear so it stands upright. From the base, scoop out the core with a melon baller or the tip of a small spoon, about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep.
Cut a circle of parchment the size of the pan with a small hole in the centre: this is the cartouche.
Pare the orange zest. Measure the sugar and spices.

timeline.do: Peel and core the pears; make the cartouche.
Dissolve sugar in the wine with the spices.
Pears in; poach at a shiver 20 to 35 minutes, turning once.
Lift out the pears. Reduce the syrup with the cassis.
Cool the syrup slightly; glaze the pears.
Serve warm or chilled with crème fraîche. Better still, poach a day ahead.

steps.do: Put the wine, sugar, cinnamon, orange zest, peppercorns, clove and vanilla in the saucepan. Warm over medium heat, stirring, until every grain of sugar has dissolved; check by running the spoon across the base.
steps.look: A clear, dark red liquid with no grit on the base of the pan.
steps.mistake: Leaving undissolved sugar on the base, where it scorches and makes the syrup bitter.
steps.fix: Keep stirring over gentle heat until the spoon feels smooth across the bottom.

steps.do: Bring to a simmer, then lower the pears in on their sides. They should be almost covered; add a little water if needed.
steps.look: Pears bobbing in the wine, mostly submerged.
steps.mistake: Using too large a pan, so the pears are only half covered and colour unevenly.
steps.fix: Use a smaller pan or add water until they are nearly covered.

steps.do: Lay the cartouche on the surface and set a small plate on top to keep the pears submerged. Lower the heat until the liquid barely shivers: an occasional bubble, never a boil.
steps.look: The surface trembles gently with a few small bubbles at the edge.
steps.mistake: Boiling the pears, which knocks them about, leaches the colour back out and cooks the outside to mush before the core is done.
steps.fix: Turn the heat down or move the pan half off the burner.

steps.do: Poach 20 to 35 minutes depending on ripeness, turning the pears once halfway. Start testing at 20 minutes by sliding the skewer into the thickest part, near the core.
steps.look: The skewer slides in with only slight resistance at the centre, like testing a cooked potato that still holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Overcooking until the pears slump and the skewer falls through, or pulling them while the core is still hard.
steps.fix: Test each pear separately; lift each out as soon as it is ready.

steps.do: Lift the pears out with the slotted spoon and stand them in a shallow dish.
steps.look: Evenly ruby pears that hold their shape.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in while you reduce the syrup, which overcooks them.
steps.fix: Always lift them out before boiling the syrup.

steps.do: Strain out about 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) of the poaching liquid into the small saucepan, add the cassis and boil 8 to 12 minutes until reduced to about 1/2 cup (120 ml) and syrupy. Keep the rest of the liquid for storing the pears.
steps.look: Large, glossy bubbles; the syrup coats the back of a spoon and a drop on a cold plate holds its shape.
steps.mistake: Reducing too far, so it sets hard and sticky as it cools.
steps.fix: Pull it while it still flows; it thickens as it cools. If too thick, add a splash of the poaching liquid.

steps.do: Cool the syrup for 5 minutes, then spoon it over the pears, letting it run down from the stalk, until they shine.
steps.look: A glossy, deep red coat on every pear.
steps.mistake: Pouring very hot syrup that runs straight off.
steps.fix: Let it cool slightly so it clings.

steps.do: Serve warm, or for the best colour, put the pears back in the remaining poaching liquid, cool, cover and refrigerate overnight; the colour travels deeper inside. Glaze again before serving and add a spoon of crème fraîche.
steps.look: Overnight pears are deep ruby right to the core when sliced.
steps.mistake: Serving straight away when the colour is still only skin deep, if you have time to wait.
steps.fix: Poach a day ahead whenever you can.

dishes.science: Poaching cooks fruit gently in a liquid held below boiling, around 175 to 185°F (80 to 85°C), so the pectin that glues the pear cells together softens slowly and evenly without the fruit falling apart. The sugar matters as much as the heat. A syrup of about a fifth sugar by weight balances the sugar inside the fruit, so water is not drawn out of the pear into the liquid; too weak a syrup and the flesh turns woolly. The red colour comes from anthocyanins in the wine, which seep into the flesh over time; boiling knocks them back out, while an overnight rest in the cooled liquid carries them deeper.
dishes.plating: Stand each pear upright on a chilled shallow plate, slightly off centre. Spoon the glossy syrup over the top so it runs down and pools around the base. Add a neat quenelle of crème fraîche beside it, shaped between two spoons, and a thin crisp biscuit or a sprig of mint at the stalk.

pairing.drink: A glass of the same young Beaujolais, lightly chilled, or a fortified Banyuls whose red fruit and warmth echo the spiced wine.
pairing.brennans: Louis Jadot Beaujolais-Villages 2021 (375 ml): the Gamay on the list, the same grape as the poaching wine

variations: Pears in white wine with vanilla and lemon for a pale, golden version.
Pears poached in port with star anise.
Peaches poached in rosé for summer, peeled after poaching.
safety: The reduced syrup is very hot and sticky; never taste it straight from the pan.
Peel away from your hand, and keep the peeler at a shallow angle.

dishes.title: Lemon Posset with Shortbread Fingers
dishes.summary: A British dessert of cream boiled with sugar and set by lemon juice alone, served with crisp shortbread fingers. Three ingredients set by acid sit beside a shortbread that teaches the first pastry skill, rubbing cold butter into flour.
equipment: Heavy medium saucepan, at least 2 quarts (2 litres), because boiling cream rises
Four small glasses or ramekins, about 5 oz (150 ml) each
8.5 x 4.5 inch (21 x 11 cm) loaf tin, lined with parchment

ingredients.item: Heavy (double) cream, at least 36 percent fat

ingredients.note: zest of 1, then 1/4 cup (60 ml) strained juice
cold, cut in 1/2 inch (1 cm) cubes

mise: Zest one lemon finely, avoiding the bitter white pith. Juice both and strain the juice; measure 1/4 cup (60 ml).
Set the glasses on a small tray that fits in the fridge.
Cube the butter and keep it cold. Line the loaf tin. Heat the oven to 300°F (150°C) when you start the shortbread.

timeline.do: Zest and juice the lemons; boil the cream 3 minutes.
Lemon in off the heat; stand 10 minutes; strain into glasses.
Chill at least 4 hours.
Rub in and bake the shortbread 35 to 40 minutes.
Cut while hot; cool in the tin.
Serve the possets cold with the shortbread.

steps.do: Put the cream, sugar and lemon zest in the saucepan. Bring to the boil over medium heat, stirring so the sugar dissolves.
steps.look: The cream rises in the pan with large bubbles.
steps.mistake: Using a small pan, so the cream boils over.
steps.fix: Use a tall pan, at least four times the volume of the cream, and stay with it.

steps.do: Once boiling, lower the heat just enough to stop it rising over, and keep it at a rolling boil for 3 minutes, stirring constantly.
steps.look: A steady boil; the cream thickens very slightly and coats the spoon more heavily.
steps.mistake: Pulling it off as soon as it boils; without the 3 minutes it may not set firmly.
steps.fix: Time it: 3 full minutes.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the lemon juice.
steps.look: The cream thickens noticeably within seconds as the acid works.
steps.mistake: Adding the lemon while it is still on a hard boil, which can make it grainy.
steps.fix: Always off the heat.

steps.do: Leave the mixture to stand 10 minutes, then pour it through the fine sieve into the jug to remove the zest.
steps.look: A smooth, pale yellow cream, slightly thickened.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, leaving zest strands in the set cream.
steps.fix: Always strain for a silky set.

steps.do: Pour into the glasses, leaving 1/2 inch (1 cm) at the top. Cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 4 hours, uncovered for the first hour, then covered.
steps.look: After chilling, the surface is glossy and the posset holds when you tilt the glass.
steps.mistake: Moving the glasses while setting, which wrinkles the surface.
steps.fix: Set them somewhere they will not be disturbed.

steps.do: For the shortbread, mix both flours, the sugar and salt in the bowl. Add the cold butter and rub it in with your fingertips, lifting the mixture and letting it fall, until it looks like fine breadcrumbs with no large pieces of butter.
steps.look: Even, sandy crumbs that hold together when squeezed in your fist.
steps.mistake: Using warm palms instead of cool fingertips, so the butter melts and turns greasy.
steps.fix: If it turns greasy, chill the bowl 10 minutes and continue.

steps.do: Tip the crumbs into the lined loaf tin and press firmly and evenly with the back of a spoon. Mark into 8 fingers with a knife and prick each finger twice with a fork.
steps.look: A flat, even layer about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.mistake: Pressing unevenly, so the thin parts burn.
steps.fix: Level it with the flat bottom of a glass.

steps.do: Bake at 300°F (150°C) for 35 to 40 minutes until an even pale sand colour, firm at the edges.
steps.look: A uniform pale gold; the kitchen smells of butter.
steps.mistake: Baking hotter to save time, which browns the edges while the centre stays raw.
steps.fix: Low and slow; shortbread should be pale.

steps.do: Sprinkle with the extra sugar, cut along the marks while hot, and cool completely in the tin. Lift out by the parchment.
steps.look: Clean, crisp fingers that snap.
steps.mistake: Cutting cold, which shatters the shortbread.
steps.fix: Cut while warm.

steps.do: Serve the possets cold with two shortbread fingers each and a few raspberries on top.
steps.look: A spoon glides into a smooth, tangy, rich cream.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from a long time at room temperature, when it softens.
steps.fix: Keep them chilled until the last minute.

dishes.science: Posset sets with no gelatine or egg. Boiling the cream drives off some water and concentrates the fat and milk proteins. When lemon juice is added, its acid lowers the pH, and the casein proteins in the cream, which normally stay dispersed, lose their negative charges and begin to cling to one another, forming a soft network that traps the fat as it cools. That only works with high-fat cream; below about 36 percent fat there is too little structure, and the result stays liquid. Shortbread depends on cold fat: rubbed into flour, butter coats the starch and limits gluten, so the result is crumbly and short rather than chewy.
dishes.plating: Set each glass on a small plate lined with a folded napkin. Lay two shortbread fingers crossed beside the glass, and place three raspberries and a tiny strip of lemon zest on top of the posset. Wipe the rim of the glass clean.

pairing.drink: A late-harvest Sauternes, whose honeyed sweetness and acidity match lemon and cream.
pairing.brennans: Château Suduiraut Sauternes 2016 (375 ml): the Sauternes on the list, honeyed acidity for lemon and cream

variations: Lime posset with a coconut shortbread.
Orange and cardamom posset: half orange juice, half lemon, with 2 crushed cardamom pods in the cream.
Posset served in hollowed lemon halves.
safety: Boiling cream foams up suddenly and causes serious burns: use a tall pan and stay with it.
Keep the possets refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

dishes.title: Panna Cotta
dishes.summary: Italian cooked cream set with the least gelatine that will still hold, perfumed with vanilla and turned out so it trembles on the plate. Gelatine is measured to the gram here because the goal is the softest set that still stands.
skills: unmoulding a set cream with a tremble
equipment: Four 5 oz (150 ml) ramekins, dariole moulds or glasses
Thin knife and a bowl of hot water for unmoulding

ingredients.note: or 3 sheets of silver-grade leaf gelatine, about 7.5 g, which sets to roughly the same strength
split and scraped; or 1 tsp (5 ml) vanilla bean paste
to grease the moulds, if unmoulding

mise: Weigh the gelatine. Sprinkle powdered gelatine evenly over the cold water in a small bowl and leave 5 to 10 minutes until it swells into a firm, spongy mass. If using sheets, soak them in a bowl of cold water for 5 minutes until floppy, then squeeze out the water.
Wipe the inside of each mould with a very thin film of oil on a paper towel if you plan to unmould. Set them on a small tray.
Split the vanilla bean and scrape out the seeds.
Toss the berries with the sugar and lemon juice and leave them to macerate in the fridge.

timeline.do: Weigh and bloom the gelatine; oil the moulds.
Warm the cream, milk, sugar and vanilla to steaming.
Gelatine in off the heat; strain; cool, stirring.
Pour into moulds; chill at least 5 hours.
Unmould onto chilled plates.
Berries beside; serve.

steps.do: Put the cream, milk, sugar, vanilla seeds and pod and salt in the saucepan. Warm over medium heat, stirring, until steaming and small bubbles appear at the edge, about 180°F (82°C). Do not boil.
steps.look: Wisps of steam and tiny bubbles around the rim; the sugar fully dissolved.
steps.mistake: Boiling the cream, which gives a cooked taste and a skin.
steps.fix: Pull it off the heat at the first bubbles at the edge.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Add the bloomed gelatine and whisk for 1 minute until completely dissolved.
steps.look: No granules or clear strands visible when you lift the whisk; the liquid is smooth.
steps.mistake: Adding gelatine to boiling liquid, which weakens its set, or not dissolving it fully, leaving rubbery lumps.
steps.fix: If you see granules, warm gently for 30 seconds while whisking, never boiling.

steps.do: Pour through the fine sieve into the jug. Remove the vanilla pod.
steps.look: Smooth, speckled cream with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve.
steps.fix: Always strain.

steps.do: Leave the jug to cool for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring every few minutes, until it is just warm and slightly thickened, about 75°F (24°C). This keeps the vanilla seeds suspended.
steps.look: The cream coats the back of a spoon slightly more thickly and the seeds stay spread through it.
steps.mistake: Pouring it hot, so the seeds sink and the fat rises, leaving a waxy layer on what becomes the base.
steps.fix: Stir until it cools; you can set the jug in a bowl of iced water to speed it up, stirring constantly.

steps.do: Stir once more and pour into the moulds. Cover with plastic wrap without touching the surface and refrigerate at least 5 hours, or overnight.
steps.look: A smooth, flat surface with seeds evenly spread.
steps.mistake: Moving the tray around while it sets.
steps.fix: Find a level, quiet spot in the fridge.

steps.do: To test the set, tilt a mould: the panna cotta should come away slightly from the side and wobble as one piece.
steps.look: A gentle tremble across the whole surface, like a soft jelly.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding too early, so it collapses.
steps.fix: Give it another hour.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin knife around the very top edge to break the seal. Dip the mould in hot water up to the rim for 3 to 5 seconds. Lay a chilled plate upside down on top, hold both firmly and turn over with one decisive shake. Lift the mould.
steps.look: It slides free with sharp edges and trembles on the plate.
steps.mistake: Dipping too long, so the outside melts into a puddle.
steps.fix: If it will not release, dip for 2 more seconds. If the surface is melted, return it to the fridge for 15 minutes to firm.

steps.do: Spoon the macerated berries and their juice beside the panna cotta and serve chilled.
steps.look: The panna cotta keeps trembling when the plate is moved.
steps.mistake: Leaving it on a warm plate for a long time.
steps.fix: Unmould onto chilled plates just before serving.

dishes.science: Gelatine is collagen extracted from animal tissue. Bloomed in cold water, its protein strands absorb water and swell; heated, they unwind and disperse; cooled, they reconnect into a mesh that traps liquid as a gel. The set depends on concentration. Around 1 percent of the liquid weight, as here with 5 g in about 500 g of cream and milk, gives a gel that just holds its shape and melts at body temperature, which is why panna cotta dissolves on the tongue. More gelatine makes it rubbery. Boiling damages the gelatine strands and weakens the set. Pouring the cream cool and slightly thickened keeps the vanilla seeds and fat evenly distributed.
dishes.plating: Turn the panna cotta out slightly off centre on a chilled white plate. Spoon a small pile of berries to one side with a drizzle of their juice running towards it, and set one perfect berry and a tiny mint leaf on top. Leave space on the plate so the tremble is the star.

pairing.drink: A Moscato d’Asti, gently sparkling and lightly sweet, or a Vouvray demi-sec whose honeyed acidity lifts the cream.
pairing.brennans: Domaine Huet ‘Le Mont’ Vouvray Demi-Sec 2023 (375 ml): the Vouvray demi-sec on the list, honeyed acidity to lift the cream

variations: Buttermilk panna cotta: replace the milk with buttermilk, stirred in once the cream has cooled.
Coffee panna cotta with a shot of espresso in the cream.
Agar version: 1/2 tsp (1.5 g) agar powder boiled with the cream for 2 minutes; it sets firmer and at room temperature.
safety: Keep panna cotta refrigerated and eat within 3 days.
Gelatine is made from animal collagen; tell guests if they ask.

dishes.title: Ginger Milk Curd
dishes.summary: A Cantonese pudding of hot sweetened milk poured onto fresh ginger juice, which sets in minutes into a silky curd with no gelatine or egg. An enzyme in ginger does the setting, so the lesson is that temperature, not time, decides whether it works.
skills: heating milk to the right temperature
equipment: Clean muslin, cheesecloth or a thin kitchen towel for squeezing
Four small heatproof bowls, about 5 oz (150 ml) each

ingredients.note: old, knobbly ginger with tan skin; young ginger has too little enzyme

ingredients.item: Whole milk, at least 3.5 percent fat
ingredients.note: not ultra-pasteurised (UHT) if you can avoid it

mise: Scrub the ginger and grate it finely, skin and all, on the Microplane.
Gather the pulp in the muslin and squeeze hard over a bowl to collect about 1/4 cup (60 ml) of juice. Let it stand 1 minute; a white starch will settle at the bottom.
Set the four bowls on a tray where they can sit undisturbed.
Spoon 1 tbsp (15 ml) of juice into each bowl, stirring the juice first so each gets some of the settled starch.

timeline.do: Grate and squeeze the ginger; portion the juice.
Heat the milk with sugar to 167°F (75°C).
Cool to 158 to 167°F (70 to 75°C); stir the juice; pour from a height.
Leave untouched 10 minutes to set.
Test with a tilt.
Serve warm.

steps.do: Heat the milk and sugar in the saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring, until the sugar dissolves and the thermometer reads 167°F (75°C).
steps.look: The milk steams and the surface shivers, but not a single bubble breaks.
steps.mistake: Boiling the milk, which is too hot and destroys the enzyme.
steps.fix: If it boils, let it cool back down to the target range; it will still work once in range.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and pour the milk into the jug. Check the temperature: you want 158 to 167°F (70 to 75°C) at the moment of pouring.
steps.look: The thermometer settles in the range.
steps.mistake: Pouring too hot (above about 176°F, 80°C), which kills the enzyme, or too cool (below about 149°F, 65°C), when the enzyme works too slowly to set.
steps.fix: Wait a minute if too hot; warm gently if too cool.

steps.do: Stir the ginger juice in the first bowl so the settled white starch is lifted back into it.
steps.look: Cloudy, evenly mixed juice.
steps.mistake: Leaving the starch on the bottom; it carries much of the enzyme.
steps.fix: Stir each bowl just before you pour into it.

steps.do: Hold the jug about 8 inches (20 cm) above the bowl and pour 1/3 cup (100 ml) of milk in one quick, steady stream so it lands hard in the centre and mixes itself with the juice.
steps.look: The milk swirls vigorously in the bowl and settles.
steps.mistake: Pouring slowly from close up, which does not mix the juice in, or pouring in two goes.
steps.fix: One confident pour per bowl, then move to the next.

steps.do: Repeat with the other bowls, stirring each juice before pouring. Do not stir after pouring, and do not move the bowls.
steps.look: A still, smooth surface in each bowl.
steps.mistake: Stirring or jostling the bowls, which breaks the forming gel so it never sets.
steps.fix: Leave them completely alone.

steps.do: Wait 10 minutes. Test by tilting one bowl to about 45 degrees.
steps.look: The surface holds firm and does not flow; a spoon pressed on it leaves a dent, like soft tofu.
steps.mistake: Testing too early and disturbing the set.
steps.fix: If it is still liquid after 15 minutes, the milk was the wrong temperature or the ginger was too young; note it and try again with older ginger.

steps.do: Serve warm, as it is traditionally eaten, with a spoon. A few drops of whey may appear around the edge; that is normal.
steps.look: A silky, quivering curd with a warm, spicy ginger bite.
steps.mistake: Chilling it, which makes it weep more whey.
steps.fix: Eat within the hour.

dishes.science: Ginger contains a protease, a protein-cutting enzyme called zingibain, which acts on milk the way rennet does in cheesemaking. Milk’s casein proteins float in clusters protected by a hairy outer layer of kappa-casein. The enzyme snips off that outer layer, and the bared clusters stick together into a gel that traps the milk. Enzymes are proteins with a working temperature: zingibain works fastest at around 140 to 160°F (60 to 70°C) and is destroyed above roughly 176°F (80°C). Below about 149°F (65°C) it works too slowly to set the milk before it cools. That is why the thermometer is the most important tool in this recipe.
dishes.plating: Serve in the bowl it set in, on a small saucer with a spoon. Do not garnish heavily: one thin sliver of candied ginger or a tiny pinch of finely grated fresh ginger on the centre is enough, so the smooth surface stays the focus.

pairing.drink: A cup of hot jasmine or oolong tea, the classic partner, or a light, sweet Moscato.

variations: Double-skin milk pudding: a steamed milk and egg white pudding, another Cantonese classic.
Ginger curd with brown sugar syrup drizzled over at the table.
Pineapple and kiwi also contain proteases; compare how they react with milk as an experiment, not a dessert.
safety: Hot milk scalds: pour carefully and keep hands clear of the stream.
Use pasteurised milk.

dishes.title: Muhallabia
dishes.summary: A Levantine milk pudding thickened with cornstarch and ground rice, perfumed with rose water and mastic and scattered with pistachios. A starch-thickened pudding shows that cornstarch must truly boil to thicken and lose its raw, chalky taste.
skills: perfuming with rose or orange blossom
equipment: Balloon whisk and a heatproof spatula
Four small bowls or glasses, about 5 oz (150 ml) each

ingredients.note: optional; sold at Middle Eastern grocers

mise: Freeze the mastic tears for 15 minutes, then grind them in the mortar with 1 tsp (4 g) of the sugar to a fine powder. Cold resin grinds cleanly; warm resin gums up.
In a small bowl, whisk the cornstarch and ground rice into 1/2 cup (120 ml) of the cold milk until completely smooth, with not one lump.
Chop the pistachios finely. Set out the bowls.

timeline.do: Grind the mastic; make the slurry.
Bring the remaining milk and sugar to a bare simmer.
Whisk in the slurry; cook, stirring, until it bubbles and thickens, about 6 minutes.
Off the heat: mastic and rose water; pour into bowls at once.
Chill 3 hours.
Pistachios and rose petals on top; serve.

steps.do: Pour the remaining 1 1/2 cups (360 ml) milk and the rest of the sugar into the saucepan and bring to a bare simmer over medium heat, stirring so the sugar dissolves and nothing catches.
steps.look: Steam and small bubbles at the edge of the pan.
steps.mistake: Leaving it unstirred, so the milk catches on the base.
steps.fix: Stir often across the bottom.

steps.do: Whisk the slurry once more (the starch settles fast), then pour it into the hot milk in a thin stream, whisking hard and continuously.
steps.look: The milk turns slightly cloudy and begins to thicken almost at once.
steps.mistake: Adding the slurry without restirring, so a lump of starch drops to the bottom.
steps.fix: Whisk any lumps out at once; if they persist, strain the pudding before pouring into bowls.

steps.do: Cook over medium-low heat, stirring constantly with the whisk or spatula, reaching into the corners, for about 6 minutes, until it thickens and one or two slow bubbles heave up and pop on the surface.
steps.look: Thick enough to coat the back of a spoon heavily; a finger drawn across it leaves a clean line. Slow, thick bubbles break the surface.
steps.mistake: Stopping when it first thickens, before it bubbles. It will taste chalky and loosen in the fridge.
steps.fix: Keep stirring until the slow bubbles appear, then cook 1 minute more.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat. Stir in the mastic sugar and the rose water.
steps.look: A floral, resinous perfume rises.
steps.mistake: Adding rose water during boiling, which drives off its scent.
steps.fix: Add flavourings off the heat.

steps.do: Pour immediately into the bowls while it still flows. Tap each bowl on the counter to level the surface.
steps.look: Smooth, glossy surfaces.
steps.mistake: Waiting, so it begins to set in the pan and has to be spooned out in lumps.
steps.fix: Pour at once. Never stir it once it has started to set.

steps.do: Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface of each to stop a skin forming, or leave uncovered if you like the skin. Cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 3 hours.
steps.look: Set firm with a gentle wobble.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uncovered in the fridge, where it absorbs other smells.
steps.fix: Cover once cool.

steps.do: Just before serving, scatter the chopped pistachios and rose petals over the top.
steps.look: Bright green pistachios on a white pudding.
steps.mistake: Adding nuts too early, which soften.
steps.fix: Garnish at the last moment.

dishes.science: Cornstarch is made of tightly packed starch granules. In cold milk they simply float, which is why the slurry is made cold: added dry to hot milk, the outsides would swell instantly into lumps around dry centres. As the milk heats, the granules absorb water and swell, and they burst and release their starch molecules only near boiling, around 194 to 203°F (90 to 95°C). That burst gives full thickening and removes the raw taste. Stop at a mere simmer and the granules stay partly intact, the pudding tastes chalky, and its structure is weak. Once set, the starch network is fragile; stirring breaks it permanently, so it is poured while still fluid.
dishes.plating: Serve chilled in the bowls it set in. Scatter the pistachios in a neat crescent across one side rather than all over, add a few rose petals beside them and a single drop of rose water in the centre if you like.

pairing.drink: A cup of mint tea, or a late-harvest Gewurztraminer whose rose and lychee scents echo the rose water.
pairing.brennans: Trimbach Gewurztraminer Vendanges Tardives 2007: the late-harvest Gewurztraminer on the list, rose scented like the pudding

variations: Orange blossom muhallabia topped with a spoon of orange syrup.
Muhallabia with apricot: top with apricots poached in syrup.
Chocolate version: whisk 1 oz (30 g) chopped dark chocolate into the hot pudding.
safety: Thickening starch puddings spit as they bubble: stir with a long-handled spoon and keep your hand back.
Pistachios are a tree nut: tell guests.
