dishes.title: Tembleque
dishes.summary: A Puerto Rican coconut pudding thickened with cornstarch, cooked until it truly bubbles, set in a mould and turned out under a heavy dusting of cinnamon. It repeats the starch set of muhallabia with coconut milk in place of cow’s milk, and adds unmoulding a whole pudding.
skills: a coconut milk and cornstarch pudding
equipment: 2 cup (500 ml) mould or four 4 oz (125 ml) ramekins
mise: Shake the can well and pour out 1/2 cup (120 ml) into a bowl. Whisk in the cornstarch and salt until no grain is left on the bottom of the bowl.
Rinse the mould or ramekins with cold water and shake out the excess, leaving them wet. A wet mould releases cleanly.
Have the plastic wrap and a spatula ready by the stove.

timeline.do: Slurry made; mould wetted.
Heat the rest of the coconut milk with sugar and cinnamon to steaming.
Slurry in; stir constantly until it bubbles and holds a furrow for a full minute.
Into the wet mould; cover the surface.
Chill at least 4 hours.
Unmould and dust heavily with cinnamon.

steps.do: Pour the remaining coconut milk into the saucepan with the sugar and cinnamon stick. Heat over medium heat, stirring, until it steams and the sugar dissolves. Remove the cinnamon stick.
steps.look: Steam rising, fine bubbles at the edge, a warm cinnamon scent.
steps.mistake: Letting it boil hard, which can make the coconut fat separate.
steps.fix: Keep it just below a simmer.

steps.do: Whisk the slurry again and pour it into the pan in a thin stream, whisking constantly.
steps.look: The mixture begins to thicken within a minute.
steps.mistake: Pouring without whisking, which forms lumps.
steps.fix: Whisk hard; a few small lumps will smooth out as you stir.

steps.do: Switch to the spatula and stir constantly over medium-low heat, reaching into the corners of the pan, until the pudding is very thick. Keep going until slow bubbles burst through the surface.
steps.look: Thick, glossy pudding with large, slow bubbles popping like a volcano.
steps.mistake: Pulling it off at the first thickening; it tastes chalky and slumps when unmoulded.
steps.fix: Keep cooking until the bubbles come.

steps.do: Hold it at that slow bubble for 1 more minute, stirring. Drag the spatula through the centre: the furrow should hold its shape.
steps.look: A clean furrow that stays open; the pudding pulls away from the sides of the pan.
steps.mistake: Stopping stirring, so the coconut fat settles and scorches on the base.
steps.fix: Stir right into the corners the whole time.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat and stir in the vanilla. Pour immediately into the wet mould and smooth the top with the spatula.
steps.look: A level, glossy surface.
steps.mistake: Waiting, so it sets in the pan.
steps.fix: Pour at once.

steps.do: Press plastic wrap directly onto the surface. Cool 20 minutes, then refrigerate at least 4 hours.
steps.look: After chilling, the pudding is firm and pulls slightly from the edges of the mould when tilted.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding too early.
steps.fix: If it still feels soft in the centre, chill another hour.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin wet knife around the edge. Set the serving plate upside down on top, hold both together and turn over with a firm shake. Lift the mould.
steps.look: The tembleque slides out in one piece and wobbles: its name comes from the Spanish word for trembling.
steps.mistake: Not wetting the mould or the knife, so it sticks and tears.
steps.fix: If it sticks, dip the mould in warm water for 5 seconds and try again.

steps.do: Dust heavily and evenly with ground cinnamon through a small sieve. Serve chilled, cut into wedges or spooned.
steps.look: A smooth white pudding under a russet blanket of cinnamon.
steps.mistake: Dusting hours ahead, which turns the cinnamon damp and patchy.
steps.fix: Dust just before serving.

dishes.science: Like muhallabia, tembleque relies on cornstarch granules swelling and bursting as the liquid nears boiling, around 194 to 203°F (90 to 95°C). That is when the starch molecules spill out and form a network strong enough to hold a moulded shape after chilling. Coconut milk complicates it: its fat separates and settles when heated, and fat on the pan base scorches quickly, so constant stirring is essential. Stopping at the first thickening leaves granules unburst, so the pudding tastes floury and slumps. A wet mould leaves a thin film of water between pudding and mould so it slides free instead of bonding to the surface.
dishes.plating: Turn the tembleque out onto a flat white plate, dust it with cinnamon so the top is evenly covered, and cut it at the table into wedges. For individual moulds, set each slightly off centre, dust with cinnamon and add a few toasted coconut flakes or a slice of fresh mango beside it.

pairing.drink: A small glass of aged rum, or a coquito-style coconut and rum drink served very cold.

variations: Tembleque with orange blossom water and a little orange zest.
Mango tembleque: replace a third of the coconut milk with smooth mango purée.
Layered with toasted coconut and a passion fruit topping.
safety: Bubbling starch pudding spits and sticks to skin: stir with a long spatula and keep your forearm back.
Keep refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

dishes.title: Kheer
dishes.summary: Indian rice pudding: basmati simmered slowly in a large volume of milk until it reduces and thickens, sweetened at the end and scented with cardamom and saffron. It brings the slow grain simmer to dessert, with milk that must never be allowed to catch on the pan.
equipment: Heavy, wide saucepan, at least 4 quarts (4 litres), so the milk can reduce without boiling over
Heatproof spatula with a flat edge

ingredients.note: plus a splash more to loosen
optional, for frying the nuts and raisins

mise: Rinse the rice in the sieve until the water runs clear, then soak it in cold water for 20 minutes and drain. Crush it lightly between your fingers into broken grains if you like a thicker kheer.
Crush the cardamom pods, remove the seeds and grind them fine.
Crumble the saffron into the 1 tbsp (15 ml) warm milk and leave to steep.
Sliver the nuts.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice; steep the saffron.
Bring the milk to a boil; add rice; simmer, stirring and scraping, about 35 to 40 minutes.
Sugar in; cook 5 minutes more.
Cardamom, saffron milk, most of the nuts.
Serve warm, or chill for at least 2 hours.

steps.do: Rinse the saucepan with cold water and leave a film of water in it: this helps stop the milk sticking. Pour in the milk and bring it to a boil over medium heat, stirring often.
steps.look: The milk froths up as it reaches the boil.
steps.mistake: Walking away; milk boils over in seconds.
steps.fix: Lower the heat the moment it rises and stir it down.

steps.do: Add the drained rice. Lower the heat so the milk simmers gently with steady small bubbles.
steps.look: A gentle, rolling simmer with a thin skin forming and being stirred back in.
steps.mistake: Simmering too hard, which scorches the milk solids on the base.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to the point where the bubbles barely break.

steps.do: Simmer 35 to 40 minutes, stirring every 2 to 3 minutes and scraping the base and sides with the spatula. Scrape the creamy deposits from the sides of the pan back into the milk; they add flavour.
steps.look: The milk reduces by about half, turns ivory and creamy, and the rice grains swell and soften.
steps.mistake: Letting the milk catch and burn on the base, which gives the whole pudding a scorched taste.
steps.fix: Stir often across the base. If it catches, pour into a clean pan without scraping the burnt layer.

steps.do: Check the rice by crushing a grain between your fingers.
steps.look: The grain squashes completely with no hard centre.
steps.mistake: Adding sugar before the rice is fully soft.
steps.fix: Keep simmering until it is tender.

steps.do: Stir in the sugar and cook 5 minutes more, stirring constantly.
steps.look: The kheer loosens slightly as the sugar melts, then thickens again.
steps.mistake: Adding sugar too early, which slows the rice softening.
steps.fix: Sugar goes in only once the rice is soft.

steps.do: Test the thickness: drag a spoon through it. It should leave a trail that slowly closes.
steps.look: A thick, creamy pudding, loose enough to pour slowly.
steps.mistake: Over-reducing, so it turns stiff, especially once cooled.
steps.fix: Add a splash of milk; kheer thickens a lot as it cools.

steps.do: Take it off the heat. Stir in the ground cardamom, the saffron and its milk, and most of the nuts.
steps.look: Golden streaks of saffron and a warm, floral cardamom scent.
steps.mistake: Adding cardamom early and cooking off its perfume.
steps.fix: Add the aromatics at the end.

steps.do: If you like, fry the remaining nuts and the raisins in the ghee for 1 to 2 minutes until the nuts are golden and the raisins puff. Serve the kheer warm or chilled, scattered with them.
steps.look: Golden nuts and plump raisins on a creamy pudding.
steps.mistake: Serving cold kheer without loosening it; it sets thick in the fridge.
steps.fix: Stir in a little cold milk before serving chilled.

dishes.science: Kheer thickens in two ways at once. The rice releases starch as its grains swell and soften in the hot milk, and the milk itself reduces as water evaporates, concentrating its proteins, fats and lactose. Over a long simmer, those milk sugars and proteins begin to brown gently through the Maillard reaction, giving kheer its faint caramel depth; that is the same chemistry behind the deposits on the sides of the pan, which is why they are scraped back in. Sugar is added late because dissolved sugar competes with the rice for water and slows the softening of the grains.
dishes.plating: Spoon into small bowls or glasses, filling them three quarters. Scatter the pistachios and almonds in a small mound in the centre, set a few saffron threads on top and add a single fried raisin or two. For a celebration, lay a small square of edible silver leaf in the centre.

pairing.drink: A cup of masala chai, or a sweet Riesling Auslese whose honeyed fruit suits cardamom.
pairing.brennans: Dr. Hermann ‘Erdener Prälat’ Riesling Auslese 2014 (375 ml): the Riesling Auslese on the list, honeyed fruit for cardamom

variations: Semiya payasam: toasted vermicelli in place of rice, cooked 10 minutes.
Gur kheer: sweeten with jaggery off the heat, once the milk has cooled slightly, so it does not curdle.
Coconut kheer with coconut milk replacing half the milk.
safety: Cool any leftover kheer quickly and refrigerate within 1 hour; cooked rice and milk both support bacteria at room temperature.
Boiling milk froths over suddenly: use a large pan and stay with it.
Contains nuts: tell guests.

dishes.title: Mango Sticky Rice
dishes.summary: Thai glutinous rice, soaked and steamed until chewy, soaked in sweetened coconut milk and served warm with cold ripe mango and a lightly salted coconut sauce. It teaches steaming grain rather than boiling it, and shows how a little salt sharpens sweetness.
equipment: Steamer: a bamboo or metal steamer basket over a wok or pot, or a sieve set over a pot with a lid
Cheesecloth, muslin or a clean thin cotton towel to line the steamer
Large heatproof bowl with a lid or plate
Sharp knife and board for the mango

ingredients.note: divided: 1 cup (240 ml) for the rice, the rest for the sauce
fragrant and yielding slightly when pressed, chilled

ingredients.item: Toasted mung beans or toasted sesame seeds

mise: Rinse the rice in several changes of cold water, rubbing gently, until the water runs nearly clear. Cover with plenty of fresh water and soak at least 4 hours or overnight.
Toast the sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking, until golden, if using.
Chill the mangoes.
Wet the cheesecloth and wring it out.

timeline.do: Rinse and soak the rice at least 4 hours.
Drain the rice; set the steamer over boiling water.
Steam 20 to 25 minutes, turning once.
Warm the sweet coconut milk; pour over the hot rice; cover 20 minutes.
Make the salted coconut sauce; cut the mango.
Plate warm rice with cold mango and sauce.

steps.do: Drain the soaked rice. Fill the pot or wok with 2 inches (5 cm) of water and bring it to a boil. Line the steamer with the damp cloth, spread the rice over it in an even layer about 1 inch (2.5 cm) deep and fold the cloth over the top.
steps.look: Steam rising strongly through the basket.
steps.mistake: Letting the rice touch the water, so it boils and turns to paste.
steps.fix: The water must stay below the basket; top up only with boiling water.

steps.do: Cover and steam over medium-high heat for 20 to 25 minutes. Halfway through, lift the cloth and flip the rice over as one cake so it cooks evenly.
steps.look: The grains turn from opaque white to translucent and glossy.
steps.mistake: Letting the pot boil dry.
steps.fix: Check the water level at the halfway turn and top up with boiling water.

steps.do: Taste a few grains.
steps.look: Chewy and tender all the way through, sticky, with no hard white centre.
steps.mistake: Stopping while the centres are still chalky.
steps.fix: Steam 5 minutes more and taste again.

steps.do: While the rice steams, warm 1 cup (240 ml) coconut milk with the 1/3 cup (65 g) sugar and 1/2 tsp (3 g) salt in a saucepan over medium-low heat, stirring until dissolved. Do not boil.
steps.look: Steaming, smooth, sweet coconut milk.
steps.mistake: Boiling it, which can split the coconut fat.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the sugar dissolves.

steps.do: Tip the hot rice into the bowl and pour the warm coconut milk over. Stir gently to coat every grain, cover and leave 20 to 30 minutes.
steps.look: The rice drinks the coconut milk and turns glossy and plump, with no liquid left in the bowl.
steps.mistake: Pouring cold milk over cold rice; it will not absorb.
steps.fix: Both must be hot; the absorption happens during the rest.

steps.do: For the sauce, warm the remaining coconut milk with 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar and 1/4 tsp (1.5 g) salt. Stir in the cornstarch slurry and simmer 1 minute, stirring, until slightly thickened. Cool.
steps.look: A pourable sauce, thicker than the milk, tasting noticeably salty against the sweet.
steps.mistake: Leaving out the salt; the dessert then tastes cloying.
steps.fix: Taste and add another pinch of salt if it tastes only sweet.

steps.do: Cut the mango: stand it on its end, slice down either side of the flat stone to remove the two cheeks, then scoop each cheek out of its skin with a large spoon and slice crossways into 1/2 inch (1 cm) slices.
steps.look: Neat, glistening slices, kept in the cheek shape.
steps.mistake: Cutting into the stone, which is fibrous and hard.
steps.fix: Feel for the stone with the knife and follow its curve.

steps.do: Serve the rice warm with the cold mango alongside, the sauce spooned over the rice and a scatter of mung beans or sesame.
steps.look: Warm, chewy rice, cold sweet mango and a salty-sweet sauce.
steps.mistake: Refrigerating the rice before serving, which makes it hard.
steps.fix: Serve the rice warm or at room temperature on the day.

dishes.science: Glutinous rice contains almost no amylose, the straight-chain starch, and is nearly all amylopectin, a branched starch that turns sticky and chewy when cooked. Boiled, it absorbs too much water and collapses to paste. Soaking hydrates the grains in advance, so steam alone can cook them through, keeping each grain whole. The sweetened coconut milk is absorbed after steaming while the starch is still hot and open. Salt makes sweetness taste rounder and less flat because it suppresses bitterness and boosts our perception of other flavours, which is why Thai desserts so often carry a salty coconut cream.
dishes.plating: Press a scoop of rice into a small bowl or ring and turn it out onto one side of a plate. Fan the mango slices beside it, keeping the cheek shape. Spoon the sauce over the top of the rice so it runs down the sides, and scatter the mung beans or sesame over the rice only.

pairing.drink: A late-harvest Riesling or a Moscato, whose tropical fruit matches the mango, or a cup of jasmine tea.
pairing.brennans: Dönnhoff ‘Oberhäuser Brücke’ Riesling Auslese Goldkapsel 2023 (375 ml): the Auslese on the list, tropical sweetness for ripe mango

variations: Pandan sticky rice: steam the rice with a knotted pandan leaf for a green, vanilla-like scent.
Black sticky rice with coconut cream, steamed 10 minutes longer.
With durian or ripe peach when mangoes are out of season.
safety: Cooked rice should not sit at room temperature for more than 2 hours; refrigerate leftovers promptly. Spores of Bacillus cereus survive cooking.
Steam burns: lift the steamer lid away from you.

dishes.title: Chè Chuối (Banana and Coconut Tapioca)
dishes.summary: A Vietnamese sweet soup of bananas poached in coconut milk with tapioca pearls and pandan, finished with toasted sesame and peanuts. It teaches how tapioca starch cooks and how coconut desserts are seasoned with salt.
equipment: Mortar and pestle or a zip-top bag and rolling pin for the peanuts

ingredients.note: Asian finger bananas are traditional; cut in 1 1/4 inch (3 cm) pieces
about 1/8 inch (2 to 3 mm), not instant

mise: Peel and cut the bananas, toss them with 2 tbsp (24 g) of the sugar and leave 20 minutes; they release juice and firm up.
Toast the sesame seeds in the dry pan over medium heat for 2 to 3 minutes, shaking, until golden. Crush the peanuts coarsely.
Knot the pandan leaf so it releases its scent.
Bring a medium pan of water, about 4 cups (1 litre), to the boil for the tapioca.

timeline.do: Sugar the bananas; toast sesame; crush peanuts.
Boil the tapioca until a white dot remains; cover off the heat; rinse.
Warm coconut milk, water, pandan, salt and sugar; poach the bananas.
Tapioca and coconut cream in; warm through without boiling.
Serve warm or cold with sesame and peanuts.

steps.do: Pour the tapioca pearls into the boiling water and stir immediately so they do not stick together. Boil 8 to 10 minutes, stirring often.
steps.look: The pearls turn from white to translucent from the outside in, until only a small white dot remains in the centre.
steps.mistake: Not stirring at the start, so the pearls fuse into a lump.
steps.fix: Stir hard for the first minute. Break up clumps with the spoon.

steps.do: Take the pan off the heat, cover it and leave 5 minutes.
steps.look: The white dots disappear and the pearls are clear all through.
steps.mistake: Boiling until the centres are clear; by then the outsides have dissolved into slime.
steps.fix: Let the covered pan finish the centres.

steps.do: Drain the pearls in the sieve and rinse under cold water, stirring with your fingers, to wash off surface starch. Leave them in a bowl of cold water.
steps.look: Separate, glossy, translucent pearls.
steps.mistake: Leaving them in the sieve, where they stick into one mass.
steps.fix: Keep them in cold water until needed.

steps.do: In the second saucepan, bring the coconut milk, water, pandan, salt and remaining sugar to a bare simmer over medium-low heat.
steps.look: Small bubbles at the edge, a sweet pandan scent.
steps.mistake: Boiling hard, which splits the coconut milk.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low.

steps.do: Slide in the bananas and their juice and poach gently 5 to 7 minutes.
steps.look: The banana edges turn slightly translucent and a skewer goes in with no resistance, but the pieces keep their shape.
steps.mistake: Stirring vigorously, which breaks the banana into mush.
steps.fix: Move the pan gently rather than stirring.

steps.do: Drain the tapioca and add it with the coconut cream. Warm 1 to 2 minutes, stirring gently, until heated through. Do not let it bubble. Take off the heat and remove the pandan.
steps.look: A creamy, ivory soup with pearls suspended in it.
steps.mistake: Boiling the coconut cream, which splits it into an oily slick.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as it is hot.

steps.do: Taste: it should be sweet with a clear salty edge. Add a pinch more salt if it tastes flat. Ladle into small bowls warm or let it cool and serve cold, scattered with sesame and peanuts.
steps.look: Glossy bananas, clear pearls, a sprinkle of golden sesame and peanuts.
steps.mistake: Serving without the salt.
steps.fix: Salt is what makes it taste of coconut rather than sugar.

dishes.science: Tapioca pearls are pure starch from cassava, with no protein or fibre to hold them together. As they cook, the outer layer gelatinises and turns clear first, while the centre stays raw and white. Boiling until the centre clears dissolves the outside into slime, so the pearls come off the heat with a white dot and finish in the retained heat. Rinsing removes loose surface starch that would make the soup gluey. Coconut cream is fat suspended in water by a thin layer of coconut protein; boiling denatures that protein, the droplets merge and the fat separates, so it goes in last. Sugaring the bananas first draws out water and firms them.
dishes.plating: Ladle into small glass bowls so the pearls show. Arrange three or four banana pieces on top, scatter the sesame and peanuts in a line across one side and add a tiny knot of pandan leaf or a mint leaf as garnish.

pairing.drink: Vietnamese iced coffee with condensed milk, or a cup of jasmine tea.

variations: Chè bắp: sweet corn in place of banana.
Chè chuối nướng style: grill the bananas first for a caramelised edge.
With sweet potato cubes poached alongside the banana.
safety: Peanuts and sesame are common allergens: tell guests.
Refrigerate leftovers and eat within 2 days; tapioca hardens when chilled, so warm it gently to soften.

dishes.title: Thiakry
dishes.summary: A Senegalese dessert of fine millet couscous, steamed twice until tender, cooled and folded into sweetened soured milk and crème fraîche with vanilla, raisins and nutmeg. It brings steamed grain and cultured milk together cold, and teaches why the grain must be fully steamed and fully cooled first.
equipment: Couscoussier, or a fine sieve or steamer basket that fits snugly over a pot
Cheesecloth or muslin if your sieve has large holes
Clean kitchen towel to seal any gap between pot and steamer
Large wide bowl or tray for working the grain

ingredients.note: from West African grocers; fine wheat couscous works differently, see variations

ingredients.item: Thick plain whole-milk yoghurt or lait caillé (soured milk)

ingredients.note: seeds scraped; or 1 tsp (5 ml) vanilla extract

mise: Spread the millet in the wide bowl. Sprinkle over half the water and the oil and rake it through with spread fingers until every grain is damp and separate, with no clumps.
Fill the bottom of the couscoussier or pot with 2 inches (5 cm) of water and bring to the boil. If your sieve has large holes, line it with damp cheesecloth.
If there is a gap between pot and steamer, wrap a damp twisted towel around the join so steam goes up through the grain.

timeline.do: Moisten the millet; bring the steamer water to the boil.
First steaming, 15 to 20 minutes.
Break up, moisten again, second steaming 15 to 20 minutes.
Spread out and cool completely, fluffing.
Whisk the cream; fold in cold millet and raisins; chill 1 hour.
Grate nutmeg over and serve cold.

steps.do: Tip the moistened millet into the steamer basket without packing it down. Set it over the boiling water and steam, uncovered, for 15 to 20 minutes, timing from when steam rises through the surface of the grain.
steps.look: Steam visibly escaping through the whole surface of the millet.
steps.mistake: Pressing the grain down, so steam cannot pass through and it cooks unevenly.
steps.fix: Loosen it gently with a fork.

steps.do: Tip the millet back into the wide bowl. Break up every lump with a fork, then sprinkle with the remaining water and a pinch of salt, raking with your fingers.
steps.look: Separate, slightly swollen grains with no clumps.
steps.mistake: Leaving lumps, which stay raw in the middle.
steps.fix: Rub lumps gently between your palms.

steps.do: Return the millet to the steamer and steam a second time for 15 to 20 minutes.
steps.look: Fluffy, swollen grains.
steps.mistake: Skipping the second steaming.
steps.fix: Two steamings are essential for millet.

steps.do: Test a few grains by crushing them between your teeth.
steps.look: Tender all the way through, no chalky or gritty centre.
steps.mistake: Serving millet with a hard core, which stays hard however long it sits in the yoghurt.
steps.fix: Steam 5 to 10 minutes longer if needed.

steps.do: Spread the millet out on a tray and cool it completely to room temperature, fluffing it with a fork every 10 minutes to release steam and keep the grains separate.
steps.look: Cold, dry, separate grains.
steps.mistake: Folding warm grain into the cold dairy, which can split the soured milk and makes the dessert grainy and dry as the grain keeps absorbing.
steps.fix: Be patient; put the tray in the fridge for the last 10 minutes if needed.

steps.do: Whisk the yoghurt, crème fraîche, sugar, vanilla seeds and orange blossom water until smooth and pourable, like thick cream.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, sweet cream.
steps.mistake: Leaving it too thick; it will thicken more as the millet absorbs liquid.
steps.fix: Thin with 1 to 2 tbsp (15 to 30 ml) milk.

steps.do: Fold the cold millet and the raisins into the cream until evenly coated. Cover and chill 1 hour so the raisins plump and the flavours meld.
steps.look: A loose, creamy porridge; the grains suspended in cream.
steps.mistake: Serving straight away when the raisins are still hard.
steps.fix: Give it the hour.

steps.do: Spoon into bowls, grate fresh nutmeg over and serve cold.
steps.look: Creamy, tangy, gently sweet, with soft millet and plump raisins.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit at room temperature for long.
steps.fix: Keep it cold until serving.

dishes.science: Millet is a hard, small grain. Its starch must absorb water and gelatinise, and steam does this gently, cooking the grain through while keeping it separate. One steaming hydrates only the outside; breaking up and moistening between steamings lets more water reach the core. Gelatinisation needs heat, so cold yoghurt cannot finish an undercooked grain; the core stays chalky. The grain must be fully cooled because warm starch keeps absorbing liquid fast, drying the cream, and heat makes the casein proteins in soured milk tighten and separate into grainy curds. Cold into cold keeps the cream smooth.
dishes.plating: Spoon into small glass bowls or cups, smoothing the top. Grate nutmeg in a fine, even dusting over the surface, then add three or four plump raisins and a thin curl of orange zest in the centre.

pairing.drink: Bissap, the chilled hibiscus drink of Senegal, or a glass of sweet Muscat.

variations: With fine wheat couscous: pour 3/4 cup (180 ml) boiling water over 3/4 cup (125 g) couscous, cover 5 minutes, fluff and cool completely before folding in.
Thiakry with mango or pineapple folded through.
Dégué: the same dessert made with larger millet pellets, popular in Burkina Faso and Mali.
safety: Keep the finished dessert refrigerated and eat within 2 days.
Steam escapes from the gap around a couscoussier: wrap the join with a damp towel and use a mitt.

dishes.title: Brigadeiros
dishes.summary: Brazil’s party sweet: condensed milk, cocoa and butter cooked until the mass pulls away from the pan, then cooled, rolled into balls and coated in chocolate sprinkles. It is a pure lesson in heat control and in reading thickness as the pan is tilted.
skills: cooking condensed milk until it pulls from the pan
equipment: Heavy non-stick saucepan, about 2 quarts (2 litres)

ingredients.note: plus extra for your hands and the plate

mise: Butter a plate or shallow dish.
Sift the cocoa to remove lumps.
Tip the sprinkles into a small bowl. Set out the paper cases.

timeline.do: Butter the plate; sift the cocoa.
Cook the mixture on medium-low, stirring constantly, 10 to 14 minutes.
Spread on the buttered plate; cool completely, about 1 hour.
Butter your palms; roll into balls; roll in sprinkles.
Set in paper cases and serve.

steps.do: Put the condensed milk, cocoa, butter and salt in the cold saucepan. Stir over medium-low heat until the butter melts and the cocoa is fully blended.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, dark brown liquid.
steps.mistake: Starting on high heat, which scorches the milk sugars on the base.
steps.fix: Keep the heat at medium-low throughout.

steps.do: Keep stirring constantly, scraping the bottom and sides of the pan in a figure-of-eight motion, for 10 to 14 minutes.
steps.look: The mixture thickens, bubbles slowly and becomes glossier and heavier on the spatula.
steps.mistake: Stopping stirring; condensed milk catches and burns in seconds.
steps.fix: Never leave it. If it scorches, transfer without scraping the base.

steps.do: Test it: drag the spatula across the base of the pan. When the mixture parts and you can see the pan bottom for a full second before it flows back, and the whole mass slides as one when you tilt the pan, it is done. If you have a thermometer, it reads about 225°F (107°C).
steps.look: A thick, shiny mass that pulls away from the sides and moves together as one when the pan is tilted.
steps.mistake: Stopping too soon, so the brigadeiros will not hold a shape; or going too far, so they turn stiff and fudge-like.
steps.fix: Too soft: return to the heat 1 to 2 minutes. Too firm: warm with 1 tbsp (15 ml) milk and stir until smooth, then retest.

steps.do: Scrape the mixture onto the buttered plate and spread it out a little. Cool completely at room temperature, about 1 hour, or 30 minutes in the fridge once warm rather than hot.
steps.look: Cool to the touch, firm enough to scoop but still pliable.
steps.mistake: Trying to roll it warm; it sticks to your hands and will not hold a shape.
steps.fix: Wait until it is completely cool.

steps.do: Rub a little butter on your palms. Scoop a teaspoon of the mixture, about 1/2 oz (15 g), and roll it between your palms into a smooth ball about 3/4 inch (2 cm) across.
steps.look: Smooth, round, glossy balls of even size.
steps.mistake: Rolling with dry hands, so the mixture sticks and the balls are ragged.
steps.fix: Re-butter your palms every few balls.

steps.do: Drop each ball into the sprinkles and roll it around until fully coated, pressing lightly. Set each in a paper case.
steps.look: An even coat of sprinkles all over.
steps.mistake: Letting the balls sit before coating, so the sprinkles do not stick.
steps.fix: Coat each ball straight after rolling.

steps.do: Serve at room temperature. They keep, covered, for 2 days at cool room temperature or 5 days in the fridge.
steps.look: Soft, fudgy centres under a crunchy chocolate coat.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the fridge, when they are hard.
steps.fix: Bring chilled ones to room temperature for 20 minutes.

dishes.science: Sweetened condensed milk is milk with most of its water removed and a large amount of sugar added. Cooking it drives off more water, raising the sugar concentration, which raises the temperature at which the mass boils, much as in candy making. Around 225°F (107°C), there is little enough water that the mixture holds its shape when cooled: soft enough to bite, firm enough to roll. The milk proteins and sugars also brown gently, adding a caramel note under the cocoa. Constant stirring matters because the dense, sugary mass sits on the pan base where it is hottest; left still, the sugars burn.
dishes.plating: Set the brigadeiros in their paper cases in neat rows on a flat platter or board, or stack a few in a small pyramid. For a party, alternate chocolate sprinkles with some rolled in desiccated coconut or chopped nuts for contrast.

pairing.drink: A small, strong coffee, or a tawny or vintage port, whose dried fruit and warmth suit chocolate and caramel.
pairing.brennans: Dow’s Vintage Port 2000 (375 ml): the vintage port on the list, dark fruit for chocolate and caramel

variations: Beijinho: no cocoa, a little coconut stirred in, rolled in desiccated coconut with a clove on top.
Brigadeiro de colher: stop cooking earlier and eat it warm from a cup with a spoon.
Gourmet brigadeiros: stir in 1 oz (30 g) chopped dark chocolate at the end and roll in cocoa nibs.
safety: Hot condensed milk sticks to skin and burns badly: stir with a long spatula, and never touch or taste it until cool.
Keep children away from the pan while it cooks.

dishes.title: Crêpes
dishes.summary: French crêpes made from a rested, lump-free batter, cooked paper thin in a well seasoned pan and folded around lemon and sugar. It refines the thin pancake with the first lessons in batter rest and pan temperature, and the first crêpe is always the test that tunes the pan.
skills: the first crêpe as a test
equipment: 8 to 9 inch (20 to 23 cm) crêpe pan or non-stick skillet
Blender or a mixing bowl and whisk
Ladle or a 1/4 cup (60 ml) measure
Thin, flexible spatula or palette knife
Plate and a clean kitchen towel to stack the crêpes
Paper towel for buttering the pan

ingredients.note: plus 2 to 3 tbsp (30 to 45 ml) to loosen after resting
plus 1 tbsp (14 g) for the pan

mise: Melt the butter and let it cool slightly.

Put the milk, eggs, flour, sugar, salt and melted butter in the blender, liquids first, and blend 20 seconds until smooth. Scrape down and blend 5 seconds more. By hand: whisk the eggs and half the milk into the flour to a thick smooth paste, then whisk in the rest of the milk and the butter, and pass it through the sieve.
Cover and rest the batter at least 30 minutes at room temperature, or up to 24 hours in the fridge.
Set a plate and towel by the stove for the finished crêpes.

timeline.do: Blend the batter; rest at least 30 minutes.
Stir and loosen the batter; heat the pan.
Cook the test crêpe and adjust heat and batter.
Cook the rest, about 2 minutes each, stacking under a towel.
Fill with lemon and sugar and fold into quarters.
Serve warm.

steps.do: Stir the rested batter. It should be the thickness of single (light) cream and run freely off a spoon. Add milk a tablespoon at a time if it has thickened.
steps.look: A smooth, thin, pourable batter with no lumps and a few small bubbles.
steps.mistake: Using batter that is too thick, which makes heavy, pancake-like crêpes.
steps.fix: Thin it with milk until it coats a spoon thinly.

steps.do: Heat the pan over medium-high heat for 2 minutes. Wipe it with a paper towel dipped in melted butter: a thin film, not a pool.
steps.look: A sheen of butter that sizzles gently; a drop of water dances across the surface.
steps.mistake: Too much butter, which fries the batter into a lacy, greasy edge and stops it spreading.
steps.fix: Wipe out excess with a dry paper towel.

steps.do: Lift the pan off the heat, pour in about 3 tbsp (45 ml) of batter for an 8 inch pan, or 1/4 cup (60 ml) for a 9 inch (23 cm) pan, at one side, and immediately tilt and swirl the pan in a circle so the batter runs to the edges in a thin, even layer.
steps.look: The batter spreads to a complete, thin circle and sets almost at once.
steps.mistake: Pouring into the centre of a level pan and hoping, or pouring too slowly, so it sets thick in one place.
steps.fix: Pour and swirl in one movement. Fill any holes with a drop of batter.

steps.do: Return to the heat and cook 45 seconds to 1 minute, until the edges look lacy and dry and start to lift away from the pan and the underside is golden in patches.
steps.look: Edges curling up and turning golden; the surface no longer looks wet.
steps.mistake: Flipping too early, so the crêpe tears.
steps.fix: Wait until the edge lifts by itself and the centre is matte.

steps.do: Slide the spatula under the edge, lift and flip the crêpe (or pick up the edge with your fingertips, carefully, and turn it). Cook the second side 15 to 20 seconds.
steps.look: The second side has only faint pale spots; the first side is lace-mottled gold.
steps.mistake: Cooking the second side too long, which makes the crêpe dry and brittle.
steps.fix: A few seconds is enough. The paler side goes on the inside when filled.

steps.do: Judge the first crêpe honestly: it is the test. Too pale and thick: the pan is too cool or the batter too thick. Burnt spots: the pan is too hot. Adjust the heat and the batter, then continue.
steps.look: From the second crêpe on, each is thin, even and golden.
steps.mistake: Carrying on without adjusting.
steps.fix: Eat the first crêpe yourself, as French cooks do, and fix the pan.

steps.do: Stack each finished crêpe on the plate under the towel. Butter the pan lightly every two or three crêpes and stir the batter each time, as the flour settles.
steps.look: A neat stack of soft crêpes that peel apart easily.
steps.mistake: Forgetting to stir the batter, so the later crêpes are thinner and the last are thick.
steps.fix: Stir before every pour.

steps.do: To serve, lay a crêpe paler side up, squeeze over a little lemon juice and sprinkle with 1 tsp (4 g) sugar. Fold in half, then in half again into a triangle.
steps.look: A soft triangle with a glossy, sugary interior and crisp lacy edges.
steps.mistake: Overfilling, which makes them soggy.
steps.fix: A light squeeze and a light sprinkle is all.

dishes.science: Resting the batter does two things. The flour’s starch absorbs liquid and swells, so the batter becomes smoother and cooks more evenly, and the gluten formed during mixing has time to relax, so the batter flows thinly instead of springing back. Air bubbles from blending also rise out. The lacy brown pattern comes from the Maillard reaction between the milk sugars and egg proteins on the hot metal. A very thin film of fat matters: too much and the batter fries at the edges and will not spread; too little and it sticks. The first crêpe calibrates the pan, setting the oil film and showing you the true temperature.
dishes.plating: Fold two crêpes into triangles and overlap them on a warm plate, points facing the same way. Dust with a light snow of sugar, set a lemon wedge beside them and, if you like, a small spoon of crème fraîche. For a grander finish, warm them in a pan with orange butter sauce for crêpes Suzette.

pairing.drink: A glass of Normandy cider, dry or lightly sweet, or a sparkling demi-sec wine. Brennan’s own tableside flambé dessert, Bananas Foster, is a natural crêpe filling: try the variation below.
pairing.brennans: World Famous Bananas Foster: Brennan's tableside flambé, which makes a natural crêpe filling

variations: Bananas Foster crêpes: fill with sliced bananas cooked in butter, brown sugar and cinnamon, and spoon the warm sauce over.
Crêpes Suzette: warm folded crêpes in butter, sugar, orange juice and zest.
Savoury buckwheat galettes: replace half the flour with buckwheat flour, leave out the sugar and fill with ham, Gruyère and an egg.
safety: Keep raw batter refrigerated if resting more than 2 hours, and use within 24 hours.
Raw batter contains raw egg and flour: do not taste it.
Use a spatula rather than fingers to flip until you are confident; the pan is very hot.

dishes.title: Kaiserschmarrn
dishes.summary: An Austrian torn pancake: a thick batter lightened with whipped egg whites, cooked in butter, torn into ragged pieces in the pan and caramelised with sugar, served under icing sugar with stewed plums. It introduces whipping egg whites and folding them in without losing the air.
skills: tearing and caramelising in the pan
dishes.serves: 2 as a main, 4 as a dessert
equipment: Two clean mixing bowls (one completely grease-free for the whites)
Two forks or two wooden spatulas for tearing

ingredients.note: 1 tbsp (12 g) in the whites, 1 tbsp (12 g) to caramelise
soaked 20 minutes in 2 tbsp (30 ml) rum or warm water, drained

mise: Soak the raisins in rum or warm water.
Separate the eggs carefully: not a speck of yolk in the whites, or they will not whip. Put the whites in the grease-free bowl.
Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a rack in the centre.
Warm the plum compote gently.

timeline.do: Soak raisins; separate eggs; heat the oven.
Make the yolk batter; whip the whites; fold.
Cook in foaming butter on the stove 3 to 4 minutes.
Into the oven 6 to 8 minutes to set the top.
Tear into pieces; caramelise with butter and sugar.
Dust with icing sugar; serve with plums.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks, milk, flour, salt and vanilla in a bowl until smooth with no lumps. The batter will be thick, like heavy cream.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, pale yellow batter.
steps.mistake: Leaving lumps of flour, which stay as raw pockets.
steps.fix: Whisk longer, or press lumps against the side of the bowl.

steps.do: Whip the egg whites until foamy, then add 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar and keep whipping until they form soft to medium peaks that bend over at the tip when the whisk is lifted.
steps.look: Glossy, white, smooth foam that holds a peak which curls over at the top.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping until dry and grainy, which makes them hard to fold and they collapse.
steps.fix: If grainy, add a little unwhipped white and whisk briefly to smooth them.

steps.do: Stir one large spoonful of whites into the batter to loosen it. Then add the remaining whites and fold gently with the spatula: cut down through the centre, sweep along the bottom and up the side, turning the bowl a quarter turn each time, until no white streaks remain.
steps.look: A light, airy batter with no streaks, noticeably increased in volume.
steps.mistake: Stirring or beating, which knocks out the air and gives a flat, dense pancake.
steps.fix: Fold slowly and stop as soon as the streaks are gone.

steps.do: Melt 1 1/2 tbsp (21 g) butter in the skillet over medium heat until foaming. Pour in the batter and level it gently. Scatter the drained raisins over the top.
steps.look: The batter sets around the edge within a minute and the butter sizzles underneath.
steps.mistake: Pan too hot, so the base burns before the inside cooks.
steps.fix: Lower the heat to medium-low.

steps.do: Cook 3 to 4 minutes until the underside is golden brown when lifted at the edge and the edges are set. Then put the skillet in the oven for 6 to 8 minutes.
steps.look: The pancake puffs up and the top sets and turns pale golden; a skewer comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Taking it out while the centre is still wet.
steps.fix: Give it 2 more minutes in the oven.

steps.do: Using a mitt (the handle is very hot), return the pan to the stove over medium heat. With two forks or spatulas, tear the pancake into rough, bite-sized pieces about 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) across.
steps.look: Ragged, irregular pieces with soft, fluffy insides.
steps.mistake: Cutting neat squares; the ragged edges are what catch the caramel.
steps.fix: Tear, do not cut.

steps.do: Add the remaining butter and 1 tbsp (12 g) sugar. Toss the pieces for 2 to 3 minutes until the edges caramelise and turn crisp and golden.
steps.look: Shiny, caramelised edges, and a sweet buttery smell.
steps.mistake: Burning the sugar on too high a heat.
steps.fix: Keep tossing on medium; lower the heat if it smokes.

steps.do: Pile onto warm plates, dust heavily with icing sugar through the sieve, and serve with the warm plum compote.
steps.look: A golden, sugar-dusted heap with crisp edges and fluffy middles.
steps.mistake: Letting it sit, so it loses its crispness.
steps.fix: Serve straight from the pan.

dishes.science: Egg whites are about 90 percent water and 10 percent protein. Whisking unfolds those proteins, which then link up around air bubbles to form a stable foam. Any fat, even a trace of yolk, coats the proteins and prevents them from bonding, which is why the bowl must be grease free. Sugar added once the whites are foamy stabilises the foam and makes it glossy. Folding keeps those bubbles intact; in the heat of the pan and oven they expand and the proteins set around them, giving a puffed, airy pancake. Tearing exposes rough surfaces where the butter and sugar caramelise, adding crisp edges to soft insides.
dishes.plating: Pile the torn pieces high in the centre of a warm plate in a loose, generous heap, raisins showing. Dust heavily with icing sugar through a sieve held high so it falls like snow. Spoon the warm plum compote into a small bowl on the side or in a pool beside the heap.

pairing.drink: A sweet Austrian wine such as a Burgenland Auslese, or a coffee with whipped cream in the Viennese style.
pairing.brennans: Kracher ‘Cuvée’ Auslese Burgenland 2017: the Burgenland Auslese on the list, an Austrian sweet wine for an Austrian pudding

variations: Apfelschmarrn: fold thinly sliced apples into the batter.
Without raisins, served with lingonberry jam.
Stovetop only: cut the pancake into quarters, flip each quarter and cook 3 minutes more before tearing.
safety: The skillet handle is dangerously hot after the oven: keep a mitt on it or a towel over the handle the whole time.
Cook until no wet batter remains inside the pieces; eggs should reach 160°F (71°C).

dishes.title: Chocolate Chip Cookies
dishes.summary: Classic American chocolate chip cookies made by creaming softened butter with two sugars, resting the dough, and baking to crisp edges and a soft, slightly underdone centre. The first bake on a tray teaches creaming, why rested dough spreads less, and how far a hot tray keeps cooking after it leaves the oven.
equipment: Stand mixer with paddle, or a hand mixer and a large bowl
Two sheet pans lined with parchment
3 tbsp (45 ml) cookie scoop or two spoons
Oven thermometer, if your oven runs hot or cold

ingredients.note: about 65°F (18°C): it should dent when pressed but not look greasy
half chips, half a bar chopped into 1/2 inch (1 cm) pieces

mise: Take the butter and egg out of the fridge 1 hour ahead. The butter is ready when a finger leaves a dent without sinking in.
Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt together in a bowl.
Chop the chocolate bar. Line the sheet pans with parchment.
Clear space in the fridge for the dough bowl.

timeline.do: Soften butter and egg; weigh dry ingredients.
Cream, add egg, fold in dry and chocolate.
Rest the dough in the fridge at least 1 hour, ideally overnight.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C). Scoop the dough.
Bake one tray at a time, 11 to 13 minutes.
Rest 5 minutes on the tray, then on a rack. Serve warm.

steps.do: Beat the softened butter with both sugars on medium speed for 3 to 4 minutes, scraping down the bowl once, until noticeably paler and fluffy.
steps.look: The mixture lightens from tan to pale beige, increases in volume and looks like soft, fluffy frosting.
steps.mistake: Using melted or very soft butter, which cannot hold air, or cold butter, which stays in lumps.
steps.fix: If the butter is too warm and greasy, chill the bowl 10 minutes and beat again. If lumpy and cold, keep beating; friction warms it.

steps.do: Add the egg and vanilla and beat 1 minute until fully combined and smooth. Scrape the bowl.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy mixture, not curdled.
steps.mistake: Adding a cold egg, which makes the creamed butter seize and look curdled.
steps.fix: Beat a little longer; a slight curdle usually smooths once the flour goes in.

steps.do: On low speed, or by hand with the spatula, mix in the flour mixture just until no dry flour shows.
steps.look: A soft, thick dough with no streaks of flour.
steps.mistake: Mixing on high for a long time, which develops gluten and makes tough cookies.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as the flour disappears.

steps.do: Fold in the chocolate with the spatula.
steps.look: Chocolate evenly scattered through the dough.
steps.mistake: Overmixing at this stage.
steps.fix: A few turns are enough.

steps.do: Cover the bowl and refrigerate at least 1 hour, up to 72 hours. Longer rests give deeper, toffee-like flavour.
steps.look: Firm, cold dough that holds a scoop.
steps.mistake: Baking straight away, which spreads thin and flat.
steps.fix: Even 30 minutes helps; overnight is best.

steps.do: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Scoop the dough into 12 balls of about 1 3/4 oz (50 g) each and set 6 on each tray, at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) apart.
steps.look: Evenly sized, round balls with chocolate showing on the surface.
steps.mistake: Crowding the tray, so the cookies merge.
steps.fix: Bake six to a tray.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time for 11 to 13 minutes, turning the tray halfway.
steps.look: Golden brown edges, puffed centres that look pale and slightly underdone and soft when gently pressed.
steps.mistake: Baking until the centre looks fully done; it will be hard once cool.
steps.fix: Pull them when the edges are golden and the centres still look shiny and soft. The hot tray finishes them.

steps.do: As soon as they come out, sprinkle a few flakes of sea salt on each. Leave them on the hot tray for 5 minutes, then move to the rack with a spatula.
steps.look: The centres sink slightly and set; the edges firm up.
steps.mistake: Moving them straight away, so they break.
steps.fix: Wait the full 5 minutes.

steps.do: Bake the second tray. Serve warm or at room temperature; store airtight for up to 3 days.
steps.look: Crisp edges, soft, chewy middles, pools of melted chocolate.
steps.mistake: Putting the second batch on a hot tray, which melts the dough before it bakes.
steps.fix: Let the tray cool, or use a fresh tray and parchment.

dishes.science: Creaming beats air into butter. The sharp edges of sugar crystals cut tiny pockets into the solid fat, and those air cells expand in the oven, lightening the cookie. That only works when butter is cool and pliable, around 65°F (18°C); melted butter cannot trap air. Brown sugar contains molasses, which holds moisture and makes cookies chewy, while white sugar crisps the edges. Resting the dough lets the flour absorb liquid and the butter firm up, so the cookies spread less and brown more evenly, and enzymes break some starch into sugars for deeper flavour. Baking soda raises the pH, speeding browning. A hot tray keeps cooking the cookies after the oven, so they come out looking underdone.
dishes.plating: Stack three cookies slightly offset on a small plate or a sheet of parchment on a board, with a cold glass of milk or a coffee beside them. Break one in half and lay it on top so the melted chocolate shows.

pairing.drink: A cold glass of milk, an espresso, or a tawny or vintage port, whose dried fruit and nuttiness suit chocolate and brown sugar.
pairing.brennans: Dow’s Vintage Port 2000 (375 ml): the vintage port on the list, dried fruit for chocolate and brown sugar

variations: Brown butter cookies, the library’s version: brown the butter, cool it to soft, then whisk rather than cream; the result is chewier and nuttier.
Oatmeal raisin: replace 1/2 cup (60 g) flour with rolled oats and the chocolate with raisins and 1/2 tsp (1 g) cinnamon.
Double chocolate: replace 1/4 cup (25 g) flour with cocoa powder.
safety: Raw cookie dough contains raw egg and raw flour, which can carry harmful bacteria. Do not taste it.
Sheet pans stay very hot; use a mitt and set them on a heatproof surface.

dishes.title: Anzac Biscuits
dishes.summary: Australian and New Zealand oat and coconut biscuits made by the melting method: butter and golden syrup are melted, foamed with bicarbonate of soda and stirred into the dry ingredients. A melted-butter biscuit is the counterpoint to creaming, and it shows how bicarbonate reacts with syrup and how minutes in the oven decide chewy against crisp.
equipment: Two sheet pans lined with parchment

ingredients.note: such as Lyle’s; or light corn syrup with 1 tsp (5 ml) honey

mise: Heat the oven to 320°F (160°C) with a rack in the centre. Line the trays.
Mix the oats, flour, coconut, sugar and salt in the large bowl.
Measure the bicarbonate into a small cup and boil the kettle.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; mix the dry ingredients.
Melt butter and syrup; foam with bicarbonate; mix the dough.
Roll 12 balls; flatten on the trays.
Bake 12 minutes for chewy, up to 18 for crisp.
Cool on the tray 10 minutes.
Serve, or store airtight for a week.

steps.do: Melt the butter and golden syrup in the saucepan over low heat, stirring, until just melted and smooth. Do not let it bubble.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, golden liquid.
steps.mistake: Boiling it, which starts to caramelise the syrup and makes harder biscuits.
steps.fix: Take it off the heat as soon as the butter melts.

steps.do: Pour the boiling water onto the bicarbonate and stir to dissolve, then tip it straight into the warm butter mixture and stir.
steps.look: The mixture foams up pale and roughly doubles in volume.
steps.mistake: Letting the foam sit and collapse before using it.
steps.fix: Use the foam immediately; it is the leavening.

steps.do: Pour the foaming mixture into the dry ingredients and stir with the wooden spoon until every bit is moistened.
steps.look: A stiff, slightly greasy, crumbly dough that holds together when squeezed.
steps.mistake: Adding the butter mixture cold, so it does not bind.
steps.fix: If the dough is too crumbly to hold, add 1 tsp (5 ml) warm water.

steps.do: Roll the dough into 12 balls, each about the size of a walnut, roughly 1 1/2 tbsp (25 g). Set 6 on each tray, 2 inches (5 cm) apart, and flatten each lightly with your palm to 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) thick.
steps.look: Even, round discs with rough edges.
steps.mistake: Pressing very thin, which makes them burn at the edges.
steps.fix: Keep them a little thick; they spread in the oven.

steps.do: Bake one tray at a time: 12 minutes for chewy biscuits, or 15 to 18 minutes for crisp ones.
steps.look: Spread and deep golden; the edges darker than the centres, which still look soft.
steps.mistake: Baking until the centres feel firm in the oven, which makes them rock hard once cool.
steps.fix: Judge by colour: deep gold at the edge. They harden as they cool.

steps.do: Leave on the tray for 10 minutes to firm, then move to the rack to cool completely.
steps.look: Biscuits that are soft when hot and set as they cool.
steps.mistake: Moving them while hot, so they fold or break.
steps.fix: Give them the 10 minutes.

steps.do: Store airtight. Chewy ones keep their chew 3 to 4 days; crisp ones stay crisp for a week.
steps.look: A caramel, oaty, coconut biscuit with a crisp edge.
steps.mistake: Storing them with soft cakes, which makes them go soft.
steps.fix: Store on their own in a tin.

dishes.science: There is no egg here, so texture comes from sugar, syrup and baking time. Golden syrup is largely invert sugar, glucose and fructose, which holds onto water and keeps the centre chewy. Bicarbonate of soda is an alkali: when it meets the slightly acidic syrup and hot water it releases carbon dioxide, which is the foam you see and the only lift the biscuits get. It also raises the pH of the dough, and alkaline conditions speed the Maillard browning, which is why Anzacs turn such a deep amber. More minutes in the oven drive off more water, so the same dough can be chewy or crisp.
dishes.plating: Stack five or six biscuits in a leaning tower on a small wooden board or plate, with a cup of tea beside them. For a dessert plate, set two biscuits against a scoop of vanilla ice cream with a drizzle of golden syrup.

pairing.drink: A cup of strong black tea or a flat white, or a small glass of Australian fortified Muscat.

variations: Ginger Anzacs: add 1 tsp (2 g) ground ginger and 2 tbsp (24 g) chopped crystallised ginger.
Macadamia Anzacs: add 1/3 cup (45 g) chopped macadamias.
Anzac slice: press the dough into a lined 8 inch (20 cm) square tin and bake 20 minutes, then cut into bars.
safety: The foaming butter mixture is hot: stir it carefully.
Tell guests the biscuits contain coconut, oats and wheat.

dishes.title: Cantucci di Prato
dishes.summary: Tuscan almond biscuits from Prato: a firm egg dough shaped into logs, baked, sliced on the diagonal and baked again until dry right through. Twice-baking explains how dryness keeps a biscuit crisp for weeks.
equipment: Large mixing bowl and a spatula
mise: Heat the oven to 340°F (170°C) with a rack in the centre. Line the sheet pan.
Zest the orange. Separate one egg, keeping the white for the glaze.
Mix the flour, sugar, salt and zest in the bowl.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; mix the dry ingredients.
Make the dough; shape two logs; glaze.
First bake, 25 to 30 minutes.
Cool the logs 15 minutes; slice at 45 degrees.
Second bake at 300°F (150°C), 15 to 20 minutes.
Cool completely; they crisp as they cool.

steps.do: Add the whole egg and the yolk to the dry ingredients and work them in with the spatula, then your hand, until a stiff, sticky dough forms with no dry flour left.
steps.look: A thick, tacky dough that holds together in a ball.
steps.mistake: Adding water or extra egg because it looks dry at first; it comes together as you work it.
steps.fix: Keep pressing and folding for a minute before deciding it needs anything.

steps.do: Add the almonds and knead them in until evenly spread through the dough.
steps.look: Almonds visible throughout.
steps.mistake: Using toasted almonds, which can burn in the double bake.
steps.fix: Use raw almonds; they toast as the biscuits bake.

steps.do: Dust your hands with flour, divide the dough in two and shape each half into a log about 10 inches (25 cm) long and 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) wide on the tray, 3 inches (7.5 cm) apart. Flatten the tops slightly.
steps.look: Two even logs of the same width and height.
steps.mistake: Making uneven logs, so slices bake unevenly.
steps.fix: Pat and roll them straight with floured hands.

steps.do: Brush the logs with the beaten egg white.
steps.look: A thin, even, glossy coat.
steps.mistake: Pooling egg white along the base, which burns.
steps.fix: Brush lightly; wipe pools from the parchment.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes until firm and pale golden.
steps.look: The logs have spread slightly, turned light gold and feel firm when pressed, with a few cracks on top.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the logs squash when sliced.
steps.fix: Give them 5 more minutes if they feel soft.

steps.do: Cool on the tray for 15 minutes. Lower the oven to 300°F (150°C).
steps.look: Warm logs, firm enough to cut.
steps.mistake: Cutting hot logs, which squash, or cold logs, which shatter at the almonds.
steps.fix: Cut them warm, neither hot nor cold.

steps.do: Move the logs to a board. With the serrated knife, cut each log on a 45 degree angle into slices about 5/8 inch (1.5 cm) thick, using a gentle sawing motion.
steps.look: Clean, even slices with whole almonds cut through.
steps.mistake: Pressing straight down, which cracks the slices.
steps.fix: Saw gently and let the knife do the work.

steps.do: Lay the slices cut side down on the tray and bake again 15 to 20 minutes, turning them over halfway, until dry all the way through.
steps.look: Pale golden cut surfaces; they feel dry and firm, though they may still flex slightly while hot.
steps.mistake: Pulling them when the cut faces are still soft and damp; they go stale fast.
steps.fix: Bake longer than looks necessary; judge by the snap once cool.

steps.do: Cool completely on the rack. Test one: it should snap cleanly.
steps.look: A crisp snap, a dry, crunchy biscuit.
steps.mistake: Storing while warm, which traps steam and softens them.
steps.fix: Cool fully, then store airtight for up to a month.

dishes.science: Cantucci keep for weeks because of water. Biscuits go stale or soft when they hold moisture, and mould needs water to grow. The first bake sets the egg proteins and cooks the dough through; slicing exposes the moist interior; the second, low bake is a drying bake, driving water from the cut faces until the biscuit is almost completely dry. With little water left, there is nothing to make it soft. The Prato tradition uses no chemical leavening, so the dough rises only slightly from the eggs and stays dense and even, perfect for dunking. A low second bake dries without overbrowning.
dishes.plating: Stand a handful of cantucci upright in a small glass, or lay five in a fan on a small plate beside a little glass of sweet wine or an espresso. In Tuscany, they are dunked.

pairing.drink: Tuscan Vin Santo for dunking, as in Prato, or a sweet Moscadello di Montalcino; an espresso works too.
pairing.brennans: Castello Banfi ‘Florus’ Moscadello di Montalcino 2011: the Moscadello di Montalcino on the list, a Tuscan sweet wine for a Tuscan biscuit

variations: Chocolate and hazelnut: replace the almonds with toasted hazelnuts and add 2 tbsp (14 g) cocoa.
Pistachio and cranberry, with lemon zest in place of orange.
Anise biscotti: add 1 tsp (2 g) anise seeds and a splash of anise liqueur.
safety: Use a serrated knife with a sawing motion and keep your guiding hand flat on top of the log, fingers clear.
Almonds are a tree nut: tell guests.

dishes.title: Fudgy Brownies
dishes.summary: Dense, fudgy brownies made with gently melted dark chocolate, butter and cocoa, eggs and sugar beaten for a shiny crackled top, and very little flour, baked until just underdone and cooled completely. Melting chocolate so it never seizes and judging an underbake by skewer are skills used to the top of the course.
skills: beating eggs and sugar for a crackled top
equipment: 8.5 x 4.5 inch (21 x 11 cm) metal loaf tin, lined with a parchment sling overhanging the long sides
Saucepan and a heatproof bowl that sits on top without touching the water
Sharp knife and a jug of hot water for cutting
mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Line the loaf tin with a parchment sling.
Chop the chocolate into small, even pieces so it melts evenly.
Take the eggs out of the fridge 30 minutes ahead, or stand them in warm water for 5 minutes.
Whisk the flour, cocoa and fine salt together.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; line the tin; bring eggs to room temperature.
Melt chocolate and butter gently; cool 5 minutes.
Whisk eggs and sugars a full 2 to 3 minutes; combine; fold in dry.
Bake 25 to 30 minutes, until a skewer shows moist crumbs.
Cool completely in the tin, about 2 hours.
Lift out and cut with a hot, wiped knife.

steps.do: Put 1 inch (2.5 cm) of water in the saucepan and bring it to a bare simmer. Set the bowl with the chocolate and butter over it; the bowl must not touch the water. Stir gently until melted and smooth. Take the bowl off the heat and cool 5 minutes.
steps.look: A glossy, smooth, flowing mixture with no lumps.
steps.mistake: Letting steam or a drop of water into the chocolate, or overheating it, which makes it seize into a thick, grainy paste.
steps.fix: Keep the heat low and wipe the base of the bowl. If it seizes, stir in 1 tbsp (15 ml) boiling water vigorously; it may smooth out for baking.

steps.do: In a separate bowl, whisk the egg, yolks, both sugars and vanilla hard for 2 to 3 minutes (1 to 2 minutes with a mixer) until thick, pale and glossy.
steps.look: The mixture lightens in colour and falls from the whisk in a thick ribbon; the sugar has largely dissolved.
steps.mistake: Stirring briefly, which gives a dull, matte top with no crackle.
steps.fix: Keep whisking; this step makes the shiny crust.

steps.do: Pour the warm chocolate into the eggs in a steady stream, whisking constantly, until evenly combined and glossy.
steps.look: A thick, shiny, dark batter.
steps.mistake: Adding hot chocolate, which can scramble the eggs.
steps.fix: Let the chocolate cool to warm first; it should feel only warm on your lip.

steps.do: Sift the flour and cocoa mixture over the top and fold it in with the spatula, just until no streaks remain.
steps.look: A thick, glossy batter that falls from the spatula in ribbons.
steps.mistake: Overmixing, which develops gluten and makes them cakey.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as the flour disappears.

steps.do: Scrape into the tin and level it. Sprinkle the flaky salt over the top.
steps.look: An even, glossy surface.
steps.mistake: Leaving it uneven, so one end overbakes.
steps.fix: Smooth with the back of the spatula.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes. At 25 minutes, insert the skewer into the centre and pull it out.
steps.look: The top is shiny and crackled; the edges are set; the skewer comes out with dark moist crumbs and a little smear, not wet batter and not clean.
steps.mistake: Baking until the skewer comes out clean, which means you have baked cake.
steps.fix: If wet batter clings, bake 3 minutes more and test again.

steps.do: Set the tin on the rack and cool completely, about 2 hours. The centre sets as it cools.
steps.look: Firm to the touch and slightly sunken in the centre.
steps.mistake: Cutting warm, so they ooze and fall apart.
steps.fix: Be patient. To hurry, chill 30 minutes once at room temperature.

steps.do: Lift out by the parchment sling. Cut into 8 bars with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped dry between every cut.
steps.look: Clean, sharp edges with a dense, fudgy interior and a papery top.
steps.mistake: Cutting with a cold, dirty knife, which drags.
steps.fix: Dip and wipe after every cut.

dishes.science: Chocolate is cocoa solids and sugar suspended in cocoa butter. A single drop of water makes the sugar and solids clump together into a stiff paste: the chocolate has seized; too much heat does the same as it scorches. Melting it gently over steam avoids both. The shiny, crackled crust comes from dissolved sugar: beating the eggs and sugar for a few minutes dissolves the sugar into the eggs, and in the oven it rises to the surface and dries into a thin, glossy meringue-like skin. Fudginess comes from a high ratio of fat and sugar to flour and from underbaking: the centre stays moist, and carryover heat and cooling set it.
dishes.plating: Serve one bar on a small plate, slightly warm if you like (10 seconds in the microwave), with a quenelle of vanilla ice cream or crème fraîche beside it and a light dusting of cocoa on the plate. The crackled top should face up.

pairing.drink: A glass of cold milk, an espresso, or a Banyuls or ruby port, whose red fruit sweetness is made for dark chocolate.
pairing.brennans: Domaine La Tour Vieille Banyuls Reserva NV: the Banyuls on the list, made for dark chocolate

variations: Espresso brownies: dissolve 1 tsp (1 g) instant espresso powder in the vanilla.
Pecan brownies: fold in 1/2 cup (55 g) toasted pecans, a New Orleans favourite.
Swirled: dot the top with 2 tbsp (32 g) peanut butter or raspberry jam and marble with a skewer before baking.
safety: Raw brownie batter contains raw egg and raw flour: do not taste it.
Steam from the bain-marie burns: lift the bowl with a cloth.

video.search: fudgy brownies shiny crackle top technique

dishes.title: Victoria Sponge
dishes.summary: The British teatime cake: two light sponges made with equal weights of butter, sugar, egg and flour, sandwiched with raspberry jam and whipped cream and dusted with caster sugar. It is the purest test of creaming, where the air beaten in becomes the rise.
equipment: Two 6 inch (15 cm) round cake tins, at least 1 1/2 inches (4 cm) deep, greased and base lined with parchment
Stand mixer or hand mixer and a large bowl
Whisk and a bowl for the cream

ingredients.metric: about 113 g out of the shell
ingredients.note: at room temperature; weigh them out of the shell, and if they come to more or less, match the butter, sugar and flour to their weight

mise: Take the butter and eggs out of the fridge 1 hour ahead.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C), or 325°F (160°C) with a fan, with a rack in the centre.
Grease the tins with butter, line the bases with parchment circles and grease the paper.
Weigh the eggs in their shells and subtract about 7 g per egg for the shell; weigh the butter, sugar and flour to match. Sift the flour, baking powder and salt together.
Beat the eggs lightly in a jug.

timeline.do: Soften butter and eggs; prepare tins; heat oven.
Cream butter and sugar a full 5 minutes.
Add eggs gradually; fold in flour and milk.
Bake 20 to 22 minutes.
Cool 5 minutes in the tins, then completely on a rack.
Whip the cream; sandwich with jam and cream; dust with sugar.

steps.do: Beat the butter and sugar on medium-high speed for a full 5 minutes, scraping down the bowl twice.
steps.look: The mixture turns from yellow to very pale, almost white, and is light, fluffy and noticeably larger in volume.
steps.mistake: Stopping after a minute, when it has barely changed colour; the sponge will be dense.
steps.fix: Time it. Five minutes is not too long.

steps.do: Add the beaten egg a little at a time, about a tablespoon at once, beating well after each addition. If the mixture starts to look curdled, add a spoonful of the flour.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, thick batter after each addition.
steps.mistake: Adding the eggs all at once or cold, so the mixture curdles and loses its air.
steps.fix: Add a spoon of flour and beat; it usually comes back. Cold eggs are the usual cause.

steps.do: Sift the flour mixture over the batter in two additions, folding gently with the spatula after each, cutting through the middle and lifting from the bottom. Fold in the milk and vanilla.
steps.look: A soft batter that drops easily from the spatula, called a dropping consistency.
steps.mistake: Beating the flour in, which knocks out air and develops gluten.
steps.fix: Fold just until no flour shows. If the batter is too stiff to drop, add another teaspoon of milk.

steps.do: Divide the batter evenly between the tins, weighing them for accuracy. Level the tops with the back of a spoon.
steps.look: Two tins holding equal weights of batter, level surfaces.
steps.mistake: Uneven amounts, so the layers bake differently.
steps.fix: Use the scale.

steps.do: Bake on the centre rack for 20 to 22 minutes. Do not open the door for the first 15 minutes.
steps.look: Golden brown, risen and level; the sides just shrinking away from the tins; the top springs back when pressed lightly with a fingertip; a skewer comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Opening the oven early, which can make the sponges sink.
steps.fix: If a fingertip leaves a dent, bake 2 to 3 minutes more.

steps.do: Cool in the tins for 5 minutes, then run a knife around the edge, turn out onto the rack, peel off the paper, and turn them top side up. Cool completely.
steps.look: Smooth, golden sponges with straight sides.
steps.mistake: Filling while warm, which melts the cream.
steps.fix: Wait until completely cool.

steps.do: Whip the cream with 1 tsp (4 g) sugar to soft peaks that just hold their shape.
steps.look: Soft, billowy cream that holds a gentle peak which flops at the tip.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping into grainy, buttery cream.
steps.fix: Stop early; if slightly over, fold in a spoon of unwhipped cream.

steps.do: Choose the less handsome sponge for the base and set it top side down on a plate. Spread the jam to within 1/4 inch (6 mm) of the edge, then spread the cream over it. Set the second sponge on top, top side up, and press lightly.
steps.look: Neat layers of red jam and white cream visible at the side.
steps.mistake: Spreading the cream right to the edge so it squeezes out.
steps.fix: Leave a margin; the weight of the top layer spreads it.

steps.do: Dust the top with caster sugar. Serve within 2 hours, or refrigerate.
steps.look: A golden cake with a sparkling sugar top and straight sides.
steps.mistake: Leaving a cream-filled cake out for hours.
steps.fix: Refrigerate if not eating within 2 hours; bring out 15 minutes before serving.

dishes.science: Creaming is the engine of this cake. Beating butter with sugar crystals drives tiny air bubbles into the fat; the longer you cream, the more and finer the bubbles. In the oven, baking powder releases carbon dioxide into those existing bubbles, and steam from the eggs and butter expands them further, so the sponge rises on the air you beat in. Adding egg gradually keeps the butter and egg emulsified; too much at once and the water in the egg overwhelms the fat, it curdles and air escapes. Folding the flour gently keeps the bubbles and limits gluten, keeping the crumb tender. Equal weights give a balanced, reliable cake.
dishes.plating: Set the whole cake on a cake stand or a plain plate with a doily. Cut into four wedges with a long, sharp knife, wiping it between cuts so the cream stays clean. Lay a wedge on its side on a small plate so the jam and cream layers show, with a few fresh raspberries beside it.

pairing.drink: A pot of English breakfast tea, or a glass of English sparkling wine, whose bright acidity suits jam and cream.
pairing.brennans: Ridgeview ‘Bloomsbury’ Brut Sussex NV: the English sparkling wine on the list, bright acidity for jam and cream

variations: With buttercream: beat 4 tbsp (56 g) butter with 1/2 cup (60 g) icing sugar instead of whipped cream; it keeps at room temperature.
Lemon sponge: add lemon zest to the batter and fill with lemon curd and cream.
Strawberry sponge: fresh sliced strawberries over the cream in summer.
safety: A cream-filled cake must be refrigerated if it will not be eaten within 2 hours.
Raw batter contains raw egg and flour: do not taste it.

dishes.title: Tarta de Santiago
dishes.summary: The almond cake of Santiago de Compostela: eggs and sugar whisked to the ribbon stage, ground almonds folded in, baked and dusted with icing sugar around a stencil of the cross of Saint James. An almond cake raised only by whisked eggs shows a second way, after creaming, to put air into a cake.
skills: whisking eggs and sugar to the ribbon
ground almonds in place of flour
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) springform tin, buttered and base lined with parchment
Stand mixer with whisk or a hand mixer
Paper stencil of the cross of Saint James (print and cut one out), about 4 inches (10 cm) tall
mise: Take the eggs out of the fridge at least 1 hour ahead, or stand them in warm water for 10 minutes. Warm eggs whip to far greater volume.
Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Butter the tin and line the base.
Mix the ground almonds, lemon zest, cinnamon and salt in a bowl, breaking up any lumps with your fingers.
Print and cut out the stencil.

timeline.do: Warm the eggs; prepare tin and stencil; heat the oven.
Whisk eggs and sugar to the ribbon, 5 to 7 minutes.
Fold in almonds in three additions; add sherry.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
Cool completely in the tin.
Stencil the cross with icing sugar; serve in slim wedges.

steps.do: Whisk the eggs and sugar on medium-high speed for 5 to 7 minutes until very thick, pale and roughly tripled in volume.
steps.look: The mixture turns from yellow to pale cream, and when the whisk is lifted, it falls in a thick ribbon that sits on the surface for 3 seconds before sinking. This is the ribbon stage.
steps.mistake: Stopping too early, when the ribbon sinks at once; the cake will be flat and dense.
steps.fix: Keep whisking. Test by drawing a figure of eight with the falling batter: it should hold its shape briefly.

steps.do: Sprinkle a third of the almond mixture over the foam and fold it in gently with the spatula, cutting down through the centre, sweeping across the bottom and up the side, turning the bowl as you go.
steps.look: The almonds disappear into the foam with minimal loss of volume.
steps.mistake: Stirring or beating, which collapses the foam you just built.
steps.fix: Fold slowly and gently. A little deflation is normal.

steps.do: Fold in the remaining almonds in two more additions, then fold in the sherry. Stop as soon as no dry almond remains.
steps.look: A thick, mousse-like batter with no streaks.
steps.mistake: Overfolding, so the batter turns runny and flat.
steps.fix: Stop when evenly mixed.

steps.do: Pour into the tin and gently level the top. Tap the tin once on the counter to release any large bubbles.
steps.look: An even surface.
steps.mistake: Banging the tin hard, which knocks out the air.
steps.fix: One gentle tap only.

steps.do: Bake 30 to 35 minutes until deep golden, risen and firm to the touch.
steps.look: An even, deep golden top; the edges pulling away from the tin; a skewer in the centre comes out with a few moist crumbs, not wet batter.
steps.mistake: Underbaking, so the centre collapses; or overbaking, so it turns dry.
steps.fix: If the top browns too fast before the centre sets, lay a sheet of foil loosely over it.

steps.do: Cool completely in the tin on a rack, at least 45 minutes. The cake sinks a little and firms as it cools.
steps.look: A firm, slightly sunken cake with a thin, crisp crust.
steps.mistake: Releasing the cake while hot, which can tear it.
steps.fix: Leave it until fully cool, then run a knife around the edge and open the springform.

steps.do: Set the cake on a plate. Lay the stencil in the centre of the cake. Dust the whole surface heavily with icing sugar through the sieve held high.
steps.look: A thick, even white coat on the cake and stencil.
steps.mistake: Dusting while the cake is warm, so the sugar melts.
steps.fix: Wait until completely cool.

steps.do: Lift the stencil straight up with both hands in one smooth movement.
steps.look: A crisp, dark golden cross showing through the white sugar.
steps.mistake: Sliding the stencil sideways, which smudges the design.
steps.fix: Lift straight up. If it smudges, dust lightly again and use the stencil once more.

dishes.science: Whole eggs can trap a lot of air when whisked with sugar, but only if they are warm: warmth makes the proteins more flexible and the sugar dissolves more easily, so they unfold and wrap around bubbles quickly. At the ribbon stage, the foam is stable enough to carry heavy ground almonds without collapsing. In the oven, the air bubbles expand and the egg proteins set around them, holding the rise without baking powder or creaming. Almonds bring fat and protein rather than starch, so the crumb is moist, dense and tender. As the cake cools, the structure contracts slightly and firms, which is why it is left in the tin.
dishes.plating: Serve the whole cake on a plain plate so the cross shows. Cut slim wedges with a sharp knife, wiping it between cuts, and lay each on its side on a small plate with a spoon of lightly whipped cream and a small glass of sherry beside it.

pairing.drink: A glass of cream or pale cream sherry, nutty and gently sweet, the Spanish choice with almond cake; or a sweet Galician aguardiente for the brave.
pairing.brennans: Barbadillo ‘Pale Cream’ Sherry NV: the pale cream sherry on the list, the Spanish match for almond cake

variations: Orange and almond: replace the lemon zest with orange zest and add a splash of orange liqueur.
With a short pastry base, as in some Galician bakeries: blind bake a thin base and pour the batter over.
Individual cakes in a muffin tin, baked 18 to 20 minutes.
safety: Almonds are a tree nut: tell guests the whole cake is built on them.
Raw batter contains raw egg: do not taste it.
