dishes.title: Malva Pudding
dishes.summary: A South African baked pudding: a light, apricot-scented sponge baked until deep brown, then soaked while hot with a hot butter and cream syrup until it drinks every drop. It teaches how a hot sponge absorbs a hot syrup, and how beating egg and sugar to a pale foam lightens a simple batter.
skills: pouring a hot cream syrup over a hot cake
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square baking dish or a 1 1/2 quart (1.5 litre) oval dish, buttered
Stand mixer or hand mixer and a large bowl
Small jug or measuring cup for the milk mixture
mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre. Butter the dish.
Sift the flour, baking soda and salt together.
Stir the milk, melted butter and vinegar together in a jug; it may look slightly curdled, which is fine.
Measure the sauce ingredients into the small saucepan.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; butter the dish; sift the dry ingredients.
Beat egg, sugar and jam until pale and thick.
Fold in dry ingredients and milk mixture alternately.
Bake 30 to 35 minutes until deep brown.
Heat the sauce; poke the hot pudding; pour the sauce over.
Rest 15 minutes; serve warm with ice cream or custard.

steps.do: Beat the egg, sugar and apricot jam on medium-high speed for 4 to 5 minutes until pale, thick and roughly doubled.
steps.look: A pale, creamy foam that falls in a thick ribbon from the beaters.
steps.mistake: Stopping after a minute, which gives a dense, heavy sponge.
steps.fix: Keep beating; this foam is what makes it light.

steps.do: Add a third of the flour mixture and fold it in gently, then half the milk mixture, then another third of flour, the rest of the milk, and the last of the flour, folding after each until just combined.
steps.look: A smooth, loose batter with no pockets of flour.
steps.mistake: Beating hard, which knocks out the air.
steps.fix: Fold with the spatula and stop as soon as it is smooth.

steps.do: Pour into the dish and level it. Bake 30 to 35 minutes.
steps.look: Risen, deep golden brown all over, springing back when pressed; a skewer in the centre comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Pulling it pale; it needs a deep colour for the caramel flavour.
steps.fix: Bake a few minutes longer until deeply browned.

steps.do: Five minutes before the pudding is ready, heat the sauce ingredients over medium heat, stirring, until the butter melts and the sugar dissolves. Bring just to a simmer.
steps.look: A smooth, golden, steaming sauce.
steps.mistake: Boiling the sauce hard, which can split the cream.
steps.fix: Keep it just below a boil.

steps.do: As soon as the pudding comes out, poke holes all over it with a skewer, about 3/4 inch (2 cm) apart, right to the bottom.
steps.look: Dozens of holes across the whole surface.
steps.mistake: Poking only the top, so the sauce sits on the surface.
steps.fix: Push the skewer all the way down.

steps.do: Pour the hot sauce slowly and evenly over the hot pudding. It will look like far too much.
steps.look: The sauce pools, then sinks in and is gradually absorbed.
steps.mistake: Pouring cold sauce or letting the pudding cool first, so it does not absorb.
steps.fix: Hot sauce onto hot pudding is the rule.

steps.do: Rest 15 minutes until the pudding has drunk almost all the sauce, leaving a shallow, glossy moat at the edges.
steps.look: A dark, glossy, sticky top and a soft, saturated sponge.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, when the sauce is still on top.
steps.fix: Wait the full 15 minutes.

steps.do: Serve warm in squares with vanilla ice cream or custard, spooning any sauce from the dish over the top.
steps.look: A soft, caramel-soaked sponge with a slight crust at the edges.
steps.mistake: Serving it cold, when the butter in the sauce firms.
steps.fix: Rewarm leftovers gently, covered, in a low oven.

dishes.science: Baking soda is an alkali that needs an acid to release carbon dioxide; here the vinegar and the apricot jam supply it, and the beaten egg and sugar foam adds air of its own. Baking until deep brown matters because the Maillard reaction and caramelisation on the crust bring the toffee flavour that defines malva. The soaking works because both sponge and sauce are hot: the sponge’s air cells are open and its starch is still soft and swollen, so it draws the liquid in by capillary action, the way a hot sponge soaks up water. Let it cool and the crumb tightens and absorbs far less.
dishes.plating: Cut a generous square and lift it onto a warm shallow bowl, glossy top up. Spoon a little of the remaining sauce over and around it, set a scoop of vanilla ice cream against one side so it begins to melt into the sauce, and finish with a thin strip of orange zest or a single mint leaf.

pairing.drink: A cream liqueur, or a sweet South African Muscat or a Sauternes. Brennan’s own float made with Amarula, the South African cream liqueur, vanilla ice cream and root beer is a natural partner.
pairing.brennans: Floating in South Africa: Brennan's Amarula float, a South African cream liqueur beside a South African pudding

variations: Sticky toffee pudding, a close cousin: add chopped dates soaked in boiling water to the batter and use a toffee sauce.
Orange malva: add orange zest to the sponge and orange juice in place of the water in the sauce.
Brandy sauce: replace 2 tbsp (30 ml) of the water with brandy, as some Cape cooks do.
safety: The sauce is hot and fatty: pour it slowly and keep your hand back.
Refrigerate leftovers within 2 hours; the sauce contains cream.

dishes.title: Peach Cobbler
dishes.summary: A Southern cobbler of ripe peaches macerated with sugar, lemon and spice, topped with a rubbed-in buttermilk biscuit dough and baked until the biscuits are golden and the fruit bubbles thickly at the centre. It puts the rubbing-in skill from the shortbread to work over juicy, thickened fruit.
skills: baking until bubbling at the centre
equipment: 8 inch (20 cm) square or 9 inch (23 cm) round baking dish, about 1 1/2 quarts (1.5 litres)
Saucepan of boiling water and a bowl of iced water for peeling
Slotted spoon and a paring knife

ingredients.note: fragrant and yielding slightly; or 1 1/2 lb (680 g) frozen sliced peaches, thawed and drained
adjust to the sweetness of the peaches

mise: Heat the oven to 400°F (200°C) with a rack in the centre. Set the baking dish on the sheet pan.

To peel the peaches, cut a shallow X in the base of each, lower into boiling water for 30 to 45 seconds, then into iced water. The skins slip off. Halve, stone and slice into 1/2 inch (1.25 cm) wedges.
Cube the butter and put it back in the fridge, or the freezer for 10 minutes.
Whisk the biscuit flour, sugar, baking powder, baking soda and salt in a bowl.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; peel and slice the peaches.
Macerate the peaches 20 minutes.
Fruit into the dish; bake alone 10 minutes. Make the biscuit dough.
Top with biscuits; bake 25 to 30 minutes until bubbling in the centre.
Cool at least 10 minutes so the juices thicken.
Serve warm with vanilla ice cream.

steps.do: Toss the peaches with the sugar, lemon juice, cornstarch, cinnamon, nutmeg and a pinch of salt. Leave 20 minutes.
steps.look: The peaches release a syrupy juice that pools in the bowl and the cornstarch dissolves.
steps.mistake: Leaving out the cornstarch, so the cobbler floods with thin juice.
steps.fix: Check the cornstarch is fully dissolved in the juice before baking.

steps.do: Tip the peaches and all their juice into the dish and bake alone for 10 minutes while you make the topping.
steps.look: The juices begin to bubble at the edges.
steps.mistake: Putting raw dough on cold fruit, which leaves the underside of the biscuits doughy.
steps.fix: The head start heats the fruit so the biscuit bottoms cook through.

steps.do: Add the cold butter cubes to the flour mixture and rub them in with your fingertips or the pastry blender until the mixture looks like coarse crumbs with some pea-sized pieces of butter left.
steps.look: Crumbly mixture with visible flakes and small lumps of butter.
steps.mistake: Rubbing until fine and warm, so the butter melts and the biscuits are heavy.
steps.fix: Work fast with cold fingertips; chill the bowl 5 minutes if the butter softens.

steps.do: Pour in the buttermilk and stir with a fork just until a shaggy, sticky dough forms. Do not knead.
steps.look: A rough, lumpy dough with no dry flour at the bottom of the bowl.
steps.mistake: Overmixing into a smooth dough, which makes tough biscuits.
steps.fix: Stop as soon as it holds together.

steps.do: Take the dish out of the oven. Drop the dough over the hot fruit in 6 to 8 rough spoonfuls, leaving gaps between them for steam to escape. Sprinkle with the turbinado sugar.
steps.look: Rustic mounds of dough on bubbling fruit, with fruit showing between them.
steps.mistake: Spreading the dough in a solid sheet, which steams underneath and stays raw.
steps.fix: Leave gaps; they let the fruit bubble up and the biscuits bake.

steps.do: Bake 25 to 30 minutes until the biscuits are deep golden and the fruit bubbles thickly, not just at the edges but in the centre too. A biscuit should read about 200°F (93°C) in the middle if you check.
steps.look: Golden, crisp-topped biscuits; thick, glossy juices bubbling slowly in the centre of the dish.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when only the edges bubble; the cornstarch has not thickened the centre, so it runs.
steps.fix: Bake until the centre bubbles. If the biscuits brown too fast, cover loosely with foil.

steps.do: Cool on a rack for at least 10 minutes, ideally 20, so the juices set into a syrup.
steps.look: Juices that thicken as they cool.
steps.mistake: Serving immediately, when the filling is runny and very hot.
steps.fix: Wait; it is better warm than hot.

steps.do: Spoon into bowls with a biscuit on top and a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside it.
steps.look: Glossy peaches, a tender, flaky biscuit, ice cream melting into the juices.
steps.mistake: Burying the biscuit under the ice cream, so it goes soggy.
steps.fix: Put the ice cream beside the biscuit.

dishes.science: Sugar draws juice out of the peaches by osmosis, which is the macerating, and dissolves into it. Cornstarch thickens that juice, but only once it reaches a boil, around 203°F (95°C), when the starch granules burst; that is why the cobbler must bubble in the centre, not just at the edges. Lemon juice brightens flavour and keeps the peaches from browning. The biscuit topping is tender because the cold butter pieces stay solid until the oven, where they melt and release steam, leaving flaky layers. Buttermilk is acidic, so it reacts with baking soda for extra lift, while baking powder supplies the rest.
dishes.plating: Spoon a portion into a warm shallow bowl so the fruit and juice settle first, then set a whole biscuit on top, golden side up. Place a scoop of vanilla ice cream beside the biscuit and spoon a little extra syrup over the fruit. A sprig of mint or a fresh peach slice finishes it.

pairing.drink: A late-harvest white or a peach-forward cocktail. Brennan’s own OBX, built on gin, peach and lemon, echoes the fruit.
pairing.brennans: OBX: Brennan's gin, peach and lemon cocktail, which echoes the fruit

variations: Georgia batter cobbler, the library’s version: pour a thin batter over melted butter, spoon the peaches on top without stirring and bake; the batter rises up around the fruit.
Blackberry and peach cobbler: replace a third of the peaches with blackberries.
Bourbon peach cobbler: add 1 tbsp (15 ml) bourbon to the fruit.
safety: Fruit fillings bubble far hotter than they look: let the cobbler cool at least 10 minutes before serving.
Lower peaches into boiling water with a slotted spoon, never by hand.

dishes.title: Smulpaj (Swedish Crumble Pie)
dishes.summary: Swedish crumble pie: sliced apples tossed with sugar and a little starch, covered with a loose crumble of oats, flour, butter and cardamom, and baked until the juices bubble up through the golden top. It takes rubbing in to a free crumble and adds the warmth of Swedish cardamom.
equipment: 8 or 9 inch (20 or 23 cm) pie dish or shallow baking dish
Mortar and pestle or spice grinder for cardamom
Peeler, corer and a sharp knife

ingredients.item: Tart, firm apples (Granny Smith, Braeburn or a mix)
ingredients.note: or 3 cups (450 g) blueberries or bilberries

ingredients.item: Granulated or light brown sugar for the crumble

ingredients.note: best from the seeds of about 8 green pods, freshly ground

ingredients.item: Vanilla ice cream or vanilla custard sauce

mise: Heat the oven to 375°F (190°C) with a rack in the centre.
Split the cardamom pods, tip out the black seeds and grind them finely. The scent of freshly ground cardamom is far stronger than bought powder.
Peel, quarter and core the apples and cut into slices 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
Cube the butter and keep it cold.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; grind cardamom; slice apples.
Toss the fruit straight into the dish.
Rub the crumble to rubble; scatter loosely over the fruit.
Bake 35 to 40 minutes until juices bubble through.
Cool 10 minutes.
Serve warm with vanilla sauce or ice cream.

steps.do: Toss the apple slices with the sugar, cornstarch and lemon juice directly in the pie dish and spread them in an even layer.
steps.look: Glossy, evenly coated slices, packed fairly level.
steps.mistake: Leaving the cornstarch in dry clumps, which turn into gluey lumps.
steps.fix: Toss until no white powder remains visible.

steps.do: In a bowl, mix the flour, oats, sugar, cardamom and salt. Add the cold butter and rub it in with your fingertips until the mixture forms a rough rubble with some pea-sized clumps and visible pebbles of butter.
steps.look: A loose, uneven crumble that holds in small clumps when squeezed.
steps.mistake: Rubbing it to fine sand or working it until it becomes a dough, which bakes into a hard lid.
steps.fix: If it turns pasty, chill 10 minutes and break it up again with your fingers.

steps.do: Scatter the crumble loosely over the fruit to the edges. Do not press it down.
steps.look: An even, loose, bumpy layer with a few gaps.
steps.mistake: Pressing the crumble flat, which makes it dense instead of crisp.
steps.fix: Air between the crumbs is what crisps them.

steps.do: Set the dish on the sheet pan and bake 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: A golden brown top, and thick juices bubbling up through the crumble at the edges and in the centre.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when the top is golden but the juices are not bubbling; the apples will be firm and the juice thin.
steps.fix: Bake until you see bubbles. Cover loosely with foil if the top browns too quickly.

steps.do: Test the apples by pushing a knife through the crumble into the centre.
steps.look: The knife slides in with no resistance.
steps.mistake: Serving with crunchy apples.
steps.fix: Bake 5 to 10 minutes more.

steps.do: Cool 10 minutes so the juices thicken.
steps.look: Juices settle into a glossy syrup.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the oven, when it is scalding.
steps.fix: Wait 10 minutes.

steps.do: Serve warm with vanilla custard sauce poured over or a scoop of vanilla ice cream.
steps.look: Crisp, fragrant crumble, soft tart apples, cold cream.
steps.mistake: Making it hours ahead and serving cold; the crumble softens.
steps.fix: Rewarm briefly in a 350°F (175°C) oven for 10 minutes.

dishes.science: Rubbing cold butter into flour coats some of the flour in fat and leaves small pebbles of butter. In the oven, those pebbles melt, fry the surrounding flour and oats and leave little air pockets, which is why a loose crumble turns crisp and an over-worked one turns hard. Oats add chew and a toasty flavour. Cardamom’s aroma comes from volatile oils inside its seeds, mostly a compound called cineole, which fade within weeks once ground, so fresh grinding gives a far stronger scent. The cornstarch thickens the apple juices once they reach a boil; that is why the bubbling at the edges signals doneness.
dishes.plating: Spoon a generous portion into a warm shallow bowl, crumble side up, letting some juice run out around it. Pour a ribbon of vanilla custard sauce across one side, or set a scoop of ice cream against it, and dust lightly with a pinch of ground cardamom mixed with sugar.

pairing.drink: A glass of sweet cider or an apple brandy. Brennan’s Apple Crumble cocktail, with bourbon, cider, maple and cinnamon, is the dessert in a glass.
pairing.brennans: Apple Crumble: Brennan's bourbon, cider, maple and cinnamon cocktail, the dessert in a glass

variations: Blåbärspaj: blueberries or bilberries in place of apples, with 1 tbsp (8 g) more cornstarch.
Rhubarb smulpaj in spring, with 2 tbsp (24 g) extra sugar.
Quick vaniljsås: warm 1 cup (240 ml) half milk, half cream with 2 yolks, 2 tbsp (24 g) sugar and vanilla, stirring, until it coats a spoon at 170 to 175°F (77 to 80°C), then strain.
safety: Fruit fillings bubble far hotter than they look: cool before serving, especially for children.
Keep your fingers clear when coring apples: cut them in quarters first and core each quarter flat on the board.

dishes.title: Key Lime Pie
dishes.summary: The Florida Keys pie: a pressed graham cracker crust filled with condensed milk, egg yolks and key lime juice, baked briefly until just set, chilled and topped with softly whipped cream. Acid thickening returns from the posset, now in a baked custard with a pressed crumb crust.
skills: a custard set by lime acid and a short bake
equipment: 7 inch (18 cm) pie plate or tart tin with a removable base
Zip-top bag and rolling pin, or a food processor, for the crumbs
Flat-bottomed glass or measuring cup for pressing
Microplane zester and a citrus juicer

ingredients.note: about half a 14 oz (397 g) can
from about 10 key limes, or 2 Persian limes, or bottled key lime juice
for zest and thin slices to garnish

mise: Heat the oven to 350°F (175°C) with a rack in the centre.
Crush the crackers into fine, even crumbs with no large pieces.
Zest the limes before juicing them. Juice and strain.
Separate the eggs; keep the whites for another use.

timeline.do: Make and bake the crust 10 minutes; cool slightly.
Lower the oven to 325°F (160°C). Whisk the filling.
Bake the filling 12 to 15 minutes until just set.
Cool 30 minutes on a rack.
Chill at least 3 to 4 hours.
Whip the cream; top, garnish and slice.

steps.do: Stir the crumbs, melted butter, sugar and salt together until the mixture looks like wet sand and holds together when squeezed.
steps.look: Evenly moistened crumbs with no dry patches.
steps.mistake: Too little butter, so the crust crumbles apart when sliced.
steps.fix: Add 1 tsp (5 g) more melted butter if it will not hold when squeezed.

steps.do: Tip into the pie plate and press firmly and evenly over the base and up the sides with the bottom of a glass, about 1/4 inch (6 mm) thick.
steps.look: A compact, even shell with a neat top edge.
steps.mistake: Leaving it thick in the corner where base meets side, which bakes hard.
steps.fix: Press the corner with your thumb to even it out.

steps.do: Bake the crust 10 minutes until fragrant and a shade darker. Cool on a rack for 10 minutes. Lower the oven to 325°F (160°C).
steps.look: A lightly toasted, firm crust that smells of biscuit.
steps.mistake: Overbaking, so it turns bitter and hard.
steps.fix: Ten minutes is enough; it bakes again with the filling.

steps.do: Whisk the yolks and lime zest for 1 minute until pale. Whisk in the condensed milk until smooth, then whisk in the lime juice.
steps.look: The mixture thickens noticeably in the bowl as the lime juice goes in: this is the acid setting the milk.
steps.mistake: Adding the juice to the yolks alone, before the condensed milk, which can curdle the yolks.
steps.fix: Follow the order: yolks, milk, then juice.

steps.do: Pour the filling into the warm crust and smooth the top. Bake 12 to 15 minutes.
steps.look: The edges are set and the centre wobbles slightly, like a jelly, when the plate is nudged. For the yolks to be fully safe, the centre should reach 160°F (71°C) on a probe.
steps.mistake: Baking until firm all over or browned, which makes it grainy and cracked.
steps.fix: Probe the centre; if short of 160°F (71°C), bake 2 to 3 minutes more and check again. Or use pasteurised yolks.

steps.do: Cool on the rack for 30 minutes, then refrigerate uncovered for 1 hour, then covered for at least 3 hours more.
steps.look: Firm, smooth filling that slices cleanly.
steps.mistake: Slicing before it is fully chilled, so it runs.
steps.fix: Give it the full chill; overnight is fine.

steps.do: Just before serving, whip the cream with the powdered sugar to soft peaks. Spread or pipe it over the pie, leaving a border of filling showing if you like.
steps.look: Soft, billowy cream that holds gentle peaks.
steps.mistake: Over-whipping, so the cream turns grainy.
steps.fix: Stop when it just holds a peak that curls at the tip.

steps.do: Grate a little lime zest over the cream and add thin lime slices. Cut with a sharp knife dipped in hot water and wiped between cuts.
steps.look: Clean slices showing a pale yellow filling and crisp crust. A true key lime pie is pale yellow, never green.
steps.mistake: Adding green colouring, which is not traditional.
steps.fix: Let the natural pale yellow speak for itself.

dishes.science: Key lime filling begins to set before it reaches the oven. Sweetened condensed milk is concentrated milk proteins and sugar; the citric acid in lime juice lowers the pH, and the milk proteins, mainly casein, lose their electrical charge and bond into a thickened network, the same chemistry as a lemon posset. The egg yolks add richness and, as they heat, their proteins coagulate around 150 to 160°F (66 to 71°C), firming the custard. A brief, gentle bake sets the yolks without curdling or browning. The crust is held together by melted butter, which solidifies as it cools and binds the crumbs.
dishes.plating: Cut a neat wedge and lay it on its side on a chilled plate so the layers show. Pipe or spoon a small rosette of extra whipped cream at the wide end, top it with a twist of lime slice, and grate fresh lime zest across the plate. A few crumbs of graham cracker scattered beside it add crunch.

pairing.drink: A demi-sec Champagne, whose sweetness meets the condensed milk and whose acidity matches the lime.
pairing.brennans: Laurent-Perrier ‘Harmony’ Demi Sec NV (375 ml): the demi-sec Champagne on the list, sweetness for condensed milk and acidity for lime

variations: Meringue top, the other Keys tradition: whip the 2 leftover whites with 1/4 cup (50 g) sugar and brown it in the oven.
Key lime tartlets in four 4 inch (10 cm) tins, baked 8 to 10 minutes.
Lemon or grapefruit pie with the same method.
safety: The filling contains egg yolks. Bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C), or use pasteurised eggs, especially for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weakened immune system.
Keep the pie refrigerated and eat within 3 days.

dishes.title: Leche Flan
dishes.summary: The Filipino caramel custard: a dark dry caramel poured into moulds, then a rich custard of egg yolks, condensed and evaporated milk, strained twice and baked gently in a water bath until it barely trembles. It unites caramel and a gently set custard, the two pillars of classic desserts.
skills: baking or steaming gently in a water bath
equipment: Four 6 oz (180 ml) ramekins, or a small loaf tin or llanera mould
Small heavy stainless saucepan with a light interior (to judge caramel colour)
Mixing bowl and a spoon or whisk (stir, do not beat)
Roasting tin or deep baking dish for the water bath

ingredients.note: keep the whites for another use
about half a 14 oz (397 g) can
about half a 12 oz (354 ml) can

mise: Heat the oven to 325°F (160°C) with a rack in the centre.
Set the ramekins in the roasting tin, close to the stove, before you start the caramel: you must pour it the moment it is ready.
Boil a kettle of water for the water bath.
Separate the eggs, letting no white into the yolks.

timeline.do: Heat the oven; set out ramekins; boil the kettle.
Make the dry caramel; pour and tilt to coat the bases.
Stir the custard gently; strain twice; pour over set caramel.
Bake in a water bath 35 to 40 minutes.
Cool in the bath, then chill at least 6 hours or overnight.
Run a knife around, invert onto plates, let the caramel flow.

steps.do: Sprinkle the sugar in an even layer over the base of the dry saucepan. Set over medium heat and leave it until the edges begin to melt.
steps.look: The sugar at the edges turns to clear liquid, then pale gold.
steps.mistake: Stirring at the start, which makes the sugar clump and crystallise.
steps.fix: If clumps form, keep heating gently; they will melt. Swirl rather than stir.

steps.do: As the sugar melts, swirl the pan gently to move the dry sugar into the liquid. Keep heating until all the sugar has melted and turned a deep amber, like the colour of maple syrup or a copper coin.
steps.look: A clear, deep amber caramel with a rich, slightly bitter, toasty smell and a few wisps of smoke.
steps.mistake: Taking it too far, so it turns black and acrid; or stopping at pale gold, which gives a weak, sweet caramel.
steps.fix: If it smells burnt and acrid, it is too far; let it cool, soak the pan, start again. Never taste hot caramel.

steps.do: Immediately pour about 2 tbsp (30 ml) of caramel into each ramekin and tilt each quickly to coat the base. Work fast: it sets within seconds. Leave to harden.
steps.look: A glossy amber layer covering each base.
steps.mistake: Hesitating, so the caramel hardens in the pan.
steps.fix: If it hardens, warm the pan briefly to loosen it. To clean the pan, fill it with water and boil.

steps.do: In the bowl, gently stir the yolks, condensed milk, evaporated milk, vanilla and zest with a spoon until just evenly combined. Stir, do not whisk.
steps.look: A smooth, pale yellow liquid with almost no bubbles.
steps.mistake: Whisking vigorously, which beats in air; the bubbles become holes in the set custard.
steps.fix: If foam forms, let it stand 5 minutes and skim it off.

steps.do: Pour the custard through the fine sieve into a jug. Strain it a second time.
steps.look: A completely smooth custard with no strands of egg.
steps.mistake: Skipping the straining; chalazae and bits of white leave specks and holes.
steps.fix: Two strains give a glass-smooth flan.

steps.do: Pour the custard over the set caramel, dividing it evenly. Skim any bubbles from the surface. Cover each ramekin tightly with foil.
steps.look: Smooth surfaces with no bubbles; foil sealed tight.
steps.mistake: Leaving the ramekins uncovered, so a skin and bubbles form on top.
steps.fix: Cover tightly so condensation cannot drip in.

steps.do: Pull out the oven rack, set the roasting tin on it and pour hot water from the kettle into the tin to come halfway up the ramekins. Slide the rack back in gently. Bake 35 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: The water bath steams but does not boil.
steps.mistake: Splashing water into the ramekins, or letting the bath boil, which makes the custard bubbly and porous.
steps.fix: Pour carefully. If the bath bubbles, lower the oven to 300°F (150°C).

steps.do: Test by lifting the foil on one ramekin and nudging it: the edges should be set and the centre should wobble like a jelly. A probe in the centre reads 170 to 175°F (77 to 80°C).
steps.look: A uniform, gentle tremble; a knife near the centre comes out clean.
steps.mistake: Overbaking until it is firm and full of holes.
steps.fix: Pull them as soon as they tremble; they firm as they cool.

steps.do: Lift the ramekins out of the bath with tongs, cool on a rack for 30 minutes, then refrigerate at least 6 hours, ideally overnight.
steps.look: A cold, firm custard; the caramel has partly dissolved into a sauce beneath.
steps.mistake: Unmoulding while warm, so it breaks.
steps.fix: Give it the full chill.

steps.do: To unmould, run a thin knife around the edge of each flan. Set a plate upside down on top, hold both firmly and turn over. Lift the ramekin; the caramel sauce pours over.
steps.look: A glossy, golden flan with amber caramel flowing around it.
steps.mistake: Not loosening the edges, so it sticks.
steps.fix: If it resists, dip the base in hot water for 10 seconds and try again.

dishes.science: A dry caramel is pure sucrose heated with no water. Around 320°F (160°C) it melts; from about 340 to 360°F (170 to 180°C) the molecules break down and recombine into hundreds of compounds that turn it amber and give it bitter, toasty depth. In the fridge, moisture from the custard slowly dissolves the hardened caramel into a sauce. The custard sets because egg yolk proteins unfold and bond as they heat, starting near 150°F (66°C). A water bath keeps the custard’s surroundings at or below 212°F (100°C), so it heats slowly and evenly; without it, the edges overcook and water inside turns to steam, leaving holes.
dishes.plating: Turn the flan out onto a small, chilled plate with a raised rim so the caramel pools around it. Leave the surface clean and glossy. A few fine strips of lime zest on top, or a single fresh berry beside it, is all it needs.

pairing.drink: A cup of strong coffee, the classic Filipino partner, or a small glass of tawny port. New Orleans chicory coffee is a fine match for the bitter caramel.
pairing.brennans: New Orleans-Style Coffee with Chicory: Brennan's chicory coffee, bitter enough for the dark caramel

variations: Steamed leche flan: steam over gently simmering water, covered, for 20 to 25 minutes.
Crème caramel: whole eggs and fresh milk with sugar in place of yolks and canned milks, for a lighter custard.
Ube leche flan: a layer of purple yam halaya beneath the custard.
safety: Caramel is much hotter than boiling water and sticks to skin. Never touch or taste it, and keep children away.
Pour the water bath with the tin already on the oven rack, and lift it out only once cooled.
Keep the flan refrigerated and eat within 4 days.

dishes.title: Basque Burnt Cheesecake
dishes.summary: The crustless cheesecake of San Sebastián: a simple batter of cream cheese, sugar, eggs and cream baked very hot until the top is caramelised almost black while the centre still sways, then cooled into a creamy, slumping custard. A custard baked hot rather than gently shows how far the wobble can be pushed for a molten centre.
skills: very high heat for a caramelised top
equipment: 6 inch (15 cm) springform tin, at least 3 inches (7.5 cm) deep
Stand mixer with paddle, or a hand mixer and large bowl
Sheet pan to set the tin on

ingredients.note: completely at room temperature, about 3 hours out of the fridge

mise: Take the cream cheese, eggs and cream out of the fridge about 3 hours ahead. Cold cream cheese leaves lumps that no amount of beating removes.
Heat the oven to 450°F (230°C) for at least 30 minutes, with a rack just below the centre.
Crumple two sheets of parchment, smooth them out and press them crossways into the tin, letting them stand at least 2 inches (5 cm) above the rim. The pleats and folds are part of the look.
Set the lined tin on the sheet pan.

timeline.do: Bring cream cheese, eggs and cream to room temperature.
Heat the oven 30 minutes; line the tin.
Beat the batter; strain into the tin.
Bake 30 to 40 minutes until the top is very dark and the centre sways.
Out of the oven; cool in the tin at room temperature at least 2 hours.
Slice at room temperature, or chill and bring back to room temperature for 1 hour.

steps.do: Beat the cream cheese and sugar on medium-low speed for 2 to 3 minutes, scraping the bowl, until completely smooth with no lumps.
steps.look: A smooth, glossy, thick mixture.
steps.mistake: Using cold cream cheese, which stays lumpy.
steps.fix: If lumpy, set the bowl over warm water for a minute and beat again.

steps.do: Add the eggs one at a time, beating on low after each until incorporated and scraping the bowl.
steps.look: A smooth, loose batter.
steps.mistake: Beating on high, which whips in air; the cheesecake puffs, then cracks and sinks unevenly.
steps.fix: Keep the mixer on low.

steps.do: Beat in the cream, vanilla and salt on low. Sift the flour over and beat just until combined.
steps.look: A thin, pourable batter, much looser than a classic cheesecake batter.
steps.mistake: Assuming the thin batter is a mistake; it is right.
steps.fix: Trust it: the batter should pour like heavy cream.

steps.do: Pour the batter through the sieve into the lined tin.
steps.look: A silky, lump-free batter filling the tin about three quarters.
steps.mistake: Skipping the sieve, so lumps show in the cut slice.
steps.fix: Press any lumps through the sieve with the spatula.

steps.do: Bake on the sheet pan for 30 to 40 minutes.
steps.look: The cheesecake puffs well above the rim, the top turns deep mahogany and nearly black at the edges, and when the pan is nudged the centre 3 inches (7.5 cm) sways like a water bed.
steps.mistake: Pulling it when the top is only golden; the burnt caramel top is the flavour and the point.
steps.fix: Leave it in until the top is very dark; if the centre is set firm, it has gone too far, and will be dense rather than creamy.

steps.do: Check the centre with the thermometer if you are serving anyone vulnerable to food poisoning: the centre should reach 160°F (71°C), which gives a softer-set, still creamy middle. A very loose centre stays below that.
steps.look: A reading in the centre of the cheesecake.
steps.mistake: Serving a liquid centre to someone pregnant, elderly, very young or with a weakened immune system.
steps.fix: For a very loose centre, use pasteurised eggs. Otherwise bake until 160°F (71°C) in the centre.

steps.do: Set the tin on a rack and cool at room temperature in the tin for at least 2 hours.
steps.look: The cheesecake sinks dramatically into a crater with a collapsed centre: this is how it should look.
steps.mistake: Chilling it hot, or cutting it warm, when the centre is still liquid.
steps.fix: Let it cool fully at room temperature; it sets as it cools.

steps.do: Open the springform, lift the cheesecake out by the parchment and peel the paper away from the sides. Serve at room temperature for the creamiest texture, cut with a hot, wiped knife.
steps.look: A dark, caramelised top and edges, and a pale, creamy, custardy interior that slumps slightly on the plate.
steps.mistake: Serving straight from the fridge, when it is firm and dense.
steps.fix: If chilled, rest it 1 hour at room temperature before slicing.

dishes.science: Most cheesecakes bake slowly in a water bath so the egg proteins set evenly without cracking. This one does the opposite. At 450°F (230°C), the sugars and milk proteins on the surface caramelise and brown deeply through the Maillard reaction, forming a bitter, toasty crust in place of a biscuit base. The heat penetrates from the outside in, so the edges set firm while the centre is still barely cooked when it comes out. As it cools, carryover heat continues to set the egg proteins, and the cream cheese firms as its fat cools, giving a soft, custardy centre. The puff and collapse come from steam that escapes as it cools.
dishes.plating: Cut a tall wedge and stand it on a plain plate with the dark top and creamy cut face both visible, leaving a little of the crinkled parchment edge if you like. Serve it unadorned, or with a spoon of fresh berries or a drizzle of sweet sherry on the side.

pairing.drink: A rich, sweet white such as Sauternes or a Barsac, whose honeyed acidity cuts the cheese and echoes the caramel top; in San Sebastián, Pedro Ximénez sherry is a favourite.
pairing.brennans: Château Climens Barsac Premier Cru Classé 2010: the Barsac on the list, honeyed acidity for cheese and burnt caramel

variations: Larger cake: double everything for a 9 inch (23 cm) tin and bake 50 to 60 minutes.
Chocolate Basque cheesecake: beat in 4 oz (115 g) melted dark chocolate with the cream.
With a little lemon zest and served with lightly sugared strawberries.
safety: A very loose centre may not reach 160°F (71°C), the temperature at which eggs are fully safe; use pasteurised eggs, or bake until the centre reaches 160°F (71°C), for anyone pregnant, elderly, very young or immunocompromised.
The oven is at 450°F (230°C): use heavy mitts and pull the rack out rather than reaching in.
Refrigerate within 2 hours of cooling and eat within 4 days.
